state: U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright today announced nine recipients of the prestigious Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award for their exceptional contributions to research and development supporting the U.S. Department of Energy’s missions in science, energy, and national security. October 13, 2026WASHINGTON—U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright today announced nine recipients of the prestigious Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award for their exceptional contributions to research and development supporting the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) missions in science, energy, and national security. “This year’s Lawrence Award recipients exemplify the ingenuity and determination that drive America’s leadership in science and technology,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “From achieving fusion ignition to advancing critical materials and high-performance computing, these scientists and engineers are tackling some of our nation’s most complex challenges and translating groundbreaking research into real-world capabilities. Their work strengthens our nation’s energy security, drives American innovation, and ensures the United States remains at the forefront of scientific discovery.” Established in 1959, the Lawrence Award recognizes mid-career U.S. scientists and engineers for groundbreaking achievements across nine scientific and engineering categories. The award is among the longest-running and most prestigious science and technology honors bestowed by the U.S. government. The 2026 Ernest O. Lawrence Award recipients are: - Eric J. Schelter, Ph.D. (University of Pennsylvania) – Atomic, Molecular, and Chemical Sciences – Honored for his “fundamental chemical studies of energy-critical metals leading to new methods for their selective and sustainable separations.” - Patrick Chain, Ph.D. (Los Alamos National Laboratory and New Mexico Consortium) – Biological and Environmental Sciences – Honored for his “pioneering work in genomics and microbiome science, including discoveries of new bacterial-fungal interactions and revolutionizing the field by democratizing access to advanced bioinformatics tools.” - Samuel W. Williams, Ph.D. (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory) – Computer, Information, and Knowledge Sciences – Honored for his “pioneering contributions in performance modeling, hardware/software design optimization, and novel computer architecture for high-performance computing, enabling modeling of complex computational solutions, and increasing analysis speed, simulation accuracy, and computational efficiency.” - Thomas Epps, III, Ph.D. (University of Delaware) – Condensed Matter and Materials Sciences – Honored for his “fundamental contributions to chemistry and materials science with applications in the chemical upcycling of polymeric waste, generation of high-performance materials from biomass feedstocks, and development of membranes for lithium-ion battery technologies.” - Gregg Beckham, Ph.D. (National Laboratory of the Rockies and University of Colorado Boulder) – Energy Science and Innovation – Honored for his “transformative research in the conversion of lignocellulosic biomass and waste plastics via biology, chemistry, and engineering, yielding building blocks for sustainable fuels, chemicals, and materials.” - Andrea L. Kritcher, Ph.D. (Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory) – Fusion and Plasma Sciences – Honored for her “exceptional design efforts leading to the first-ever achievement of fusion ignition in the Laboratory, which is of major scientific impact to institutional and national missions, the private sector, and fusion interests within academia.” - Charles C. Polly, Ph.D. (Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory) – High Energy Physics – Honored for his “exceptional scientific and technical contributions to low-energy precision measurements in particle physics, most notably leadership of the experimental measurement of the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon with the Muon g-2 experiment.” - Michael Reed, Ph.D. (Nevada National Security Site) – National Security and Nonproliferation – Honored for his “vital contributions to national and international nuclear emergency response through the Advanced Visualization & Integration of Data (AVID) software, which broke existing paradigms by simultaneously fusing all radiological data into a single interface connected seamlessly to world-wide expertise.” - Lijuan Ruan, Ph.D. (Brookhaven National Laboratory) – Nuclear Physics – Honored for her “outstanding leadership and ingenuity in the design, construction, and operation of novel detector systems in the STAR experiment, transforming dilepton final states into precision probes of heavy ion collisions.” DOE will honor the recipients at a hybrid award ceremony in Washington, D.C., on November 13, 2026. The ceremony will be broadcast live online, and a recording will be available following the event. Registration is required for both virtual and in-person attendees. Due to space and security requirements, in-person attendance is limited, with registration closing October 30, 2026. For more information and to RSVP, visit the DOE Office of Science Ernest O. Lawrence Award webpage.

state: The U.S. Department of Energy announced today that it will use up to $42 million in Defense Production Act Title III funding to advance the development of a proposed 125-mile natural gas pipeline from Pennsylvania to New York. October 19, 2026WASHINGTON—The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) announced today that it will use up to $42 million in Defense Production Act (DPA) Title III funding to advance the development of a proposed 125-mile natural gas pipeline from Pennsylvania to New York. Constitution Pipeline Company, LLC's project will transport natural gas to markets across the Northeast that currently experience limited access to the low-cost reliable fuel. By leveraging DPA authorities, DOE is helping strengthen the security of the nation’s energy system and defense industrial base. The project will also dramatically lower electricity and home heating costs across the region. “Despite America having an abundant supply of low-cost natural gas, tens of millions of Americans have limited access to this reliable energy source due to a lack of pipeline infrastructure,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “President Trump promised to lower energy costs and reverse the energy emergency he inherited that was caused by 17 years of energy subtraction policies. That is why he promised to build the Constitution Pipeline – a project that will transform the lives and economic opportunities for Americans across New York and New England. It will also reduce the risk of blackouts during periods of peak electricity demand and make our nation more secure.” “For too long, families and businesses in New York and other blue states have paid the price for anti-energy policies that kneecap production, block critical infrastructure and drive up costs,” said Secretary of the Interior and Chairman of the National Energy Dominance Council Doug Burgum. “President Trump is reversing that failed approach, choosing abundance over government-imposed scarcity. This historic investment in New York will help deliver the reliable, secure energy Americans deserve while saving families across the Northeast billions of dollars.” This investment supports President Trump’s commitment to ensuring all Americans have access to affordable, reliable, and secure energy while strengthening infrastructure critical to national defense. Thanks to the Working Families Tax Cut, $1 billion in federal funding has been appropriated for energy-related projects deemed critical to national security. Presidential Determination No. 2026-12 identifies natural gas pipelines, processing and storage as essential to national defense. The DPA funding will support eligible pre-construction and permitting activities necessary to advance the project and, after permits are completed, the deployment of complementary natural gas infrastructure. These activities may include environmental reviews and assessments, engineering and site-preparation work, and other costs associated with securing required regulatory approvals.

state: Additional funding will help states, territories, and tribes modernize critical energy infrastructure, improve grid reliability, and deliver more affordable electricity to American families and businesses. October 20, 2026WASHINGTON— The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) today announced approximately $967 million in additional funding through its Grid Resilience State and Tribal Formula Grant program to modernize critical energy infrastructure, lower electricity costs and strengthen America’s power grid. The funding will support locally driven projects across states, territories, and tribes to upgrade critical infrastructure, prevent power disruptions, and meet growing electricity demand while helping lower costs for American families and businesses. The investment advances President Trump’s American energy dominance agenda. Projects funded through the program will help states, territories, and tribes invest in infrastructure improvements that protect against disruptive events, improve system performance, and ensure communities and businesses have dependable power when they need it most. “Lowering costs and unleashing prosperity are top priorities for President Trump,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “These commonsense investments provide resources directly to states, territories, and tribes to lower electricity costs and strengthen grid reliability for American businesses and families.” “A strong and dependable grid is the backbone of American economic prosperity,” said Office of Electricity Assistant Secretary Katie Jereza. “This funding will help Americans across the country, including our tribal partners, optimize their electricity systems and prepare for future growth while strengthening energy security and deploying technologies that can lower the long-term cost of delivering reliable power.” States, tribes, and U.S. territories can view their funding allocations and application instructions here.

state: The U.S. Department of Energy Alternative Fuels and Feedstocks Office released a pre-publication draft of a federal register notice announcing the Emissions Value Request process for the 45Z fuel production tax credit. October 14, 2026WASHINGTON—The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Alternative Fuels and Feedstocks Office (AFFO) released a pre-publication draft of a federal register notice announcing the Emissions Value Request (EVR) process for the 45Z fuel production tax credit. Modified and extended under the Working Families Tax Cut, the Clean Fuel Production Tax Credit (Internal Revenue Code Section 45Z) provides a production incentive for certain feedstocks produced in the United States, Mexico, or Canada. “Thanks to President Trump’s Working Families Tax Cut, we are creating new opportunities for American farmers and fuel producers to strengthen domestic energy production, reduce costs, and unleash American energy dominance,” said Assistant Secretary of Energy Audrey Robertson. “Through the Department of Energy’s new 45Z Emissions Value Request process, we are expanding opportunities for American fuel producers to access critical tax incentives, supporting rural economies, and bringing more American-made fuels to market. In short: putting American energy first.” Transportation fuel producers seeking to claim the tax credit must obtain the life cycle greenhouse gas emissions rate of their transportation fuel using the applicable rate table for Section 45Z. If the fuel’s type, primary feedstock, or pathway is not included in the rate table, fuel producers must petition the Secretary of Treasury for a provisional emission rate (PER). The 45Z EVR process is the route through which fuel producers can obtain a rate value from DOE and petition U.S. Treasury for a PER. To request an emissions value from DOE, stakeholders must follow the EVR Application Instructions to submit the following requested materials: - Engineering information/analyses consistent with the specified section of the front-end engineering and design (FEED) study or similar indication of project maturity, as determined by DOE. - A completed EVR form. In addition to the required documents, an applicant also has the option to include additional information that may be beneficial in completing lifecycle analysis of the transportation fuel production pathway described in the EVR form and FEED study. For more detailed information on how to apply for a PER or the EVR process, visit DOE’s 45Z EVR webpage or contact 45ZEmissionsRequest@doe.gov. Questions about the 45Z tax credit and eligibility for the tax credit should be directed to the Internal Revenue Service.

state: Secretary Wright issues an emergency order to stabilize the mid-Atlantic grid and mitigate the risk of blackouts October 12, 2026WASHINGTON—U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright issued an emergency order to mitigate blackout risks in the mid-Atlantic ahead of a period of elevated demand, a high rate of planned generator outages during the autumn maintenance season, and numerous planned transmission outages. The order directs PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM) to dispatch specified units and to order their operation as needed to maintain reliability and authorizes PJM to direct backup generation resources to operate as a last resort before declaring an Energy Emergency Alert (EEA) 3 or during an EEA 3. PJM is authorized to call upon its Transmission Owners and Electric Distribution Companies to implement the order as needed. The order was issued pursuant to an application from PJM submitted on October 11, 2026. “This order will help ensure millions of American families and businesses across the mid-Atlantic have access to affordable, reliable, and secure electricity by making additional power generation, including backup power, available to use as needed,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “While past leaders’ energy subtraction policies have made the grid more vulnerable to the risk of blackouts when the sun doesn’t shine or the wind doesn’t blow, this administration remains committed to using every available tool to prevent blackouts.” DOE estimates more than 35 GW of unused backup generation remains available nationwide. The order is effective October 13, 2026, through October 16, 2026.

state: DOE urges PJM to require large new electricity users to pay for the generation and infrastructure needed to serve them. October 9, 2026WASHINGTON—The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) announced its support for the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (FERC) guidance that would help ensure lower electricity costs for American families and businesses across the PJM Interconnection LLC's (PJM) region spanning across the mid-Atlantic. DOE filed a Notice of Intervention and Statement of Position with FERC supporting its recommendation for PJM’s proposed Reliability Backstop Procurement. FERC recommends PJM submit revised tariff provisions to implement appropriate cost allocation and other reforms. FERC’s recommendations are consistent with President Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, ensuring large electricity users pay for the generation and infrastructure needed to serve them. This action follows the Trump Administration’s call in January 2026 for PJM to adopt market rules to strengthen grid reliability and reduce electricity costs. Specifically, the Administration asked PJM to hold an emergency power auction and to accelerate the development of reliable power generation. The Trump administration was joined by governors from all 13 states who participate in the PJM grid. “The Trump Administration remains committed to doing everything it can to lower electricity costs, grow the supply of American energy and strengthen grid reliability,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “That’s why President Trump created the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, and the Energy Department supports having large electricity users pay for reliable new power generation.” “In January, the Trump Administration recognized early warning signs of capacity shortfalls in PJM and joined the Governors of all 13 PJM states in issuing a Statement of Principles to PJM, calling for PJM to adopt market rules to strengthen grid reliability and reduce electricity costs for American families and businesses,” said U.S. Deputy Secretary of Energy James P. Danly. “By increasing transparency and preventing unjust cost shifts onto existing customers, the proposed reforms advance President Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge while ensuring Americans continue to have access to affordable, reliable, and secure electricity.” DOE supports an urgent procurement that would: - Lower electricity costs for Americans by ensuring large load users pay for new generation and infrastructure. - Protect households and businesses from subsidizing large loads. - Use accurate and transparent demand information. - Allow large loads to build, bring, or buy the capacity needed to serve them. DOE urges PJM to comply promptly with FERC’s order and adopt durable market reforms that support reliable generation and protect American families and businesses.

state: The U.S. Department of Energy today announced its intent to deploy Defense Production Act (DPA) funding to accelerate the expansion of transmission capacity in Virginia and West Virginia, strengthening grid reliability and infrastructure essential to national defense. October 16, 2026WASHINGTON—The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) today announced its intent to deploy Defense Production Act (DPA) funding to accelerate the expansion of transmission capacity in Virginia and West Virginia, strengthening grid reliability and infrastructure essential to national defense. Virginia Energy's Grid Enhancing Technologies for Virginia & West Virginia Large Load Growth project will receive up to $50 million in DPA funding to deploy advanced transmission technologies across existing power lines to increase electricity delivery capacity, reduce congestion, and support growing energy demand across the region. The proposed project will deploy advanced reconductoring and Dynamic Line Rating technologies along existing transmission corridors, adding an estimated 290 megawatts of transmission capacity across Appalachian Power's Virginia system, one to four years faster than conventional transmission upgrades. These improvements will make the power grid more reliable, lower electricity costs, and help ensure that communities, businesses, military operations, and government and defense-related industries across the region have dependable power, especially during times of high demand or power disruptions. Thanks to President Trump and the passage of the Working Families Tax Cut, $1 billion in federal funding has been appropriated for energy-related projects deemed critical to national security. Presidential Determination No. 2026-10 identifies transmission lines and conductors, substations, and power-control and protection equipment as essential to national defense. “President Trump is committed to doing everything possible to strengthen American energy security and lower costs for the American people,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “By deploying Defense Production Act funding to secure and expand electricity access in Virginia and West Virginia, the Trump Administration is strengthening the nation’s energy security for decades to come.” “A stronger electric grid doesn't always mean building more power lines. Sometimes it means making better use of the ones we already have,” said Office of Electricity Assistant Secretary Katie Jereza. “This investment will help unlock more power, strengthen reliability, and ensure our grid can meet the growing demands of American families, businesses, and national defense.” Led by Virginia Energy in coordination with Appalachian Power, Potomac Edison, and regional partners, the proposed 48-month project will demonstrate how advanced conductors and real-time transmission monitoring technologies can expand capacity using existing infrastructure. The project reflects the Trump Administration's focus on delivering critical energy infrastructure, strengthening domestic supply chains by creating infrastructure deployment of advance technologies and materials, and improving grid performance while protecting taxpayer dollars and ratepayers.

state: The Energy Department Announces Intention to Support Adding 2.5 GW of Grid Capacity and 800 Jobs October 13, 2026WASHINGTON—The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) today announced plans to lower electricity costs and strengthen grid reliability by supporting the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) in funding 84 transmission and distribution projects across eight states. The projects are expected to add approximately 2.5 gigawatts (GW) of grid capacity to help mitigate outages and create greater grid resilience. The TVA award is for approximately $581 million in total, including $250 million in federal funding and about $331 million in applicant cost-share funding. As part of the Resilience Amplified: Multi-Market Grid Interconnection Initiative funding award under the Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships (GRIP) project, the investments will help ensure 2.58 million families and businesses have access to the affordable, reliable, and secure power they need. The project is estimated to support about 800 jobs. “Since day one, President Trump has recognized that years of misguided energy policies under the previous administration left our bulk power system less robust than it should be,” said U.S. Deputy Secretary of Energy James P. Danly. “America is blessed with an abundance of natural resources and some of the most advanced technology in the world, but we must have the generation and transmission infrastructure necessary to support our rapidly growing economy and its electricity needs. These investments with TVA will help reduce congestion, improve efficiency, and make better use of our existing transmission system to lower costs for ratepayers while delivering affordable, reliable, and secure energy essential to American prosperity.” “America's electric grid cannot become a roadblock to economic growth,” said Office of Electricity (OE) Assistant Secretary Katie Jereza. “By bringing TVA and local utilities together, we're helping reduce costly outages and deliver more power where it's needed. That means fewer disruptions for families, more opportunities for businesses, and a stronger foundation for American jobs.” The award builds on DOE's selection of TVA for the Speed to Power through Accelerated Reconductoring and other Key Advanced Transmission Technology Upgrades (SPARK) program. Together, the GRIP and SPARK projects for TVA represent nearly $741 million in planned grid investment, including approximately $329.8 million in federal support, and are expected to add more than 4,300 MW of additional grid capacity. Under SPARK, TVA plans to upgrade about 125 miles of existing transmission lines across Tennessee, Alabama, and North Carolina using advanced conductors and grid-management technology. The $159.7 million project is expected to add approximately 1,900 MW of transmission capacity and reduce congestion. Final federal funding, project scope, schedules, and other award conditions remain subject to executed DOE agreements and applicable environmental, permitting, regulatory, and Tribal reviews.

state: - SPEECH IMFC Statement Statement by Christine Lagarde, President of the ECB, at the fifty-fourth meeting of the International Monetary and Financial Committee IMF Annual Meetings, 17 October 2026 Introduction The global economy has proven surprisingly resilient in the face of high uncertainty. The conflict in the Middle East continues to expose energy markets to sharp swings. Trade tensions and protectionist measures are weighing on confidence and contributing to a reconfiguration of trade flows. The global economy has held up thanks in part to the rise of artificial intelligence, with investment in technology supporting activity and trade, particularly in economies integrated into technology value chains. Risks nonetheless remain tilted to the downside for growth and to the upside for inflation. A return to an international economic order grounded in openness, predictability and the rule of law would help trade and investment flourish. Economic activity Despite global headwinds and the ongoing energy shock, the euro area economy has so far proved resilient. Growth was broad-based across most euro area countries and sectors in the first half of 2026. The September ECB staff projections foresee growth of 0.9% in 2026, 1.4% in 2027 and 1.5% in 2028. As the energy shock fades over the medium term, the projections see domestic demand benefitting from a recovery in real income over the medium term, driven by lower energy inflation and a resilient labour market. Rising government spending on infrastructure and defence, complemented by investment in AI and digital technologies, should also support growth. Export growth should pick up on the back of strengthening foreign demand, also driven by AI. The medium-term outlook is surrounded by uncertainty over how intense and long-lasting the Middle East conflict will be, and how the resulting shocks might propagate through the economy. Risks to growth are assessed to be on the downside. Fiscal sustainability remains a crucial anchor for broader economic stability. It is important to maintain sound fiscal policies, including by adhering to fiscal rules, and, where debt is high, to consolidate, re-prioritise spending and enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of public finances to rebuild buffers. Governments should strive to ensure that any fiscal response to the energy shock is temporary, targeted and tailored. In addition, policies that strengthen resilience to climate change can improve the economy’s ability to absorb climate-related shocks. These efforts should be complemented by structural policies that promote labour market participation, equip the workforce with the skills needed in an AI-driven economy and facilitate the diffusion of new technologies. Priorities include advancing the savings and investments union, improving access to risk capital and creating better conditions for innovative firms to scale up across the Single Market. Inflation Headline inflation increased to 3.8% in September, mostly reflecting a surge in energy inflation, and, to a lesser extent, an increase in food and services inflation. Core inflation increased slightly to 2.5%. The range of underlying inflation measures remained broadly stable in September and wages have so far shown no material response to the energy shock. Looking ahead, higher energy prices are expected to keep headline inflation well above target into the first half of 2027 and to gradually feed through to core and food inflation. Headline inflation is expected to decline after the first quarter as energy inflation falls, returning to around target towards the end of 2027. The risks to the inflation outlook are to the upside due, in particular, to the Middle East conflict and Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine. A more intense or persistent energy shock could strengthen indirect and second-round effects, resulting in higher and more persistent inflation. Extreme weather could push up food prices. By contrast, a sustainable resolution of geopolitical conflicts, weaker energy pass-through or more risk-averse financial markets could lower inflation. Monetary policy The Governing Council decided to raise the key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points in September, following an increase of the same size in June. Our interest rate decisions are based on our reaction function, which comprises three criteria: our assessment of the inflation outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data, the dynamics of underlying inflation; and the strength of monetary policy transmission. The inflation outlook points to higher inflation ahead, especially in the short term, given the latest developments in energy markets. However, we see no evidence at this stage of significant pass-through of energy prices to other prices and wages, beyond what we have already included in our projections. And while growth has been resilient, financing conditions have tightened, with long-term interest rates rising notably since our last meeting. This will slow growth and reduce pass-through by more than projected in our September exercise. Taking these three criteria together, the energy shock is too large to “look through” but a measured response remains appropriate to keep inflation in check. In setting future policy, we will make a comprehensive assessment of the incoming data based on our reaction function. In July, the Governing Council decided on the operational features and the onboarding process for the enhanced EUREP, the Eurosystem repo facility for central banks that was announced earlier this year. The new facility supports the smooth transmission of monetary policy and reinforces the international role of the euro. More than 30 central banks have expressed interest in EUREP in the past six months. Financial stability Sources of risk and vulnerabilities for euro area financial stability remain high. Continued geopolitical tensions, fiscal challenges and uncertainties around accelerated AI adoption continue to be causes for concern. The widespread concentration of critical third-party service providers introduces single points of failure for both financial and non-financial institutions. New frontier AI models have increased cyber risks and operational vulnerabilities. Euro area banks maintain strong capital and liquidity buffers and robust profitability, together with healthy and stable asset quality. These solid fundamentals should help navigate ongoing geopolitical uncertainties and effectively support lending to the economy. Strengthened prudential regulation and supervision since the global financial crisis has helped leave euro area banks in a strong position to withstand the unfolding economic challenges. Shocks could expose vulnerabilities among non-bank financial intermediaries, notably from concentrated AI-related exposures, amplifying market stress and creating spillovers across financial sectors. Banks’ exposures to non-banks and vulnerable firms could expose funding and credit vulnerabilities. Stress in private credit markets has continued, with private credit funds reporting outflows and reactivating redemption gates. Private market “semi-liquid funds” that allow for redemptions are becoming more prevalent, which could lead to greater liquidity mismatches in the future, but euro area financial institutions have limited direct exposure to private credit. This means, for now, that private credit in isolation is unlikely to be a source of financial instability in the euro area. Payment systems Central bank money must evolve to fulfil the needs of an increasingly digital economy. The Eurosystem is at the forefront of this evolution, bringing the stability and trust of central bank money to digital retail payments and tokenised finance in Europe. In the retail space we are preparing to complement cash with its digital equivalent – the digital euro – for day-to-day payments. The digital euro will further stimulate innovation and competition in retail payments, ensuring that the continued co-existence of public and private solutions underpins Europe’s strategic autonomy in payments. To lay the groundwork for a seamless and secure launch, we will run a 12-month internal pilot in the second half of 2027. Adopting the Regulation on the establishment of the digital euro by the end of 2026 is key to making this possible. In the wholesale space, the Eurosystem is developing new capabilities to ensure that central bank money can settle transactions in the growing market of tokenised assets. Pontes – the Eurosystem’s distributed ledger technology (DLT) solution that went live on 21 September – marks the first step in implementing our strategy to enable the development of a European tokenised ecosystem. This vision will be advanced under the Appia initiative, which aims to deliver a blueprint for this ecosystem based on common standards, shared network infrastructure and European governance. International cooperation We value the work of our global institutions and fora, particularly those that promote global macroeconomic and financial stability. We welcome the recent completion of the three major IMF reviews (Comprehensive Surveillance Review, Financial Sector Assessment Program Review and Review of Program Design and Conditionality), which strengthen the role of the IMF at the centre of the global financial safety net. Climate-related work should remain fully anchored in IMF operations, particularly surveillance. Multilateral efforts to help tackle global imbalances support coordination of domestic action that is required to minimise the risks from disorderly adjustment. The IMF’s analytical work on global imbalances and its improvements to the methodology for assessing external balances provide a strong basis for these efforts. state: - INTERVIEW Interview with Die Presse Interview with Frank Elderson, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB and Vice-Chair of the Supervisory Board of the ECB, conducted by Aloysius Widmann on 14 October 2026 20 October 2026 Almost without exception, banks complain about the high cost of regulation. Do they have a point? Or are these costs essential for the stability of the banking system? We shouldn’t forget the financial crisis of 2008. The costs were enormous, not only for banks, but also for households, firms, taxpayers and society as a whole. Those costs far outweigh the cost of regulation. The regulatory reforms introduced after the crisis have made European banks far more resilient. Banks today are well capitalised, have high liquidity levels and are more profitable, on average, than for many years. But wouldn’t it be possible to simplify supervision without putting the stability of the sector at risk? It’s true that regulation and the supervisory framework have become more complex over time. One of the reasons for this is that the banks themselves differ greatly and operate in an increasingly complex environment. The risks have also become more complex, ranging from geopolitical tensions, cyber risk and climate and nature risks through to artificial intelligence. But complexity is not an end in itself. We do of course ask ourselves constantly whether we could still achieve our objectives as supervisors with simpler rules and regulations. And we’ve already taken a whole range of measures. We’ve reduced reporting obligations and accelerated processes. But it’s important to remember that simplification is not the same as deregulation. And it is resilience that is the foundation of sustainable growth and competitiveness. Regulation means costs, and costs can be a competitive disadvantage. What do you see as the biggest obstacles to international competitiveness for European banks? The biggest obstacle to European competitiveness is fragmentation. Although we have made progress, Europe still doesn’t have a truly single, integrated banking market. Cross-border banking activities remain limited. Banks are not able to fully benefit from economies of scale, greater diversification or more efficient allocation of capital and liquidity across the European economy. This fragmentation leads to higher costs, lower efficiency and fewer opportunities to achieve the kind of scale that is needed to compete internationally. This doesn’t just affect the banking sector but many other sectors besides. We talk about the Single Market, but the reality is the market is not yet truly single. If fragmentation is the diagnosis, integration is the remedy – not deregulation. We need to complete the Single Market, the savings and investments union, and the banking union, including establishing a European deposit insurance scheme. Simplification and integration are two sides of the same coin, which is the competitiveness agenda. We need both and we need both at the same time. This is why it is crucial that the European Commission’s banking reform package keeps both sides together. How much would a fully integrated banking market actually encourage cross-border lending? Local banks know their customers best. And competition is already really strong in countries like Austria. I haven’t got a crystal ball. What is clear, though, is that a single jurisdiction with several hundred million customers would lead to more competition, better products and more risk sharing. Banks would also be in a position to fund future-oriented investments; the challenges associated with the climate and nature crises, the energy transition and demographics are enormous. Today, differences in legal frameworks, insolvency regimes and consumer protection rules still make cross-border banking unnecessarily complex and costly. No one is forcing us Europeans to keep these obstacles in the market. We’ve built them ourselves – we can, and should, also remove them and do so urgently. And with the enormous investment challenges in front of us, we’ve no time to lose. Other countries could relieve the burden on their banks by implementing Basel III more loosely. Wouldn’t this cause Europe to become less competitive? Banking is a global business. Capital flows across frontiers, banks are interrelated, and risks don’t normally come to a halt at national borders. That’s why international standards are so important. We want banks to compete on how efficient and innovative they are and how well they manage their risks, and not on who operates under the weakest rules. Thanks to the Basel standards, this is what’s happening, because we’ve created a broadly consistent international framework. The Basel standards create a common minimum benchmark for banking regulation and prudential supervision. Of course there is also space for national variations, where these are justified, carefully targeted and supported by evidence. But in a global financial system where shocks can propagate across borders, policymakers share a responsibility to observe minimum standards. Simply lowering the standards does not cause the risks to disappear. Supervisors will still need to assess the risks and ensure banks address them appropriately. Loosening Pillar 1 requirements could therefore simply shift the burden from regulation to supervision. You’re calling for supervision to be more proportionate, meaning it takes more account of the size and complexity of the institutions that are supervised… Proportionality is not about weakening supervision. The aim is to tailor the supervision better to the banks, using criteria such as size, complexity and risk profile. This is already embedded in the legal framework. For instance, there is the category of small and non-complex banks that are subject to significantly lighter reporting requirements. They only have to report up to 30% of the data that large banks are required to report. But there is room to do more on proportionality. And I staunchly support doing just that. Right now, the threshold for whether a bank is considered small and non-complex is €5 billion in total assets. Raising that threshold to €10 billion would enable a further 150 banks or so to come under the simplified regime. Another option would be to lengthen the periods between regulatory reviews, where risk profiles allow. And for stress tests, we could make greater use of data that we already have to hand. All these changes would reduce the workload for smaller and less complex banks. How far can such simplifications go? No further than the risk. Proportionality can only go as far as a bank’s risk profile allows, and only as far as it does not impair our ability to safeguard financial stability and ensure banks are safe and sound. There should be no change in the core prudential standards. Banks still need to have sound corporate governance, effective risk management, adequate capital and liquidity and resilience in the face of new risks. Not only would smarter and more proportionate supervision lessen the burden on banks, it would also free up resources for us supervisors to concentrate on the most important risks. What risks does artificial intelligence raise for banks? AI has enormous potential for banks. It can improve risk management, facilitate the processing of information, reinforce fraud detection and raise efficiency. But every transformative technology also creates risks. One area of concern is cyber risk. Advanced AI models can discover and exploit vulnerabilities more quickly. This is why, back in July, we asked the banks to reassess their cybersecurity measures and to review their IT budgets and staffing levels. They are expected to submit concrete action plans for dealing with AI-related cyber risks to us by the end of October. Banks should not become overly dependent on AI models either. The technology has many advantages – helping to improve credit assessments, for instance. But banks need to watch out for biases and blind spots; they can’t simply leave decisions to the algorithm. A third issue is data quality. AI is only as good as the data it is trained on. And fourthly, operational dependencies on cloud providers, for instance, are emerging. The fact that there only so many such providers is giving rise to considerable concentration risk. The AI investment boom in the United States is increasingly funded via private credit – loans extended outside of the banking sector – and corporate bonds. It remains to be seen whether the AI firms can actually generate the predicted profits that they use to justify the investment. To what extent does this create risks for European banks? The key issue here is the interconnectedness between banks and non-banks. We’re taking this topic very seriously and want to see that the banks are also well aware of these risks. A more diverse financial system is a good thing. Europe needs huge investments to address its strategic priorities, and market-based finance can play a role there alongside banks. Certain other players are better able to bear specific risks than banks. But if lending migrates out of the banking system, it does not automatically mean that all the associated risks migrate with it. Those risks can feed back into the banking system, because of the interconnections between banks and non-banks. It may be the case, for instance, that a bank not only lends money to a private credit provider but at the same time funds firms to which this provider also extends loans. This can give rise to risk concentrations that are not evident at first glance but that come to light when something goes wrong. That is why banks need to take a very close look at these linkages and make sure they can manage them appropriately. state: - SPEECH Resilience, integration and competitiveness: building the future of European banking Keynote speech by Boris Vujčić, Vice-President of the ECB, at the tenth annual conference of the European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB) Frankfurt am Main, 2 October 2026 It is a great pleasure to participate in this conference marking the ESRB’s 15th anniversary. As we know, the ESRB was established 15 years ago as the EU’s macroprudential oversight body, in response to the global financial crisis. I have contributed to its work for the past 13 years, so I feel very at home here. In 2009 the de Larosière Group recommended the establishment of an EU-level body with a mandate to oversee risks in the financial system as a whole, going beyond the supervision of individual firms. The global financial crisis, followed by the sovereign debt crisis in Europe, clearly demonstrated both the potential severity and the long-lasting costs of financial crises – and the importance of preventing them (Slide 2). Estimates put the median fiscal cost of a banking crisis at around 7% of GDP for advanced economies. And fiscal costs capture only part of the damage. Financial crises can also lead to broader and persistent losses in output, employment and investment, not least because they weaken confidence. After 15 years, however, the global regulatory reforms introduced to limit this fallout from crises are increasingly being called into question. The banking industry sees the EU regulatory framework as erring too far on the side of caution, putting European banks at a disadvantage. It suggests that capital requirements are constraining the provision of bank credit to the real economy, and that lowering them would make banks more competitive. But if we recall the generalised fragility of banks’ balance sheets 15 years ago, there is little doubt that, had banks entered the crisis with the stronger balance sheets of today, the economic costs would have been considerably lower. The fact that our banks are profitable and of sound standing today is a strategic advantage for Europe, because a resilient financial system is a prerequisite for sustainable economic growth. At the same time, I agree that such resilience does not necessarily require complex rules. The same level of resilience can, in many cases, be achieved with simpler ones. I remember much simpler rules being discussed within the ESRB some 12 or 13 years ago, when Mark Carney was First Vice-Chair and Martin Hellwig was Chair of the Advisory Scientific Committee. But there was a lot of pushback at the time, and the rules have instead become gradually more complex. Complying with EU rules has become increasingly complicated and burdensome, and there is a clear case for simplifying them. So today let me make the case for simplification – which can contribute to a prosperous financial sector – and at the same time focus on what will really make banks more competitive, namely financial integration in a truly Single Market which fosters economies of scale. Simplification At the end of last year, the Governing Council of the ECB put forward a set of high-level recommendations for simplifying the EU’s regulatory, supervisory and reporting frameworks for banks.[1] We identified the main areas where the rules could be made less complex and where legislative action would be required. First, we proposed simplifying the capital stack within the risk-based prudential framework by merging the existing capital buffers into just two: a non-releasable buffer, combining the capital conservation buffer and the global systemically important institutions or other systemically important institutions buffer; and a releasable buffer, combining the countercyclical capital buffer and the systemic risk buffer. We also proposed simplifying the leverage ratio framework by moving from four elements in the capital stack to two: a 3% minimum requirement and a single leverage ratio buffer. Second, to simplify the resolution framework, we proposed more closely aligning the frameworks for MREL (the minimum requirement for own funds and eligible liabilities) and TLAC (total loss-absorbing capacity). In other words, we suggested bringing the resolution requirements that apply to all EU banks closer to those applying to global systemically important banks under the international TLAC framework, without reducing the resources that would be available in resolution. Third, we recommended a dedicated, prudent and materially simpler regime for smaller banks, building on the existing EU regime for small and non-complex institutions, while introducing significantly greater proportionality. To preserve resilience, this simpler regime would be calibrated in a more conservative manner. The Eurosystem also responded to the European Commission’s consultation on the competitiveness of the EU banking sector.[2] The Commission subsequently published its Communication on the competitiveness of the banking sector and the Single Market in banking – an initiative that the ECB very much welcomes. In parallel, the ECB’s supervisory arm is pursuing concrete simplification measures to make European banking supervision more efficient, effective and risk-focused. These include streamlining supervisory guidance and discontinuing around 40 guidance documents out of more than 100. Competitiveness All these will be important improvements, but what will ultimately drive the competitiveness of EU banks lies elsewhere. Before addressing the broader debate, though, let me take a step back and consider what we actually mean by competitiveness. Competitiveness cannot be reduced to a single metric. It has multiple dimensions: sustained profitability, operating efficiency, the capacity to innovate, the ability to invest – for example, in IT – and the capacity to attract investment in bank equity. So, what does the evidence tell us about the relationship between capital and competitiveness? Since the global financial crisis, euro area bank capital ratios have steadily increased. The median Tier 1 ratio has more than doubled, from around 8% in 2009 to more than 16% today (Slide 3, left-hand side). After more than a decade of structurally low profitability, euro area banks’ return on equity has risen steadily since the pandemic, alongside the normalisation of monetary policy, to reach historical highs (Slide 3, right-hand side). The earlier period of low profitability was reflected in price-to-book ratios below 1, indicating a substantial undervaluation of bank equity in Europe and a large gap with US banks. That gap has narrowed considerably since 2023. The average price-to-book ratio is now around 1.5, well above its long-term median (Slide 4, left-hand side). Stronger bank performance has also translated into higher dividend payouts, while contributing to greater capital headroom through retained earnings (Slide 4, right-hand side). These developments call for caution when drawing immediate conclusions about the relationship between capital requirements and lending. It is too simplistic to suggest that the EU banks can be made more competitive simply by reducing their capital requirements. The academic evidence on the relationship between capital requirements and banks’ ability to lend is nuanced. Some studies identify a negative effect of higher capital requirements on credit supply – looking at short-term adjustments, not at effects in the long run – while others find no significant effect. The effect is state-dependent, i.e. it varies with the economic environment in which the study is conducted. Studies covering the period immediately following the global financial crisis tend to find that higher capital requirements have had a negative effect on lending. At that time, banks were dealing with the legacy of the crisis: high levels of non-performing loans, weak profitability and limited capacity to generate capital internally. Under such conditions, tighter capital requirements can induce banks to reduce lending. More recent studies, covering periods of more favourable economic and financial conditions, reach different conclusions.[3] The impact of higher capital requirements on lending appears more limited among well-capitalised banks operating in a more positive macroeconomic environment. The reason is straightforward. Comfortable capital positions and solid profitability allow banks to absorb tighter regulatory requirements through retained earnings or smaller voluntary management buffers. This limits their need to reduce the supply of credit. The current situation in the euro area is important in this respect. Banks’ financial reporting for the second quarter of 2026 confirms that profitability has improved further. Net interest income has continued to rebound and net fees and commissions have picked up. Over the past few years, retained earnings have been the main driver of capital accumulation (Slide 5, left-hand side). While some of these resources have been absorbed by growth in risk-weighted assets, dividend payouts and somewhat higher capital requirements, aggregate capital headroom has continued to increase. This suggests that regulatory capital is not currently a binding constraint on lending. Evidence from the euro area bank lending survey points in the same direction. In recent years, banks have consistently reported that tighter credit standards primarily reflect risk perceptions, risk tolerance and uncertainty about the economic outlook, rather than their capital positions. Moreover, loan demand has remained subdued (Slide 5, right-hand side). Taken together, these developments suggest that current lending dynamics are more likely to reflect the demand for credit, elevated uncertainty and broader macroeconomic conditions than a shortage of capital to meet regulatory requirements. So, under the current conditions, would a reduction in capital requirements materially increase lending? I would consider this very unlikely. Financial integration The present level of bank capital requirements is not a competitive disadvantage for European banks. Instead, the resilience of our banks is a source of strength for the euro area banking system and the EU more broadly, especially if we recall the situation 15 years ago. This resilience has been demonstrated many times in recent years. An analysis of euro area bank data finds that better-capitalised banks tend to face lower equity costs (Slide 6, left-hand side) and are more able to meet heightened credit demand when financing needs surge. This was evident during the pandemic, an unprecedented economic shock, when well-capitalised banks lent more than those with less capital. (Slide 6, right-hand side).[4] There is also evidence that banks that were more robust and better performing were less reliant on government-backed lending and other policy support measures during the pandemic.[5] In addition, euro area banks successfully weathered the market tensions following the failure of several US regional banks and Credit Suisse in 2023, supported by strong profitability and ample capital and liquidity buffers. So, I think we can agree that a resilient banking sector performs better during periods of stress and provides a solid foundation for competitiveness. But what is the most powerful tool for boosting the competitiveness of the European banking sector? In my view, it is financial integration. Only a genuine Single Market and a complete banking union can reduce fragmentation and enable European banks to realise their full potential in terms of scale and competitiveness. At present, European banks clearly lack scale. The fact remains that banking services in the euro area are still largely provided within national borders. Cross-border bank lending to non-financial firms within the euro area remains subdued, accounting for only around 16% of total corporate lending.[6] This share is lower than lending to corporate borrowers outside the euro area – primarily US and UK-based firms – which represents about 20% of total corporate lending. This suggests that the Single Market has not yet managed to facilitate cross-border corporate lending within the euro area. The euro area banking sector has become more concentrated over the past decade, but this has been driven mainly by domestic mergers and acquisitions (M&A). Banking sector concentration at the EU level is still lower than in the United States. Moreover, M&A activity in Europe often follows existing cross-border financial linkages and tends to be between neighbouring countries or remain within national markets. This is a missed opportunity, as studies suggest that, on average, banks involved in M&A activities improve their profitability and cost efficiency. They also become more diversified in terms of assets and revenues after an M&A deal.[7] In addition, more competitive banking groups tend to have greater geographical reach, which helps them to reap efficiency gains, including through lower cost-to-income ratios (Slide 7). What’s more, cross-border M&As can also help tackle the bank-sovereign nexus. Euro area banks tend to operate with, on average, lower lending margins than US banks (Slide 8, left-hand side). Cross-border integration in banking would lower borrowing costs for firms and households and benefit banks by spreading earnings and risk across countries. Further progress on the savings and investments union by completing the banking union and the capital markets union is therefore needed to help EU banks become more competitive. Establishing a European deposit insurance scheme – the missing pillar of the banking union – is essential. It would ensure that deposits are protected equally across the euro area. This would, in turn, help create a credible crisis management framework, which is a precondition for building the trust necessary for financial integration. This would lead to a more competitive and integrated banking sector that is better placed to support European priorities. Integration also offers opportunities for efficiency gains by allowing banks to exploit economies of scale. This brings me to an area where EU banks are at a distinct competitive disadvantage compared with their US counterparts: capital market transactions. US banks are far more competitive when it comes to trading or global investment banking (Slide 8, right-hand side, and Slide 9). The United States has the deepest capital market in the world in terms of liquidity and investor demand. Meanwhile, EU capital markets still have to contend with significant legal and regulatory fragmentation. Consider withholding taxes, for example: cross-border investors in the EU are confronted with 27 different regimes and face potential double-taxation burdens on dividends and interest. Insolvency laws are even more complex, with divergent national rules generating considerable uncertainty and potentially unpredictable outcomes for cross-border investments. Ultimately, if Europe wants deep capital markets comparable to those in the United States, it must also address the underlying investor base. The large pool of pension fund assets in the United States provides a deep and stable source of long-term capital (Slide 10). Developing stronger funded pension systems in Europe would play an important role in deepening EU capital markets. Growth-oriented policies require greater harmonisation to reduce national divergences in taxation, insolvency rules, labour law and corporate law that create fragmentation and frictions for cross-border investment. That is quite a list, but these are the very issues that need to be tackled if we truly want to make the European financial ecosystem more competitive. Simplification, while important, will not on its own substantially boost competitiveness, and we must make sure that it does not weaken resilience. Conclusion I would like to finish by repeating three key messages from our response to the Commission’s consultation on the competitiveness of the EU banking sector.[8] First, the resilience of banks is a prerequisite for economic growth and competitiveness. This is particularly true in today’s uncertain environment, where preparedness for shocks is critical. European firms rely heavily on banks as their main source of external funding. They therefore need banks with strong, resilient balance sheets that can continue to provide credit when conditions deteriorate. Second, simplification and further harmonisation can foster competitiveness. Substantial efforts are under way to simplify regulatory, supervisory and reporting frameworks and to address unnecessary complexity that may hamper competitiveness. These are valuable initiatives, and Europe has much to gain from designing and implementing them quickly. Third, the most powerful tool to enhance the competitiveness of the European banking sector is financial integration. Well-integrated markets and greater cross-border activity will enable banks to reap economies of scale, diversify, strengthen their business models and better support the real economy – particularly in times of stress. Completing the banking union and achieving a fully integrated Single Market is therefore vital and will allow banks to operate across the euro area as if it were a single jurisdiction. Making further progress towards a genuine capital markets union must also be our priority. Rome wasn’t built in a day, of course, and the same is true for resilience, simplification and integration. Yet while progress may take time, history also reminds us that destruction can occur rapidly – the Great Fire devastated Rome within days. Financial crises can also have devastating effects, as we witnessed 15 years ago, wiping out hard-earned gains in an instant and imposing heavy costs on taxpayers, businesses and banks. That should strengthen our resolve to preserve resilience and build a competitive financial system, based on the understanding that Europe is stronger together. state: Decisions taken by the Governing Council of the ECB (in addition to decisions setting interest rates) August-September 2026 2 October 2026 External communication Announcements related to the digital euro project On 30 July 2026 the ECB issued a press release outlining the accessibility features of the digital euro app, the design of which will go beyond the requirements set out in the European Accessibility Act, and announcing that the ECB would start usability and accessibility testing as part of the digital euro pilot in 2027. The press release, together with the related underlying documentation, is available on the ECB’s website. On 15 September 2026 the ECB issued a call for expression of interest inviting e-commerce and mobile commerce (m-commerce) merchants operating in the euro area to take part in the digital euro pilot. The deadline to submit applications is 27 October 2026. Finally, on 28 September 2026 the ECB issued another call for expression of interest inviting private companies and organisations to collaborate in exploring how the digital euro infrastructure could support them in their innovation efforts. More detailed information is available in the related announcement published on the ECB’s website. The deadline to submit applications is 9 November 2026. Strong participation in the ECB survey on the future design of the euro banknotes On 23 September 2026 the ECB issued a press release reporting that almost ten million people across Europe and beyond had completed the ECB survey on the future design of euro banknotes, which ran between 23 July and 21 September 2026. This level of participation, equal to 2.6% of the euro area population, is unprecedented for such a survey. The press release also outlined the next steps in the process. More information on the future banknotes, the shortlisted proposals and the selection process is available on the ECB’s website. Market operations Amendments to legal acts on the implementation of the Eurosystem monetary policy framework On 22 September 2026 the Governing Council adopted amendments to the legal acts implementing the Eurosystem monetary policy framework. The amending legal acts are Guideline ECB/2026/26 amending Guideline (EU) 2015/510 on the implementation of the Eurosystem monetary policy framework and Guideline ECB/2026/27 amending Guideline (EU) 2016/65 on the valuation haircuts applied in the implementation of the Eurosystem monetary policy framework. The amendments will apply from 30 November 2026 and include the changes detailed in a related press release available on the ECB’s website. Macroprudential policy and financial stability Response of the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) to the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCAR) targeted consultation On 7 September 2026 the Governing Council, with the involvement of the General Council, approved the ESCB’s response to the European Commission’s targeted consultation on the review of MiCAR. The response, which welcomes the consultation to assess areas where existing rules could be improved with a view to ensuring that MiCAR remains fit for purpose, taking into account lessons learned from the initial years of MiCAR’s implementation, evolving market dynamics and practices in other jurisdictions, is available on the ECB’s website. Market infrastructure and payments Appointment of a new member of the Market Infrastructure Board (MIB) On 30 July 2026 the Governing Council approved the appointment of Sigríður Dis Guðjónsdóttir, Head of Payments and Resilience at the Central Bank of Iceland, as a non-voting member of the MIB from a non-euro area central bank until 31 May 2029. The full list of members of the MIB is available on the ECB’s website. Agreement for and go-live of the Pontes pilot On 11 August 2026 the Governing Council approved an agreement governing the initial launch of Pontes, a solution that enables wholesale transactions in tokenised assets to be settled in central bank money. The agreement between the Eurosystem central banks and the solution-providing Eurosystem national central banks establishes a binding legal framework for a production grade system while, at the same time, reflecting the interim nature of this phase of the service. It also includes terms and conditions for market participants and market distributed ledger technology (DLT) operators that will provide contract templates for arrangements between the Eurosystem central banks and their market participants and market DLT operators. On 11 September 2026 the Market Infrastructure Board recommended proceeding with the scheduled Pontes initial launch date of 21 September 2026. A related press release is available on the ECB’s website. ECB Decision on the identification of Visa Europe Payment System as a systemically important payment system On 24 August 2026 the Governing Council adopted Decision ECB/2026/22 on the identification of the Visa Europe Payment System as a systemically important payment system pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2025/1355 on oversight requirements for systemically important payment systems. The Decision, which was notified to the German branch of Visa Europe Limited in its capacity as operator of Visa Europe Payment System for the euro area, is available on EUR-Lex. As a result of the Decision, Visa Europe Payment System will be overseen by the Eurosystem with the ECB acting as lead overseer. Progress update on the interlinking of TARGET Instant Payment Settlement (TIPS) with other fast payment systems On 24 September 2026 the Governing Council took note of a status update on progress made on interlinking the TIPS platform with other fast payment systems globally and approved the initiation of an assessment of the feasibility of interlinking with Brazil’s instant payment system, Pix. A related article is available on the ECB’s website. The Governing Council also considered a recommendation of the Market Infrastructure Board on the pricing of the TIPS interlinking service. More detailed information will be provided on the ECB’s website as further progress is made. Advice on legislation ECB Opinion on the Polish Defence Investment Fund On 28 July 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/23 at the request of the Marshal of the Polish Parliament. ECB Opinion on Ireland's participation in the International Monetary Fund’s Resilience and Sustainability Trust On 12 August 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/24 at the request of the Irish Minister for Finance. ECB Opinion on the introduction of a ban on crypto-asset activities, and measures concerning the application of Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 On 12 August 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/26 at the request of the Marshal of the Polish Parliament.
