state: - SPEECH Money in the digital age: digital euro, tokenisation and the role of central banks Speech by Piero Cipollone, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, MNI Connect Webcast Frankfurt am Main, 6 October 2026 For centuries, issuing money and safeguarding its value has been at the heart of central banks’ mandate. But the technological environment is changing. People increasingly pay digitally. Financial institutions are experimenting with distributed ledger technology (DLT). Assets are being represented as digital files, or tokens. New actors have entered markets traditionally served by banks. This transformation opens up significant opportunities. It can make payments more convenient and finance more efficient. And it can pave the way for new products and business models. But it also creates risks. If we do not provide a digital form of cash, the role of public money may continue to decline. And we may find ourselves trapped in a situation where there is no pan-European digital payment solution that caters to every type of day-to-day transaction. If tokenised finance develops on closed, incompatible platforms without a safe settlement asset, fragmentation could increase and the singleness of money could be weakened. And when Europe depends excessively on infrastructures, technologies or solutions controlled elsewhere, our resilience and monetary sovereignty is diminished. The question, therefore, is not whether payments and finance will become more digital. They already are. The question is how we can ensure that our monetary system continues to preserve the singleness of money, trust and stability, while also supporting efficiency, resilience and autonomy as this transformation unfolds. Our answer is to extend central bank money into the digital environment while preserving the two-tier monetary system in which public and private money coexist. In retail payments, this means preparing for a digital euro. In wholesale markets, it means ensuring that central bank money can be used to settle tokenised transactions – through Pontes – while working with the market – through Appia – to shape the wider digital finance ecosystem. These initiatives are often discussed separately. But they are all part of one comprehensive strategy: to keep central bank money at the heart of retail and wholesale finance, while giving European market participants the infrastructure they need to innovate, grow and remain competitive internationally. Central bank money as the anchor Our monetary system rests on the coexistence of public and private money. Central bank money is the ultimate risk-free settlement asset. And it supports the role of private money because trust in commercial bank money rests on its convertibility at par into central bank money. This convertibility ensures the singleness of money. One euro has the same value as any other, throughout the euro area. Our objective is not therefore to replace private money or private innovation. It is to provide a stable public foundation to ensure day-to-day payments are cheap, resilient and inclusive. And to enable financial innovation to develop safely, at scale, in an integrated European market. Preparing a digital euro for retail payments Let me turn first to retail payments. This is what the digital euro is for: our day-to-day transactions. A Europe-made, Europe-wide payments solution There is still no European digital means of payment that works across all euro area countries and all major use cases. European private solutions tend to cover specific markets or payment situations. This means that banks and their customers depend heavily on international card schemes and global technology companies. Two-thirds of euro area card payments rely on international schemes. Of the 21 euro area countries, 13 have no domestic card scheme. And where a domestic payment solution exists, it does not always cater to all use cases and cannot be used in other euro area countries without co-badging with international schemes. This is not just a question of sovereignty, resilience and freedom of choice. It is also a question of competitiveness. European payment service providers have so far been unable to compete with international payment solutions on a European scale, let alone at global level. This is mainly because it would be costly for each individual provider to develop a Europe-wide acceptance network. The recent announcement of an interoperability platform that would allow private payment solutions to share customers, enabling users to pay wherever interoperable solutions are accepted, is a step in the right direction and one we very much welcome. But much remains to be done: cross-border transactions account for just 5% of the market and interoperability does not expand acceptance domestically, nor does it broaden the use cases covered. The digital euro would fill this gap. It would provide a digital form of central bank money for everyday payments, complementing cash and private solutions. It would be available both online and offline and would be usable throughout the euro area for most use cases: person-to-person payments, e-commerce transactions and payments in physical shops. But the ECB would not provide customer-facing services. Banks and other regulated payment service providers would distribute the digital euro, manage customer relationships and develop complementary services. Our objective is not to take over the role of banks. On the contrary, the digital euro would equip banks with the infrastructure they need to compete in the digital age and help them expand the reach and use cases of their own solutions. A platform payment service providers can build on The digital euro would provide a common acceptance layer across the euro area. Its legal tender status would give it pan-European reach: it would be accepted wherever digital payments can be made. The digital euro’s open standards could be used by private payment services providers, thereby simplifying acceptance at physical points of sale, online and in mobile commerce. The ECB has signed agreements with the European Card Payment Cooperation, nexo standards and the Berlin Group to reuse established European technical standards for digital euro payments. This should minimise adoption costs. Co-badging would add to these benefits. Banks could integrate the digital euro into existing cards or mobile applications alongside their own payment solutions. Where a private solution is accepted, it could remain the preferred option. Where coverage is incomplete, the digital euro would step in to ensure that private solution users can still pay. A sustainable economic model The digital euro is also being designed with a sustainable economic model in mind. The Eurosystem would bear the costs of establishing and operating its core infrastructure and would not charge any scheme or processing fees for digital euro transactions. Banks and payment service providers would be compensated for the services they provide. The precise arrangements are currently being discussed as part of the legislative process. The digital euro is not therefore simply a new public payment instrument. It would provide public infrastructure that can help private European solutions scale up, offer value-added services and compete more effectively Europe-wide. Safeguarding financial stability Whenever a central bank proposes a digital form of money, a legitimate question arises: could deposits leave banks, impairing their capacity to provide credit? We have taken this question very seriously. The digital euro is being designed as a means of payment, not an investment product. It would not be remunerated, and individual holdings would be subject to limits. Users would be able to link their digital euro holdings to a commercial bank account. A waterfall mechanism would allow users to make payments exceeding their digital euro balance by drawing the difference from that account. A reverse-waterfall mechanism could be used to automatically transfer to the linked bank account incoming amounts above the holding limit – or an even lower threshold if the customer so wishes. Behavioural research suggests that this approach could drive up digital euro adoption while reducing individual holdings.[1] The limits will have to be calibrated to balance three objectives: making the digital euro convenient to use, safeguarding financial stability and preserving the smooth implementation and transmission of monetary policy. Detailed analysis supports these safeguards.[2] At the request of the European Parliament, the ECB examined the possible effects of hypothetical holding limits from €500 to €3,000 on the balance sheets of 2,025 banks, including both significant and less significant institutions. It considered two scenarios: business-as-usual and flight-to-safety. The flight-to-safety scenario is an extreme tail scenario that has not occurred over the first 25 years of the euro. It also assumes no monetary policy response, although a crisis of this sort would normally lead the central bank to consider taking action. The results are reassuring under both scenarios. Under the business-as-usual scenario the introduction of the digital euro is projected to have an extremely contained impact on banks’ liquidity and funding metrics. Indeed, digitalisation itself supports bank deposits, as payments migrate from cash to deposit-based instruments. Our analysis estimates a potential €127 billion deposit inflow by 2034, equivalent to 0.4% of banking sector assets or 1.5% of retail sight deposits. At aggregate level, this exceeds the estimated digital euro-related outflows in the business-as-usual scenario for holding limits up to and including €3,000. No aggregate outflow would thus be recorded.[3] If we disregard the deposit inflows resulting from the continuing decline in the use of cash, the aggregate liquidity coverage ratio would fall only slightly, from 166% to 163%, for a limit of €3,000. The aggregate net stable funding ratio would decline from 128% to 127%. The extreme scenario also produces manageable results, even when we take a very conservative view and ignore the trend towards digitalisation. On aggregate, regulatory liquidity metrics remain well above 100%. With a holding limit of €3,000, the liquidity coverage ratio falls to 100% for only 13 banks, representing 0.3% of total banking sector assets. And only nine of those, representing 0.1% of total banking sector assets, would be at risk of liquidity buffers going below that level. These findings must be interpreted within the scope and assumptions of the analysis. The figures are illustrative and do not represent a decision on the eventual holding limit. But the conclusion is clear: within the range assessed, holding limits are effective in containing deposit outflows and safeguarding financial stability. The digital euro is therefore not designed to disintermediate banks. It is designed to safeguard their role as the monetary system becomes increasingly digital. It is also worth noting that the discussion about the financial stability implications of the digital euro often disregards the fact that people can already easily and instantly transfer their deposits from bank accounts to other entities, where – unlike with the digital euro – they may be remunerated, unlimited or denominated in foreign currencies. Where the project stands So where do we stand? The legislative process is advancing. The Council of the European Union agreed on its position in December 2025, the European Parliament adopted its position in July 2026 and the trilogue negotiations are now under way. The European Council has called for the negotiations to be concluded by the end of this year. The Governing Council of the ECB will only decide whether to issue a digital euro after the legislation has been adopted. Assuming the legislative process is fully concluded by the end of 2026, we aim to be ready for a potential first issuance in 2029. But technical preparation must advance in parallel. The digital euro pilot is planned to begin in the second half of 2027 and run for 12 months. We have selected 36 payment service providers from across the euro area, following a call that attracted more than 50 applications.[4] Last week, the selected providers and the Eurosystem met to start work on the next stage. The objective is not merely to try out the technology. A payment system is an ecosystem, involving service providers, merchants, central banks, infrastructure operators and users. The pilot will allow that ecosystem to test the design, learn from experience and identify areas for improvement. On 15 September we opened a call for e-commerce and mobile-commerce merchants to take part in the pilot. Participants will test customer payment journeys, assess integration with existing checkout systems and provide feedback on the user experience.[5] Moreover, the digital euro is not intended just to fix any shortcomings in the existing euro area payments landscape. It is also an opportunity to think about the future and provide a platform to innovate, to enhance the quality and breadth of payment services. New opportunities are emerging, and we want to make sure that European payment service providers are fully equipped to seize them and gain a strong competitive edge. Last week we therefore launched a new wave of activities through the digital euro innovation platform, building on an initial exercise that involved around 70 market participants.[6] One workstream will experiment with integrated electronic receipts, payments involving multiple payers or recipients, conditional payments and new features offered through payment apps. A second workstream will look further ahead, exploring developments that could enhance digital euro payments in the future. This includes possible applications of artificial intelligence, such as AI-enabled payments or micropayments. The workstream will also explore digital euro use in public services, including payments for transportation, mobility and parking services or payments to and from public authorities. We cannot know precisely how Europeans will want to pay in 20 years’ time. But we can build a foundation that is open to innovation, robust enough to earn public trust and able to develop as users' needs evolve. Tokenisation and the future of finance Let me now turn to wholesale markets. Tokenisation can bring issuance, trading, clearing, settlement, custody and asset servicing into a shared digital environment. Smart contracts can automate coupon payments, collateral movements and compliance checks. Cash and assets can be exchanged atomically, meaning that either both legs of a transaction are settled together or neither is. The potential benefits include greater automation, faster settlement, lower processing costs and more efficient use of liquidity and collateral. But these benefits will only materialise fully if tokenised markets have access to a safe and scalable settlement asset. Pontes: central bank money for tokenised finance This is why the Eurosystem launched Pontes on 21 September. Pontes enables wholesale transactions in tokenised assets to be settled in central bank money. It connects market DLT platforms with Eurosystem services. It is an operational service that banks, market infrastructures, issuers and investors can use to expand safely into digital finance. The service will be enhanced progressively in line with market needs and technological developments, for instance by extending operating hours and offering immediate settlement finality on the Eurosystem DLT platform. Full implementation is expected by mid-2028, when we plan to offer a 24/7 service as well as greater programmability, state-of-the-art resilience and multi-currency capability. Appia: shaping the wider ecosystem Appia looks further in the future. Appia addresses the architecture, standards and governance required for an integrated European tokenised financial ecosystem. It covers asset interoperability, collateral management, tokenised central bank money infrastructure, cross-border transactions, resilience and interaction with the legal framework. The work on Appia is based on analysis, experimentation and cooperation between the Eurosystem and other central banks and private market participants. Our goal is to deliver a blueprint in 2028. The market is already actively involved in this work. The public consultation on the Appia roadmap received 127 responses, and 90% of respondents made at least one proposal to contribute. Our market contact group, comprising 61 entities chosen from among the more than 100 that applied, will provide continuous input and direction for the work.[7] We also plan to run concrete work involving teams that bring together market participants, national central banks and the ECB. The guiding principle is straightforward: we should lay the foundations of an integrated European digital finance ecosystem before incompatible systems become entrenched. For banks, this means access to an ecosystem in which they can issue tokenised deposits, provide custody services and asset servicing, mobilise collateral and develop programmable financial products across a European market. Together, Pontes and Appia can help European banks keep pace with the transformation of global finance, while avoiding dependence on foreign infrastructures or settlement assets denominated in foreign currencies. Supporting tokenised deposits across banks Pontes and Appia are also important for the future of commercial bank money. Tokenised central bank money is not intended to crowd out tokenised commercial bank deposits. On the contrary, it can provide the settlement anchor that allows tokenised deposits to develop safely and achieve scale. This is because it will enable deposits issued by different banks to be exchanged. Without central bank money, commercial bank money would fragment into separate tokens circulating within closed networks. This would give a built-in advantage to the largest international bank. Our approach is to preserve, in the tokenised environment, the principle that applies today: a euro issued by one regulated bank should be exchangeable at par with a euro issued by another. Pontes can thus be the bridge between private settlement assets, enabling tokenised deposits to be transferred between banks. Conclusion Let me conclude. We are modernising public money and public infrastructure so that private innovation can flourish on a stable and integrated foundation. The digital euro would give banks access to common standards and a pan-European acceptance network. It would help them maintain customer relationships, develop value-added services and compete more effectively across borders. And it would incorporate safeguards, supported by detailed analysis, protecting bank intermediation and financial stability. When it comes to digital finance, we are front-runners. Pontes is already making central bank money available for tokenised transactions. Appia looks ahead to an ecosystem in which tokenised central bank money, tokenised deposits and other regulated assets can coexist and interact across institutions and networks without friction. Together, these initiatives serve one objective: a European financial system that is innovative, integrated, resilient and internationally competitive. We will build it together. The history of money is one of continuous adaptation. Our task is to preserve what makes money trustworthy as technology evolves. That is the role of central banks in the digital age. And by playing that role in close partnership with market participants, we can ensure that the digital transformation strengthens Europe’s financial system and benefits all Europeans. Thank you. Garcia, T., Lambert, C., Pancaro, C., Rimbaud, C. and Soldà, A. (2026), “When Less Is More: Behavioural Effects of CBDC Holding Limits”, Working Paper Series, ECB, forthcoming. ECB (2025), Technical data on the financial stability impact of the digital euro, October. The model results indicate that only a few banks would lack sufficient excess reserves to sustain their preferred liquidity buffers. Among these, most would borrow from the interbank market, while banks without market access would be able to borrow from the central bank, as they retain sufficient unencumbered collateral. ECB (2026), “ECB selects 36 payment service providers to join digital euro pilot”, press release, 14 July; see also the ECB’s digital euro pilot webpage. ECB (2026), “Call for online and mobile merchants to participate in digital euro pilot now open”, press release, 15 September. ECB (2026), “Call for expressions of interest in a new wave of digital euro innovation platform activities”, MIP News, 28 September. ECB (2026), “Eurosystem selects members for the Appia contact group”, press release, 19 August. state: - SPEECH Ensuring resilience in the face of uncertainty Keynote speech by Frank Elderson, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB and Vice-Chair of the Supervisory Board of the ECB, at the ECB-Bank of England Conference on supervising climate risk in a non-linear world Frankfurt am Main, 14 October 2026 It is a pleasure to open this joint ECB-Bank of England conference. Bringing together experts across disciplines from 18 countries and three continents to discuss how we can ensure resilience in an increasingly non-linear world, this event could hardly be more timely. For much of modern finance, risk management has rested on a simple but consequential assumption: with enough data, sufficient information about borrower behaviour, robust models and a solid understanding of historical patterns, banks can estimate the losses they may face with a reasonable degree of precision. These estimates inform how banks price risk, set aside provisions for expected losses and determine how much capital they need to absorb any large, unexpected losses. This approach works well when the underlying relationships are broadly stable and has long served as a useful basis for managing financial risks. And of course, today’s modelling is already supplemented by additional layers of risk management, including model overlays, stress testing, underwriting, risk appetite setting and other processes. But the world facing us today is becoming more complex, more interconnected and more uncertain almost by the day. Think about geopolitical fragmentation, demographic change, artificial intelligence and quantum computing and, of course, the central theme of this conference: the risks from the ongoing climate and nature (C&N) crises. These macro trends differ in many respects. They differ in origin. They differ in scope. They differ in speed. Yet they all share a common denominator: they arise in complex and highly interconnected systems, which often exhibit non-linear behaviour. This means that small changes can spread and trigger disproportionately large effects. These macro trends can amplify shocks through feedback loops. They can lead to abrupt transitions through tipping points. Events that were considered remote tail risks yesterday are moving closer to tomorrow’s baseline. Addressing non-linearities is undoubtedly challenging but still manageable as long as we remain in the realm of what is measurable. However, an even bigger challenge arises when we enter a world characterised by what Frank Knight termed uncertainty, as distinct from risk, or what John Kay and Mervyn King later popularised as radical uncertainty.[1] The underlying idea is the same: a form of uncertainty in which future events, their probabilities and even the relevant outcomes cannot be measured with any meaningful degree of confidence. Today I would like to use a simple framework to explore this challenge. The distinction between what we know, what we know we don’t know, and what we don’t even know we don’t know. Or put differently: known knowns, known unknowns and unknown unknowns. The world we know: the known knowns of C&N risks Let me begin with what we already know about C&N risks. Over the past decade, banks and supervisors have made substantial progress in identifying, quantifying and managing C&N risks.[2] Together, we have built the foundational architecture needed to capture the known knowns of C&N risks in risk management, stress testing and scenario analysis.[3] Today, we not only see and feel the effects of rising temperatures; increasingly, we can measure them. Thanks to better tools, better data and better modelling, we are increasingly able to quantify the direct damage caused to the economy by C&N risks.[4] Just think about the heavy toll this summers’ extreme weather took on economic activity, labour productivity[5] and supply chains.[6] Importantly, we also increasingly understand the transmission channels to the financial risk categories facing banks. For example, with better climate hazard and geo-location data, banks can better model the financial impacts of droughts and flooding on traditional financial risk metrics such as loss given default (LGD). We know banks’ initial estimate of the impact of different transition scenarios on their capital position. And we also know that since 2022 the average share of interest income earned from carbon-intensive sectors by significant supervised banks has remained consistently above 70%. We know the average energy performance of the properties they finance. We know what share of exposures they have in areas vulnerable to physical risk and what proportion of those exposures, in turn, has deteriorating credit quality. While many of these impacts still rely on estimates, banks have made significant strides in recent years, thanks also to the availability of public data sources, which cover an increasing number of physical risk hazards.[7] But as important as this progress is, it only tells part of the story.[8] We know that many of the C&N risks that matter most are, by their very nature, forward-looking. And we know that because these risks are very different from past events, they are not fully understood and remain difficult to quantify. The progress made so far therefore provides a springboard for a more difficult, but necessary conversation: a conversation about some of the fundamental challenges of these risks and uncertainty, a conversation not only about what we know, but also about what we know we do not yet know. What remains uncertain: the known unknowns of C&N risks And that brings me to the second category in our framework: the known unknowns. These are risks that we know exist, but whose timing, magnitude or probabilities remain uncertain. This is not a new challenge. Economic forecasting operates in a similar environment. The economy, like the climate, is a complex adaptive system. We cannot forecast it with precision, but we can explore plausible scenarios and assess our resilience against them. C&N risks provide several examples: We know that tipping points exist but we do not know exactly when they will be reached. Worryingly, scientists have identified several components of the Earth system for which the tipping point may already be approaching, including the dieback of the Amazon rainforest and the collapse of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation. We also know that compound events can amplify impact. We do not know precisely how such interactions will unfold. A severe drought will likely occur alongside a heatwave. Water scarcity could coincide with a major agricultural disruption. Physical damage could occur simultaneously with pressures on energy systems.[9] And we know that nature degradation can affect economic activity through complex and interconnected channels. We know that humanity is living well beyond most of its planetary boundaries.[10] In fact, seven of the nine planetary boundaries have already been transgressed. What remains uncertain is how these forces may interact, amplify each other and ultimately propagate through the economy and the financial system. In all these examples we run into a fundamental problem: the future impacts of climate change and nature degradation are, by definition, not reflected in the historical data used in traditional risk analysis. Using scenario analysis to address known unknowns When dealing with uncertainty, scenario analysis is an indispensable tool. Scenarios are best understood not as forecasts, but rather as structured explorations of plausible futures. Their purpose is not to tell us what will happen, but to help us think more systematically about what could happen. They allow us to identify vulnerabilities, test assumptions and investigate transmission channels that may otherwise remain hidden. Encouragingly, climate scenario analysis has advanced considerably in recent years. The Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) scenarios have become the global reference point for assessing how climate change may affect economies and financial systems over both short and long horizons. These scenarios have evolved to encompass a wider range of risks while also providing financial projections. By offering a publicly accessible set of scenarios, they have significantly improved the capacity of the central banking community to quantify climate risks in a consistent, transparent and comparable manner across jurisdictions. But scenarios are a starting point, not an endpoint. When facing uncertainty, we need to avoid a scenario “tunnel vision’’ where risk identification and capital planning becomes anchored to a narrow set of scenario narratives. With heightened uncertainty, the objective of scenarios should not only be to explore baseline pathways, but also to investigate how vulnerabilities might be exposed under extreme yet plausible conditions. And we know that the current climate scenarios have their limitations. As Simon Sharpe has observed, scientists are trained not to overstate risks, while risk managers are trained not to underestimate them. This distinction also matters for climate models designed by scientists. These models capture what can be quantified robustly, but not necessarily everything scientists know is likely to occur. Take thawing permafrost, for example. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) concludes with high confidence that further warming will cause further thaw, thus releasing more carbon. Yet most global climate models do not represent this feedback directly. The separate adjustment used in the latest assessment still excludes abrupt thaw and interactions with Arctic wildfires. Research suggests that nature’s own emissions from thawing permafrost or wildfires could add as much as 0.6°C in an adverse scenario.[11] Similar limitations apply to additional emissions from warming wetlands and freshwater systems. Moreover, local transmission channels often differ substantially from global averages. The prudent conclusion is therefore to recognise that even the best available projections cannot yet fully capture every piece of relevant feedback, including some that are already well established. This is precisely why scenario analysis matters. Scenarios need to be tailored to local contexts, challenged and complemented with expert judgement. This is also why the NGFS encourages a more thoughtful and decision-relevant use of scenarios, rather than seeing climate scenarios as a box-ticking exercise.[12] Scenarios must be applied, not just adopted. They must be challenged, not just run. Many banks are still at a relatively early stage of integrating C&N risks into their core risk models. As a result, climate stress tests and scenario analysis are often used in the internal capital adequacy assessment process (ICAAP) primarily to calibrate buffers for risks that would otherwise not be covered. Yet these exercises only cover all the risk drivers that banks themselves deem material in around 15% of cases. At the same time, all the limitations and underestimations I have just mentioned also apply. It is therefore increasingly important that banks demonstrate a clear understanding of these limitations and that they take action early to build resilience and reduce their vulnerability to these growing risks over time. Scenarios must evolve, which requires a culture of continuous improvement, regular updates and close interaction between supervisors, practitioners and the research community. And that is precisely where this conference – which brings together experts across disciplines spanning the scientific and supervisory community – is invaluable because it can help to address some challenging questions. For example, how should supervisors and banks adapt scenario analysis in a world where uncertainty, non-linearity and tipping points cannot be fully captured by models? We look forward to hearing input you may have on the most effective ways to communicate model limitations, broaden the range of scenarios considered, and ensure climate risk assessments remain decision-relevant despite deep uncertainty. Or what role do expert judgement and tail-focused scenarios play in complementing quantitative analysis, and which risks require greater attention at the system level rather than at the institution level? And how can C&N risk analysis be translated into bank risk management, strategic decision-making and supervisory actions where banks underestimate risks? Radical uncertainty: building resilience for the unknown unknowns of the climate and nature crises Scenarios are well suited to exploring known unknowns, but they are less able to address radical uncertainty. This brings me to the third category: genuine unknown unknowns. The challenge with unknown unknowns is not only that we struggle to estimate probabilities or magnitudes, but that we do not yet know all the relevant states of the world and possible outcomes. We don’t even know what all the complex interactions between climate systems, ecosystems, societies and financial markets will be, so there’s no way we can actually measure them. We don’t yet know about all the complex feedback loops that only become visible once a shock unfolds. And we do not yet know about all the transmission channels that only emerge once critical thresholds have been crossed. But worryingly, there is growing evidence that the climate and nature crises are unfolding faster and more severely than expected, which may indicate that some of the complex interactions I mentioned might be coming our way sooner than we thought: Consider that the Arctic is warming at almost four times and Europe at roughly twice the global average,[13] while the most intense rainfall events are in some cases increasing faster than conventional climate models have captured. The Earth is also accumulating heat at a rate that recent observations suggest is higher than many model simulations anticipated.[14] In September the United Nations warned that El Niño is colliding with an already exceptionally warm planet, creating what it described as “being supersized before our eyes”.[15] Ocean heat has reached record levels, and the pace of ocean warming over the past two decades has been markedly faster than in earlier periods, suggesting that the earth's capacity to absorb excess heat may be changing in ways that we don’t fully understand.[16] Similarly, ecosystems are losing resilience, in some cases faster than earlier assessments anticipated.[17] Coral reefs, forests and wetlands are under growing pressure, weakening nature’s capacity to absorb shocks and increasing the risk of cascading impacts across ecological and economic systems. Until recently, many of these developments were poorly understood. Others may become visible only as shocks unfold and previously hidden interactions emerge. Their complex interactions cannot be fully anticipated, let alone incorporated into scenarios that capture every interaction across the climate, ecosystems, economies and financial markets. This brings us back to Simon Sharpe’s distinction. Scientific rigour requires caution in describing what cannot yet be demonstrated. Risk management requires similar caution in assuming that what cannot yet be modelled can be safely ignored. This is the realm of radical uncertainty rather than measurable risk. And repeated surprises on the upside should make us cautious about assuming that what remains unknown will be benign. The answer to unknown unknowns is therefore not just scenarios or risk modelling, but to build resilience against surprises. Resilience is not something we build after a disaster. Instead, it is something we invest in before shocks occur. Building resilience obviously includes maintaining sufficient capital, liquidity, operational capacity and strategic flexibility to absorb shocks that cannot be predicted in advance. But it is also about having a well-developed and risk-sensitive reaction function. This includes actively reflecting on what further role other layers of risk management, including underwriting, model overrides, risk appetite setting, portfolio steering and pricing could play. It also includes reflecting on the range of risk mitigants, such as insurance protection and governments’ more limited fiscal space to act as insurers of last resort. It also includes reflecting on climate adaptation and mitigation investment, and on how these investments can be deployed effectively to address longer-term risks. It also includes banks testing their reaction function regularly through scenarios and analysis of business model resilience to ensure their governance and decision-making structures are capable of responding swiftly when the risk landscape changes. This is at the heart of prudential transition planning.[18] Lessons for other macro trends subject to uncertainty And this brings me to my final point. Climate and nature-related risks are perhaps the clearest manifestation of non-linear dynamics and heightened uncertainty. But they are far from being the only one. The insights from addressing these challenges in climate risk are also relevant for other macro trends and risk drivers affecting banks, such as technological innovation, demographic change and geopolitical risks, to name just a few. As European banking supervision highlighted in its 2026-28 supervisory priorities, heightened uncertainty is a cross-cutting challenge spanning several risk areas, making the likelihood of extreme tail risks unprecedently high. Similarly to C&N risks, tackling these trends will require interdisciplinary cooperation well beyond prudential authorities. Take demography as a structural risk driver.[19] Now that supervisors have learned to analyse the drivers of C&N risk, they can build on the progress to interpret demographic trajectories as a structural risk driver affecting banks’ business models and risk profiles. Take rapid advances in artificial intelligence that have increased cyber and operational resilience risks. We know that these developments are already altering the cyber risk landscape, but we do not yet know the exact magnitude with which they will unfold. This is a classic known unknown for which backward-looking information alone is not useful. Yet this does not prevent supervisors from taking action.[20] Or take quantum computing as an example of a technology with non-linear effects. Quantum risk to cryptography is already a risk given that sensitive, encrypted information can be collected today and stored with the expectation that future technological advances may allow it to be decrypted in a “harvest now, decrypt later” fashion, leading to non-linear consequences. All these macro trends have a common denominator: uncertainty. There is uncertainty about the timing, impact, transmission channels and consequently the data and modelling challenges.[21] All of these macro trends could also have an impact on the sustainability of banks’ business models. They therefore all need an upscaled risk management framework, with scenario capabilities as a core pillar to help banks stay resilient and competitive over time. Conclusion Let me conclude. For much of modern finance, risk management has focused on understanding and measuring risks. That remains indispensable. But in an increasingly complex and interconnected world, building resilience requires more than that. If risk management is like driving along a winding mountain road, preparedness is not just about being able to react when a cliff suddenly appears. It is about having guardrails and contingency measures in place for when the road may veer dangerously close to the edge. For known knowns, our task is to measure. For known unknowns, our task is to prepare. And for unknown unknowns, our task is to build resilience. When reality repeatedly surprises us on the upside, prudence requires us to be careful about assuming that the risks we have not yet identified will somehow be benign. This conference, which brings together experts across disciplines, is an opportunity to deepen our understanding on all three fronts: on where we can sharpen our focus on what we can already identify and quantify, on where we need to further illuminate uncertainties that warrant further exploration, and on where we can strengthen resilience to weather radical uncertainty. Thank you for your attention and I look forward to the fruitful discussion. Kay, J. and King, M. (2020), Radical Uncertainty: Decision-making for an Unknowable Future, The Bridge Street Press. For more details on banks’ better preparedness to identify, quantify and manage C&N risks, see Elderson, F. (2025), “Banks have made good progress in managing climate and nature risks – and must continue”, The Supervision Blog, ECB, 11 July; and Elderson, F. (2025), “From charting the course to staying the course: the path ahead for climate and nature risk supervision”, keynote speech at the ECB industry dialogue on “Climate and nature risk management: taking stock and looking ahead”, Frankfurt am Main, 1 October. For more information about the increasingly sophisticated methods and tools developed by banks and shared by ECB Banking Supervision with banks across Europe, please see Elderson, F. (2026), “Good practices for advancing climate and nature-related risk management”, The Supervision Blog, ECB, 8 May; ECB (2026), Good practices for climate and nature risk management. Observations from the ECB’s five-year climate and nature risk programme (2020-25), May; and ECB (2026), ECB report on good practices for climate and nature-related risk stress testing, May. This year’s droughts are already imposing significant economic costs across Europe. Initial estimates point to losses of at least €50 billion in the short term alone. The insurance firm Allianz estimates cumulative GDP losses of up to 7% between 2026 and 2030 in major European economies, equivalent to around USD 240 billion for France, USD 147 billion for Italy, USD 131 billion for Germany and USD 120 billion for Spain. For further details, see Allianz (2026), Too hot to grow. The economic costs of extreme heat, 28 May. According to United Nations estimates, workers' productivity declines by around 2% to 3% for every additional degree of heat above certain thresholds. Estimates suggest that the June heatwave alone may have resulted in €6.3 billion in productivity losses in Germany. For further details, see the World Health Organization’s web page on workplace heat stress. The exceptionally low water levels of the Rhine this summer, the lowest since records began in 1880, have not only disrupted transport and industrial production. They could also reduce Germany's economic recovery by up to 0.2 percentage points of GDP in the third quarter. In Romania, Hungary and France, low river levels have even disrupted electricity generation, affecting both nuclear and hydropower production. See Network for Greening the Financial System (2025), Leveraging physical climate risk data, September. Despite the notable strides made by banks under ECB supervision in integrating C&N risks into their risk management procedures, more still needs to be done to ensure they apply sound practices across all material portfolios, exposures and risk categories. For example, some banks may focus only on transition risks but not on physical risks – and vice versa – in certain portfolios. Some prudential transmission channels, such as operational or market risk, receive far less attention compared with credit risk. Furthermore, not all banks have included all material risk drivers, relevant portfolios or transmission channels in their C&N risk management. For more details on the lack of comprehensive coverage see Elderson, F. (2025), “Banks have made good progress in managing climate and nature risks – and must continue”, The Supervision Blog, ECB, 11 July The experience of a major German car manufacturer is a case in point. Back in 2024 flooding damaged an upstream aluminium supplier in Switzerland, disrupting production further down the supply chain. The flood itself was a known physical hazard. The broader consequence – namely, disruptions cascading through interconnected production networks – was much harder to model. For further details, see Arnold, M. and Dempsey, H (2024), “Porsche warns on profits as flooding hits aluminium supplier”, Financial Times, 23 July. See the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research’s web page on Planetary Boundaries – defining a safe operating space for humanity. Dinneen, J. (2026), “A Missing Piece in Climate Models: Nature’s Own Emissions”, Yale Environment 360, 18 June. NGFS (2026), Guide to climate scenario analysis for central banks and supervisors – 2025 version, 24 September. Rantanen, M., Karpechko, A.Y., Lipponen, A. et al. (2022), ”The Arctic has warmed nearly four times faster than the globe since 1979”, Communications Earth and Environment, 11 August; and World Meteorological Organization (2025), European State of the Climate – Report 2024, 15 April. Hodnebrog, Ø., Myhre, G., Jouan, C., et al. (2024). “Recent reductions in aerosol emissions have increased Earth’s energy imbalance”, Communications Earth and Environment, 3 April. https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/el-nino-set-become-very-strong-raising-risks-of-extreme-weather-2027 World Meteorological Organization (2025), State of the Global Climate 2024, 19 March. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (2022), “Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability”, Working Group II contribution to the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, 28 February. For more information about prudential transition planning as a key tool for managing risk along a range of possible pathways but also for capitalising on business opportunities, see Elderson, F. (2026), “Good practices for advancing climate and nature-related risk management”, The Supervision Blog, ECB, 8 May. Montagner, P. (2025), “Europe’s demographic shift: what could it mean for banking supervision?”, The Supervision Blog, ECB, 25 November. Buch, C. (2026), “Addressing AI-enabled cybersecurity threats”, letter to the CEO of the significant institution, European Banking Supervision, Frankfurt am Main, 7 July; and Financial Stability Board (2026), “FSB Chair warns of risks arising from frontier Artificial Intelligence (AI) models”, press release, 31 August. See also Angeloni, I. and Claessens, S. (2026), “An EU Prudential Framework for Slow-Burning Risk Drivers”, European Parliament, September, for more about slow-burning risk drivers (SBRDs), which are factors that build up risks incrementally over time, adversely affecting the viability of banks beyond normal supervisory timelines.
