state: The Federal Trade Commission has taken steps to preserve competition in the digital advertising ecosystem by requiring Publicis Groupe S.A. to continue providing neutral and nondiscriminatory access to LiveRamp Holdings Inc.’s products and services, and to establish firewalls to prevent Publicis from accessing LiveRamp’s customer data, in order to complete Publicis’s acquisition of the company. The proposed consent order would address the FTC’s concerns that Publicis’s acquisition of LiveRamp, which provides data connectivity services that help facilitate the secure and confidential movement of data used for digital advertising, would harm competition in the markets for media agency services and audience data services. Under the $2.2 billion deal, Publicis, which provides media agency services including media planning and buying for digital advertising campaigns, would acquire 100% of LiveRamp. The deal would likely result in Publicis having the ability and incentive to foreclose customers of competing media agency service providers by using its control of LiveRamp to push customers to switch their media agency business to Publicis even if those customers otherwise prefer competing media agencies, according to the FTC’s complaint. “By requiring LiveRamp to continue operating as it does today as a neutral platform, this order will ensure that Publicis does not gain an unfair advantage over its competitors in the digital advertising marketplace,” said David Shaw, Principal Deputy Director of the FTC’s Bureau of Competition. “The FTC’s action today ensures that the digital advertising marketplace can continue to grow and evolve without risking harm to competition.” LiveRamp is the leading data connectivity provider in the U.S. media marketing ecosystem and the only provider with a full spectrum of data connectivity services. Publicis is the largest among the five major advertising agencies in the United States. It also provides audience data services through its Epsilon subsidiary that help companies target their advertising to particular audiences. The FTC alleged that combining Publicis and LiveRamp would decrease competition in the relevant markets for media agency services and audience data services in violation of Section 7 of the Clayton Act. The FTC also alleged Publicis would deny or degrade access to LiveRamp services on which competitors rely, which would lead to higher costs and lower quality services for customers of competing digital advertising services. In addition, the FTC alleged that under the deal Publicis would gain access to competitively sensitive data of non-Publicis clients serviced by LiveRamp, which Publicis would leverage to pressure those clients to switch to Publicis. Under the proposed order, Publicis and LiveRamp, for five years, are required to: - Provide non-discriminatory access and support on fair and reasonable terms to LiveRamp’s standalone products and services and are prohibited from denying, degrading, delaying or impairing LiveRamp customers’ continued access to LiveRamp’s standalone products and services - Establish firewalls to ensure that Publicis does not access or use LiveRamp customer data and confidential business information that it receives from a customer’s use of LiveRamp’s standalone products and services - Appoint an independent auditor to audit the company’s compliance with the proposed contractual commitments every six months for the first two years after the date that the proposed transaction closes, and then once a year thereafter for the following three years The order also provides additional protections for LiveRamp customers, including a requirement that Publicis shall not retaliate against customers that discuss compliance concerns with the Commission. Under the order, LiveRamp customers also have the option to request an audit of Publicis’s compliance with the data protection, privacy and security obligations as applied to the requesting customer. The order also provides for third-party mediation of contractual compliance disputes that remain unresolved after 30 days. The Commission vote to issue the complaint and accept the consent agreement for public comment was 2-0. The public will have 30 days to submit comments on the proposed consent agreement package. Instructions for filing comments appear on the docket. Once processed, they will be posted on Regulations.gov. NOTE: The Commission issues an administrative complaint when it has “reason to believe” that the law has been or is being violated and it appears to the Commission that a proceeding is in the public interest. state: The Federal Trade Commission today announced Greenway Auto Group has agreed that its price advertisements will prominently include the actual price a consumer must pay for a vehicle, excluding only charges the government requires consumers to pay, to settle the Commission’s lawsuit alleging the company advertised prices that were thousands of dollars below what it actually charged. In addition to requiring price transparency and prohibiting deceptive prize mailers, the proposed order prohibits specific misrepresentations, including whether charges, fees, taxes, products or services are optional or required and whether any type of or source for financing is required. “Truthful advertising in the auto industry is vital because purchasing a car is one of the most significant financial decisions consumers make,” said Christopher Mufarrige, Director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection. “Consumers can’t make informed choices when the actual price is hidden. Price transparency is critical to a properly functioning market and is a top priority for the Trump FTC.” According to the complaint, Greenway inflated the amount it charged the overwhelming majority of consumers by tacking on to the advertised price mandatory fees, packages and penalties that cost consumers thousands. The complaint alleges Greenway charged consumers more than $3,350, on average, over the advertised price in over 92% of transactions. The fees Greenway allegedly imposed on top of the advertised price included so-called administrative fees, dealer fees, delivery fees and processing fees. Greenway’s advertised prices at times also allegedly reflected conditional rebates and discounts available only to a subset of consumers. In addition, the FTC alleges Greenway lured consumers into dealerships with scam mailers representing that recipients had won thousands of dollars in cash prizes that could be collected at a Greenway dealership, but the prizes were not real. In a March 2026 letter, the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection warned Greenway about its misleading advertising practices, advising the company to ensure that the “price consumers see in advertising is the actual price they will pay.” According to the complaint, however, Greenway responded by adding false assurances of price transparency to their websites while continuing to advertise vehicles for thousands less than their actual prices. The Commission continues to promote price transparency across several markets, including grocery delivery, rental housing, sports and concert ticketing as well as auto sales and leasing. The Commission vote authorizing the staff to file the complaint and stipulated final order was 2-0. The FTC filed the complaint and stipulated final order in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida, Orlando Division. state: Albania – addressing irregular migration programme: call for proposals Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) invites organisations to submit proposals by 19 November 2026 for addressing irregular migration programme. 1. Introduction The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) invites eligible organisations to submit proposals under the Addressing Irregular Migration Programme [Bilateral] – Behavioural Insights and Social Norm Change for Migration Decision Making in Albania. The programme seeks to reduce irregular migration pressures from Albania by increasing the uptake of sustainable domestic economic, labour mobility, and reintegration opportunities, while strengthening informed migration decision-making and resilience within target communities. The programme will be delivered through an Accountable Grant Agreement following a competitive Call for Proposals process. Applicants should read this Invitation together with the accompanying Statement of Outcomes and application documentation. 2. Funding opportunity | Item | Detail | |---|---| | Funding mechanism | Accountable Grant Agreement | | Total funding available | Up to £750,000 | | Grant duration | December 2026 – March 2028 | | Geographic focus | Albania | | Primary beneficiaries | Potential migrants, returnees, and other individuals in target communities vulnerable to irregular migration from Albania to the United Kingdom | | Number of awards | FCDO reserves the right to award one or more grants | | Lead applicant eligibility | Not-for-profit organisations, civil society organisations, research institutions, international organisations and consortia | The final number and value of awards will depend on proposal quality, value for money and strategic fit. 3. Programme outcomes Applicants should set out how their proposal contributes to the following outcomes: Outcome 1: Improved understanding of migration decision-making drivers and engagement with domestic opportunities. Outcome 2: Stronger local engagement on behavioural and social influences on migration. Outcome 3: Effective behavioural and social norm approaches are identified, refined and assessed through testing and learning. Outcome 4: Evidence on effective interventions informs future programming and policy. Further information is provided in the accompanying Statement of Outcomes. 4. What we are looking for FCDO is seeking proposals that: - support informed migration decision-making and reduce drivers of irregular migration - strengthen existing systems rather than creating parallel structures - demonstrate a clear understanding of the Albanian context - are evidence-based and adaptive - deliver sustainable benefits beyond the grant period - demonstrate strong value for money - build effective partnerships with relevant stakeholders Applicants are encouraged to propose innovative approaches that contribute to the programme outcomes. 5. Eligibility requirements Applicants must: - be a legally registered organisation - have appropriate financial management and governance arrangements - demonstrate relevant organisational experience - be capable of receiving and managing grant funding - be able to comply with FCDO due diligence and safeguarding requirements Consortia are permitted. Where a consortium applies, a lead organisation must be identified. FCDO strongly encourages applications involving local Albanian organisations and institutions. 6. Proposal requirements Proposals should not exceed 10 pages excluding annexes and should include: Technical proposal Applicants should describe: - understanding of the behavioural, social, and economic factors shaping migration choices - proposed approach and theory of change - how the proposal contributes to programme outcomes - target beneficiaries and geographic focus - partnerships and stakeholder engagement - learning and adaptation approach - sustainability strategy - risk management and safeguarding arrangements FCDO expects bidders to propose a phased and adaptive delivery model. Initial delivery is expected to focus on behavioural diagnostics, stakeholder engagement, social norms analysis and intervention design, before progressing to the piloting, testing and refinement of promising approaches. Bidders should demonstrate how learning generated through implementation will be used to adapt interventions and generate practical evidence on what works, for whom and under what conditions. Budget Applicants must submit a detailed budget using the FCDO grant budget template. Budgets should clearly demonstrate how resources will contribute to outcomes and value for money. Supporting information Applicants should provide: - organisational profiles - consortium arrangements (where relevant) - relevant organisational experience - any additional information requested in the application template 7. Evaluation process Proposals will be assessed by an evaluation panel against the following criteria: | Criterion | Weighting | |---|---| | Strategic Fit and Contribution to Outcomes | 25% | | Quality of Proposed Approach and Outcomes | 25% | | Value for Money (4Es) | 20% | | Feasibility and Deliverability & Organisational Capability and Partnerships | 20% | | Risk Management and Safeguarding | 10% | | Total | 100% | All proposals will be scored using a 0-5 scoring scale and moderated by the evaluation panel. 8. Value for money Applicants should demonstrate how their proposal delivers value for money through: - economy: appropriate inputs secured at reasonable cost - efficiency: effective use of resources - effectiveness: likelihood of achieving outcomes - equity: reaching those most in need The budget narrative should clearly explain how value for money has been considered throughout the proposal. 9. Indicative timeline | Milestone | Date | |---|---| | Call for Proposals launched | 20 October 2026 | | Proposal submission deadline | 19 November 2026 | | Notification of outcome | 7 December 2026 | FCDO reserves the right to amend these dates and will communicate any changes to applicants. 10. Clarification questions All clarification questions should be submitted in writing to: British.EmbassyTirana@fcdo.gov.uk with [Clarifying Questions] Addressing Irregular Migration Programme [Bilateral] – Behavioural Insights and Social Norm Change for Migration Decision Making in Albania – Call for Proposals in the subject title by 12 November 2026. Responses will be shared with all applicants to ensure transparency and equal access to information. Applicants should not seek information from other FCDO staff concerning this opportunity. 11. Submission instructions Applications must be submitted electronically to: British.EmbassyTirana@fcdo.gov.uk with [Submission] Addressing Irregular Migration Programme [Bilateral] – Behavioural Insights and Social Norm Change for Migration Decision Making in Albania – Call for Proposals in the subject title. The submission should include: - technical proposal - completed budget template - required annexes Late submissions may not be considered. Please ensure that submission meets size and format criteria. The maximum message size that is allowed is 36 MB. This includes not only attachments but email itself as it reaches FCDO email system. Make sure to keep the overall size below the limit to ensure delivery of submission. It is responsibility of the applicant to send the submission in a timely manner and to check their email (including spam section) should they encounter delivery issues, and address them immediately, in such case. 12. Important information This Call for Proposals is conducted in accordance with FCDO’s Programme Operating Framework and Grants Standards. state: Reducing the risk of Ips typographus infestation at Whiligh Estate A Spruce Site Assessment (SSA) helped a historic Sussex estate to reduce bark beetle risk and plan a more resilient, productive woodland. Key facts - site: Whiligh Estate, East Sussex - type: priority spruce removal area with Norway spruce and Sitka spruce - size: 76-hectare site with 31.6 hectares surveyed, 688 tonnes of spruce for felling - felling method: a combination of clear fell, regeneration felling and isolated felling of individual trees using hand felling and harvester felling - species restocked: 9,100 trees at 1,100 stems per hectare, including wild cherry, wild service tree, red oak, Douglas fir, black walnut, English oak, hornbeam, sweet chestnut and common alder - grants: Spruce Site Assessment and tree health pilot (THP) scheme - timeframe: 13 working days from SSA application submission to agreement offered and 6 months to claim paid, 8.5 months to a live THP agreement Whiligh Estate’s legacy: from Westminster to Sutton Hoo Whiligh Estate is a private residential estate in the High Weald National Landscape, home to a wide range of woodland with a history stretching back over 600 years. The estate’s oldest and most famous contribution came in 1393, when King Richard II commissioned the hammerbeam roof for Westminster Hall. Whiligh’s mature pedunculate oaks provided the timber for this enormous, self-supporting structure, which remains to this day the largest medieval timber roof anywhere in Northern Europe. Twice since then, the Palace of Westminster has returned to Whiligh for help. The first occasion was in 1913, when deathwatch beetles had eaten into the original beams and new oak was needed to replace them. The second came after World War II, when the roof suffered serious damage during the Blitz and sections had to be rebuilt using timber felled at Whiligh once again. This tradition of supplying oak for significant national projects hasn’t stopped. In December 2024, the estate responded to an appeal for timber from the Sutton Hoo Ship’s Company project. Based in Woodbridge, Suffolk, the project is building a full-scale, working reconstruction of the seventh-century Anglo-Saxon burial ship discovered at Sutton Hoo, using traditional tools, authentic materials and the original archaeological findings as a guide. Assessing Whiligh Estate’s woodlands for Ips typographus risk Today, the estate’s woodlands face a new challenge. Whiligh lies within the proactive spruce removal Area, designated because of the heightened risk of Ips typographus (eight-toothed spruce bark beetle) incursion. The condition of the estate’s spruce varies significantly from healthy, resilient isolated trees to poor condition spruce crops that have had limited woodland management since planting due to access constraints and difficult terrain. In October 2025, the landowner’s forestry agent recommended applying for a Spruce Site Assessment. The agent reported that their experience of the SSA process was positive, saying that the application was straightforward and accessible, with clear guidance notes explaining exactly what information was needed and why. The timescale from submitting the application to receiving an agreement offer took just 13 working days. Crucially, the grant also funded the time needed to accurately map management and felling proposals, allowing the agent to give detailed, professional support throughout this planning process. Building on the existing woodland management plan The estate already had a woodland management plan in place. The SSA complements this by pinpointing the exact location and condition of spruce across the property, along with the operational constraints, environmental considerations and forestry operations that spruce removal would involve. A condition scoring system was used to clearly identify the condition of the spruce, helping with planning of felling and extraction. In total, the survey covered 31.6 hectares of the site, within which 4.3 hectares of Norway and Sitka spruce was identified. The survey also identified constraints the woodland management plan hadn’t accounted for. These included an active badger sett, watercourses and river placements, steep slopes and fencing that would need removing and replacing. Walking the site with a contractor to estimate costs for the work also helped identify felling constraints early, along with the risks, requirements and processes needed for effective timber and brash extraction. Laura Henderson, English Woodlands Forestry, said: To complete the SSA survey properly, we walked the site with a contractor. This helped with costing up the future works that might need to take place, meaning there were no surprises going into the tree health pilot. This level of detail wouldn’t have happened without the SSA grant. Clear data from the assessment led to confident decisions Spruce is a key productive part of Whiligh’s woodlands, so understanding the full implications of removing it mattered. The SSA gave the landowner exactly that through detailed mensuration data on timber volume, tonnage and stocking density, which fed directly into cost calculations for the THP. It identified around 700 tonnes of spruce suitable for felling, to be done through a mix of clear felling, regeneration felling and the removal of individual isolated trees. With this data, the landowner had a clear picture of likely costs, income and overall viability before committing to proactive removal of the spruce. That early clarity, combined with early contractor engagement, meant any unexpected costs and delays could be avoided once work began. The badger sett is a good example because the SSA flagged it early, so the necessary permissions and mitigation measures were all in place before any felling started. Josh Diplock, English Woodlands Forestry, said: The way the SSA assessed the Ips infestation threat and evaluated felling considerations was the key motivation for the landowner to act upon spruce removal, significantly reducing any future risk of Ips typographus infestation. Looking beyond spruce removal The SSA proved to be a valuable springboard into the next stage. Information gathered during the assessment supported a subsequent application for the THP proactive felling offer, helping to keep the project moving without losing momentum. Following a successful application, felling was proposed to start 8 to 9 months after completing the SSA, with restocking planned for the following planting season. The process also sparked wider conversations about managing the estate’s woodland, infrastructure and long-term resilience, extending well beyond spruce alone. It helped identify a range of opportunities and challenges, while raising awareness of the risks posed by Ips typographus and the consequences of leaving susceptible material unaddressed. One of the opportunities the survey identified was for permanent infrastructure improvements, including a loading bay measuring 237.5 metres2. Part funded by the THP grant, it will support woodland management and timber production long after the current spruce removal programme is complete. The estate’s long-term vision is to transform woodlands once dominated by spruce into something more resilient and productive, managed through continuous cover forestry. Once the spruce has been removed, around 9,100 trees are planned for restocking, including oak, Douglas fir and a range of other mixed broadleaves. The SSA grant covered every stage of the process, from surveying the spruce to planning the operations and costs involved, giving the landowner the confidence to make informed decisions about proactively removing the spruce. The result is a woodland that’s both safer and stronger. The risk of Ips typographus at Whiligh has been significantly reduced and poor-quality spruce is steadily being replaced with woodland designed for the future. Find out more about the Spruce Site Assessment and how to apply, along with information on grants for spruce at risk from Ips typographus in the proactive removal area. We also have guidance on Ips typographus, the demarcated area and how it affects woodlands.

state: Armed Forces, NHS and allies test UK battlefield injury response More than 100 military experts, clinicians and civil servants test plans to treat injured Armed Forces personnel during possible future operations. - The Armed Forces, NHS and international partners conduct UK medical resilience exercise. - Lessons from the war in Ukraine have been used to strengthen UK frontline care, medical resilience and innovation. - The exercise demonstrates the Strategic Defence Review’s whole-of-society approach to national security. The Armed Forces and the NHS took part in a joint exercise last week to strengthen the UK’s ability to treat Armed Forces personnel injured during conflict. The wargame, led by Defence Medical Command, explored how the Armed Forces, the NHS and healthcare providers would work together to support military patients returning to the UK from a range of future operational scenarios. Participants assessed plans for civilian health services to treat military patients returning to the UK after receiving life-saving care overseas at the point of injury and after potentially travelling vast distances. Defence Minister Lord Coaker said: Keeping people safe takes more than one organisation—it takes all of us working together. This exercise brought Defence, the NHS and our allies around the same table to put that partnership into practice. By testing our plans now, we are building the trusted relationships and readiness needed to protect our country and care for those who serve. They also explored medical lessons from Ukraine, including challenges for increasing hospital capacity, maintaining civilian access to health care, large-scale rehabilitation, likely injuries requiring treatment, and mental health care support. The exercise is part of an ongoing UK and international programme to ensure medical preparedness keeps pace with the changing character of warfare. Surgeon General Major General Phil Carter, said: Wargames like this are a vital part planning the Operational Patient Care Pathway, helping ensure Defence, NHS, our health services, and our allies can manage returning casualties while continuing to care for civilian patients. The war in Ukraine reinforces the need to keep learning, adapting and innovating. By regularly exercising together, we strengthen our readiness and national resilience. Dr Mike Prentice, National Director for NHS Resilience, said: The NHS has a vital role to play in the UK’s preparedness for future conflict. By working closely with the Ministry of Defence, we are putting our plans to the test, identifying potential challenges and strengthening the partnerships we would rely on in a crisis. Preparing together now means we can ensure the NHS is ready to care for military personnel returning home, while continuing to meet the needs of the public - whatever the circumstances. Part of routine preparedness planning, the exercise supports the Strategic Defence Review’s emphasis on resilience, readiness and a whole-of-society approach to national security. Defence Medical Command is investing in life-saving innovations, including dried blood products to more easily restore blood supplies on the battlefield, and tranexamic acid autoinjector pens which cause clotting to reduce blood loss at the point of injury, as well as modern field hospital equipment and enhanced equipment to care for casualties. Defence Medical Command is also learning lessons from the conflict in Ukraine including techniques to protect field hospitals, equipment and medical personnel from attack, advanced trauma training, stronger supply chains and the development of new technologies such as portable ultrasound equipment and uncrewed evacuation systems. Lessons from the wargame will inform future planning across the Armed Forces and civilian health services, with further exercises scheduled in the coming months. Notes to editors: Imagery of the event can be found here: 2026.10.15 RAMP Wargame - Defence Imagery

state: Serious offenders detained in hospital will no longer receive benefits Convicted killers and serious sexual offenders detained in hospital are among those who will lose their entitlement to benefits under regulations laid in Parliament today. - Serious offenders detained for treatment under a Hospital Order will no longer receive taxpayer-funded benefits worth hundreds of pounds a month. - Change ends “double provision,” whereby offenders have their living costs met by the NHS while also claiming benefits at the taxpayer’s expense. - Follows direct engagement with victims’ families who campaigned to close the loophole and a range of experts. Under the current system, an offender can be paid over £800 a month in Universal Credit – amounting to thousands in taxpayer cash over several years. The proposed change is expected to save tens of millions of pounds each year. As part of ongoing action to put fairness back at the heart of the welfare system, this intervention will stop hundreds of offenders receiving benefits from early next year – those already in hospital and future cases. Those transferred to mental health hospitals from prison are already banned from claiming. The regulations laid today will extend this to mental health hospital patients that are guilty of a dozen serious offences – focusing on violent and sexual offences. The move will end the so-called “double provision” where people detained under a hospital order can receive benefits despite already having their bed and board fully funded by the taxpayer through the NHS. Families of victims in high-profile cases - including the loved ones of Kennedi Westcarr-Sabaroche and the victims of the Nottingham attacks, Grace O’Malley-Kumar, Barnaby Webber, and Ian Coates - have bravely highlighted the loophole which sees offenders continuing to receive benefit payments. The change comes after extensive engagement between the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions and a range of experts and victims directly affected. Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, Pat McFadden said: We said we’d act to tackle this gross unfairness and we’re delivering on that promise. For too long these violent criminals have had their living costs paid by the taxpayer twice over, while their victims and families paid the price. That ends today because victims and taxpayers deserve a system that is fair and supports only those who genuinely need it. The decision to remove benefits from serious offenders will not affect people currently detained under the Mental Health Act 1983, who have not committed any offence. Anyone detained under a hospital order for any reason will continue to receive appropriate mental health support. The regulations deliver on the promise made earlier this year to close the loophole, marking the latest step in reforming the welfare system to put fairness at its core, while ensuring it works for the people who need it most. Emma Webber, Mother of Barnaby Webber said: This is long overdue, and simply the right thing to do. It was a disgrace that Calocane and offenders like him have ever received taxpayers’ money. A hospital bed does not erase the egregious crimes committed, nor the destruction they have caused. Closing this loophole finally delivers some basic accountability that victims deserve. Leon Westcarr, Uncle of Kennedi Westcarr-Sabaroche said: The loss of my niece can never be undone, but I am encouraged that this long-standing injustice has been recognised and addressed. I am grateful to the Secretary of State for listening, investigating the issue, and taking bold action to ensure that those responsible for the most serious crimes do not benefit from their actions. This is an important step towards fairness for victims and their families. Linda Westcarr, Mother of Kennedi Westcarr-Sabaroche said: I believe it is right that the Government reviews benefit entitlement for those who have committed the most serious offences, particularly where public money, funded by taxpayers, is involved. For many victims’ families, the question of whether serious offenders should continue to receive benefits raises understandable concerns about fairness, accountability and the values we uphold as a society. In my view, this is not simply a question of policy; it is also a matter of moral responsibility and ensuring that the impact on victims and their families is properly recognised. I recognise that a hospital order is a mental health disposal rather than a prison sentence, and that each case must be considered carefully. However, the seriousness of the offence and the lasting consequences for victims and their families must remain central to these decisions. For families like mine, the consequences of losing a loved one are devastating and lifelong. Kennedi’s life was taken, her child is growing up without a mother, and our family continues to live with the trauma of her death. I welcome this announcement as a step towards addressing these concerns and achieving a greater sense of fairness for victims’ families. I hope the Government will provide clarity on how and when the proposed changes will be implemented. Kennedi mattered. Her life mattered. The voices of victims’ families must be heard, and their suffering must never be overlooked when decisions are made about the consequences of serious crime. Dr Sanjoy Kumar, father of Grace O’Malley Kumar said: Our campaign has always been about accountability and fairness. Offenders with treatment orders already cost the taxpayer an enormous amount. On release, every offender gets help with housing and benefits. On the principle of fairness alone, we do not see why taxpayers should fund benefits while they are incarcerated. We are grateful to the Secretary of State Pat McFadden for taking action and listening to our campaign which always been about what is good for the country. Julian Hendy, from the Hundred Families said: This is a very welcome move and something we’ve been campaigning on for nearly a decade. Paying thousands of pounds of state benefits to mentally disordered offenders on hospital orders who have committed the most serious of crimes cannot be justified. It is unjust and morally wrong. Dangerous offenders should not be rewarded for their crimes, particularly when they have no costs and when victims’ families have to struggle so hard to get appropriate care and support. That’s why we’re very grateful the government has taken action to close this dangerous loophole, which will surely help keep patients, their families, and the public safe. Additional Information: - The Regulations will apply to individuals subject to a Section 37 order under the Mental Health Act 1983 and a Section 57A order under the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995 - The offences under scope for England and Wales (not including the Scots Law equivalents) are: - Manslaughter (whether voluntary or involuntary) - Attempted murder - Wounding (etc) with intent to cause grievous bodily harm (GBH) - Rape - Assault by penetration - Causing a person to engage in sexual activity without consent (aggravated – with penetration) - Rape of a child under 13 - Sexual assault of a child under 13 (aggravated – with penetration) - Causing or inciting a child under 13 to engage in sexual activity (aggravated – with penetration) - Sexual activity with a child - Familial sexual offences (sexual activity with a child family member) (offender 18 or over) - Familial sexual offences (inciting a child family member to engage in sexual activity) (offender 18 or over) - Murder is not included because a Hospital Order is not an available disposal for the offence of murder which attracts a mandatory life sentence. - The affirmative regulations will be laid in Parliament on 20 October and remain subject to parliamentary approval. - Without these regulations, an offender on Universal Credit, in a single household, aged over 25 and receiving the LCWRA rate, could receive over £800 a month. - The change is expected affect some 2,500 offenders already in hospital and approximately 200 a year in future. - Removal of these benefits will save in the low tens of millions of pounds each year with full financial impacts to be published as part of the 2026 budget. - Individuals in scope will no longer be entitled to either Universal Credit, Pension Credit, State Pension and Employment and Support Allowance while they remain detained in hospital. - The NHS will continue to provide appropriate mental health support. - The policy follows engagement with clinicians, victims’ groups, mental health experts and the devolved governments and the decision to remove benefits from serious offenders will not affect anyone currently detained under the Mental Health Act 1983, who has not committed an offence. - The change applies only to those convicted of a serious offence as defined in the regulations; it does not affect anyone on remand, unfit to plead, awaiting trial or those convicted of offences that are not detailed in the prescribed list. - While the change only comes into effect early next year, it will apply to both existing and future cases from the point that the regulations come into force, regardless of when their conviction was made.

state: British businesses secure £330 million of African infrastructure contracts UK firms will help deliver new schools, clean water infrastructure, electricity networks and government buildings. - Project deals announced as government backs closer trade ties with fast-growing West and Central African markets - UK Export Finance increases its exposure capacity across West and Central Africa by £1.7 billion, creating more opportunity for British exporters British businesses are set to secure more than £330 million of export contracts to help deliver nine major infrastructure projects across Guinea and Benin. The contracts will see UK companies supplying goods and services for projects spanning education, clean water, electricity transmission and government infrastructure, supporting jobs and growth at home while delivering vital infrastructure overseas. The deals are being supported by £1.1 billion in financing and guarantees from UK Export Finance (UKEF), the government’s export credit agency. They are being announced as the fifth UK-West and Central Francophone Africa Trade and Investment Forum (WCAF) opens today in Conakry, Guinea, bringing together British businesses and potential partners from across the region. UKEF is also increasing its exposure capacity across the region by £1.7 billion, giving it greater capacity to support future projects involving British exporters. Business and Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said: These deals are a major win for UK businesses, helping them secure new contracts in fast-growing markets and driving jobs and growth across the United Kingdom. By backing projects like these, UK Export Finance is helping British firms win work overseas, creating opportunities for communities here at home while strengthening our trade partnerships across West and Central Africa. Tim Reid, CEO of UK Export Finance, said: British businesses have won a huge number of contracts to support key infrastructure projects across the region in recent years, driving job creation in the UK while helping our partners in francophone Africa build the infrastructure they need. This is part of the reason we hold the WCAF, we’ve seen many deals signed over the years, and it highlights how UKEF can make a real difference around the world while driving growth in every postcode of the UK. UKEF is providing finance worth £75 million to support a large-scale education infrastructure programme delivering new primary and secondary schools across four regions, improving access to education for thousands of children through modern classrooms, sanitation and related facilities, with the contract won by Planet One. A further £91 million will back the Guinea Regional Water Project, a multi-region programme expanding access to clean, potable water through new treatment and distribution infrastructure, delivered by UK-headquartered Aqua Africa, which has previously secured UKEF-backed financing for water infrastructure in the region. UKEF is also providing £129 million towards the La Cotiere Conakry Transmission project in Guinea, part of a wider electricity network programme to improve power distribution around the country’s coastal region, with the contract secured by Elecnor and expected to create UK supply-chain opportunities in transmission equipment, grid technology and engineering services. In Benin, UKEF is providing finance of £82 million which will help fund a new government administrative complex, consolidating public services within a modern urban development, with the contract awarded to ACC UK Group Ltd and opportunities for UK firms to contribute design, engineering, security systems and specialist building services. WCAF V, hosted by UKEF in partnership with DMA Invest and the Guinean government, will take place until 21 October 2026. Atam Sandhu, CEO of DMA Invest, added: WCAF is about turning relationships into results. Over five editions, our ambition at DMA has remained clear: to bring governments, businesses and financiers together to help move priority projects from discussion towards delivery. We extend our sincere thanks to the Government and people of Guinea for hosting WCAF V in Conakry, and for the leadership, commitment and hospitality that have brought this growing partnership together.

state: Grant helps landowners survey thousands of hectares of spruce woodland The Spruce Site Assessment (SSA) grant has helped 41 landowners survey over 2,450 hectares of woodland to tackle the threat of Ips typographus. Landowners have surveyed more than 2,450 hectares of spruce woodland in the first year of a grant scheme designed to tackle the threat of a destructive tree pest. The Spruce Site Assessment launched in October 2025. It helps woodland owners to assess their spruce trees and take proactive steps to address the threat posed by Ips typographus, also known as the eight-toothed spruce bark beetle. The grant forms part of the government’s wider approach to tree health. Ips typographus is a significant threat to spruce trees across Great Britain and could have devastating effects on our forestry sector if it becomes established. The £2,000 grant helps landowners better understand the extent and condition of their spruce and identify opportunities for proactive management. This means woodland owners can take the first steps to reduce the risk of infestation and protect the health of their woodland. Building a stronger evidence base for management decisions The SSA can complement existing woodland management plans through condition scoring and location mapping, giving landowners a stronger evidence base for management decisions. The assessment also identifies operational requirements and constraints at an early stage, including access and harvesting considerations. This helps landowners and contractors plan operations and reduces uncertainty around future felling operations to support smoother project delivery. By collecting detailed data including timber volumes and stocking density, the SSA helps landowners understand both the potential value of timber and the likely costs associated with felling. As a result, they are less likely to face unexpected costs or delays later on. The SSA can also identify wider improvements for a woodland. For example, landowners have identified improvements to permanent infrastructure and access, which will facilitate proactive spruce removal and support future woodland management. Supporting proactive spruce management Since the launch, the SSA has delivered a successful first year, with woodland owners across a diverse range of sites accessing support. The surveys have recorded vital information and provided statistics to help inform future tree health initiatives. The scheme has supported a wide range of woodland types and ownership, with sites ranging from 0.5 hectares to large-scale woodlands exceeding 400 hectares. In the first year, 41 agreements have been approved. Through these, landowners and their agents have surveyed more than 2,450 hectares of spruce woodland, with high risk spruce material identified in every agreement. This highlights the value of early assessment and proactive management. Collectively, the surveys have identified an estimated 26,000 tonnes of spruce that could be removed. Landowners plan to remove 60% of surveyed spruce within 12 months of the survey date. This is a significant contribution to reducing the quantity of high risk spruce material available to the beetle, building resilience against Ips typographus infestations. The SSA is open for applications, with a limited number of spaces available. From the Spruce Site Assessment to the tree health pilot (THP) Landowners who complete an SSA may also benefit from enhanced funding rates for felling through the tree Health pilot, depending on location. This year, 17 sites that completed an SSA have gone on to access funding for proactive felling through THP. The THP grant provides funding for woodlands within the Ips typographus demarcated area, which is made up of the proactive spruce removal area and, within it, the smaller priority spruce removal area. Applicants in the priority spruce removal area are eligible to apply for funding for 80% of actual felling costs, whether or not they have completed an SSA. Applicants in the wider proactive spruce removal area (but outside the priority area) can also access funding for 80% of actual felling costs, if an SSA has identified susceptible spruce and a Woodland Officer has confirmed this. Applicants in the wider proactive spruce removal area who haven’t completed an SSA may only be eligible for 40% of actual felling costs. Find out more about the funding available through the tree health pilot. Find detailed Spruce Site Assessment guidance and email the Forestry Commission for support at: SSAenquiries@forestrycommission.gov.uk. Learn about how Whiligh Estate has used the SSA to reduce the risk of an Ips typographus infestation. Read more about the eight-toothed spruce bark beetle (Ips typographus) and find out if your land is within the proactive spruce removal area.

state: Domestic abuser who suffocated former partner now jailed after sentence increased A man who repeatedly assaulted and abused his former partner had his suspended sentence overturned after the Attorney General intervened. Aiden Ford, 40, of Hanham, Bristol, had his suspended sentence of three years increased to an immediate sentence of four years and three months’ imprisonment after the Attorney General, Ellie Reeves KC MP, referred his case to the Court of Appeal under the Unduly Lenient Sentence scheme. The court heard that Ford and the victim began a relationship in September 2024. Between February and August 2025, Ford subjected her to a campaign of repeated violent assaults and coercive and controlling behaviour including trapping her in his home, making threats to her life, and relentlessly contacting her after she tried to end the relationship. On one occasion, Ford forced the victim into his car and drove to a secluded area, where he restrained her in the passenger seat. The victim feared for her life as Ford violently assaulted her and suffocated her with his forearm. After the victim reported the abuse, the offender persistently pressured and ultimately persuaded the victim to withdraw her statements to the police. The Attorney General, Ellie Reeves KC MP said: Aiden Ford subjected his victim to a sustained and terrifying campaign of violence and coercive control, leaving her genuinely fearing for her life. There is no excuse, and no place for domestic abuse in our society. Tackling violence against women and girls is my number one priority, and I welcome the Court of Appeal’s decision to overturn Ford’s suspended sentence and increase his sentence following my referral. On 11 June 2026, at Cardiff Crown Court, Aiden Ford was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment suspended for three years for one count of controlling and coercive behaviour, one count of suffocation, one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and one count of perverting the course of justice. On 20 October 2026, at the Court of Appeal, his sentence was increased to four years and three months’ imprisonment.

state: Operational update 20 October – UK military support to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia The UK will provide additional defensive military support to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, given escalating Houthi attacks in the region. The UK will provide additional defensive military support to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, given escalating Houthi attacks in the region. The UK will fly defensive counter air missions to support the protection of Saudi cities and critical national infrastructure against aerial attack, using RAF Typhoon fighter jets. These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis. The UK will provide an RAF A400M to support the movement of defence materiel within Saudi Arabia, alongside UK military advisers to support Saudi staff officers. This support builds on the UK’s existing defensive military contribution to Saudi Arabia, including the deployment of air defence equipment to protect against missiles and drone attacks. It also includes an extension of air-to-air refuelling support for Saudi defensive air operations including to degrade Houthi military targets in Yemen that threaten the Saudi and Yemeni people. The Houthis’ attempts to destabilise the region and undermine the security and stability of the Middle East are unacceptable. This reckless behaviour deepens Yemen’s already devastating humanitarian crisis, and it is in the UK’s national economic and security interest that they do not succeed. Escalating violence in the Gulf can have a serious impact at home in the UK - driving up the cost of living, disrupting energy supplies and costs to British businesses. It is also causing devastation to the civilian population in Yemen. We unequivocally condemn the Houthi attacks on civilian targets like King Khalid International Airport and are clear that Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen have the right to defend themselves. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable. The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region. That’s why today I have approved further UK military support. RAF Typhoons will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles. This builds on the UK equipment and personnel we already have in the country to defend against Houthi air attacks.

state: Full steam ahead: new station for Bradford New station for Bradford will improve connections, support economic growth and set the foundations for new homes, jobs and opportunities across the North. - new station at Bradford Interchange to bring passengers more reliable services, better connections and faster journeys as Northern Powerhouse Rail moves one step closer - Bradford Council says delivering the new station alongside the proposed West Yorkshire Mass Transit network will unlock thousands of jobs and homes, and more than £1 billion in economic benefits - new station will transform the city’s connections with some of the North’s largest cities, including Leeds, Manchester and York Passengers across Yorkshire are set to benefit from major station improvements, as the government has today (20 October 2026) confirmed a new station at Bradford Interchange. Bradford’s connections with some of the North’s largest cities, including Leeds, Manchester and York, will be transformed as passengers will be able to benefit from more frequent trains, improved journey times and reliability. The Bradford Interchange site unlocks the potential to regenerate Bradford’s Southern Gateway, and in tandem with the proposed West Yorkshire Mass Transit, would support thousands of new homes, jobs and up to £1 billion in economic benefits. The announcement marks a major milestone in the delivery of Northern Powerhouse Rail (NPR) and the government’s mission to drive growth in every postcode. The station will also become part of Great British Railways (GBR), the new publicly owned railway that will bring track and train together, helping deliver a more reliable, efficient and passenger-focused railway. The Prime Minister is driving change to give control back to local communities by empowering Mayors to shape transport to serve the communities they know best, and that is why the location decision was made with the Mayor of West Yorkshire, Tracy Brabin. NPR will deliver a turn-up-and-go railway for passengers from Bradford, meaning multiple trains an hour will run frequently enough between major cities across the North that passengers won’t need to check a timetable before going to the station. Transport Secretary, Heidi Alexander, said: Today marks an important milestone for Bradford with a brand-new station that will transform how people travel across the North. By bringing Northern Powerhouse Rail into the heart of the city, we are unlocking the huge potential Bradford offers – improving connections, supporting economic growth and setting the foundations for new homes, jobs and opportunities across the region. The new GBR station will be delivered in the 2030s and replace the outdated 1970s station, providing the modern transport hub that Bradford deserves. The city will be at the heart of the NPR network, transforming its connections with some of the North’s largest cities including Leeds, Manchester and York, creating opportunities for investment, regeneration and economic growth. Bradford’s new city centre station is a key part of the government’s Northern Growth Strategy, which, with Northern Powerhouse Rail, is electrifying and upgrading routes between Leeds, Bradford, Sheffield and York, improving journey times and reliability across the region. Tracy Brabin, Mayor of West Yorkshire, said: Today is an exciting and important milestone for Bradford, with an ironclad commitment to a new station in the city centre. Bradford has so much untapped potential, and faster, more frequent trains to Leeds and Manchester, and the transformation of the city centre through Bradford City Village, will help to finally unleash it. Together with investment for northern powerhouse rail, a mass transit system for West Yorkshire and our brand-new Weaver Network, we are working in lockstep with the government to deliver a better-connected region. Henri Murison MBE, Chief Executive of Northern Powerhouse Partnership, said: The decision to build Bradford’s new station at the interchange in the city centre is a long-term commitment to the city and the wider North. By unlocking the regeneration of the Southern Gateway, we will see homes and jobs for this city which otherwise would not be built or come here. Working with the council and Mayor Tracy Brabin and her team, I will be doing everything I can to push on and move forward with ambitious plans that enable future phases of Northern Powerhouse Rail. This network will better connect the young people in the city with opportunities in Manchester and Liverpool as well as Sheffield. Bradford and the North’s next phase of growth will be built by business. Confidence is already building here, and this will help build it further. Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, said: This government is doing things differently. We are backing local leaders and investing in the infrastructure that people need. This is how we create good jobs where people live and growth that supports a high street you can be proud of. That is how we build a stronger future for cities like Bradford, boost West Yorkshire, and deliver our plan for growth in every part of the country. state: Ofcom Board Member Appointment The Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media & Sport has extended the first term of Will Harding as a Non-Executive Member of the Ofcom Board for six months. Will Harding Term extended from 3 October 2026 to 2 April 2027 Will has almost 30 years’ experience in the media industry. He started his career as a management consultant with KPMG, before spending five years at BBC Worldwide (now BBC Studios) where he worked across the BBC’s commercial and international operations. He later helped to launch ask.com in the UK before moving to Sky, where he became Commercial and Operations Director of its new media business. He joined GCap Media plc in 2006 as Group Strategy Director. Following Global Media & Entertainment Ltd’s acquisition of GCap Media in 2008, he was appointed Global’s Chief Strategy Officer and joined the main Global board. During his time at Global, Will was responsible for establishing the Global Academy, a state school supporting young people from all backgrounds who wish to pursue careers in the creative industries. Will stepped down from the Global Media and Entertainment Ltd board in December 2020. Since 2021 he has been a Non-Executive Director of Primedia, the leading Africa-focused media and advertising group, and was a Trustee of the Baker Dearing Educational Trust from 2021 to 2024. He became a Trustee of the Education and Employers charity in 2024. Remuneration and Governance Code Ofcom Non-Executive Board Members are remunerated at £42,519 per annum. This extension has been made in accordance with the Governance Code on Public Appointments. The appointments process is regulated by the Commissioner for Public Appointments. Under the Code, any significant political activity undertaken by an appointee in the last five years must be declared. This is defined as including holding office, public speaking, making a recordable donation, or candidature for election. Will Harding has not declared any significant political activity. Notes to Editors DCMS has around 400 regulated Public Appointment roles across 44 Public Bodies including Arts Council England, Theatres Trust, the National Gallery, UK Sport and the Gambling Commission. We encourage applications from talented individuals from all backgrounds and across the whole of the United Kingdom. state: DSCC Online: Multi-factor Authentication Multi-factor authentication (MFA) went live for DSCC Online users on 15 October 2026. MFA is a security process that requires you to provide more than one form of identification when signing in. It adds an extra layer of protection to your account and reduces the risk of unauthorised access. There are over 8,600 DSCC Online user accounts. Many thousands of users have successfully accessed the service using MFA since go live. A small number of users have experienced issues, which are explained below. Available MFA methods You must use the Microsoft Authenticator app for MFA. Do not use the Oracle app. “Sign-on policy denies access” error Around 550 users were affected by an issue that showed the error message “Sign-on policy denies access” when they tried to register. All affected users were issued with new activation invitations by 4pm on Friday 16 October 2026. Everyone who has since attempted to register has done so successfully. If you have not received your activation email, check your spam or junk folder. You should also confirm that the email address on your declaration form is correct. If you have received an activation email but have not yet used it, do this as soon as possible. The activation link expires after 7 days. New user requests Since MFA went live, DSCC has received over 1,000 new user requests. These are being processed as quickly as possible, with the aim of setting up these accounts by the end of this week. Changes to access level Some users initially requested “Solicitor” access but now need this changed to “Office” access. These requests are being processed as quickly as possible. A new form is being developed to capture this information more efficiently. Contact us If you have any queries about MFA or your DSCC Online access, please email the DSCC Administration Team: dsccadmin@dutysolicitors.org.

state: Water company bosses update National Drought Group on resilience Water companies ordered to protect customer supplies as severe drought persists across parts of England Water company chief executives were called before the National Drought Group yesterday to update on the actions they are taking to protect customer supplies after government instructed daily monitoring of reservoir and river levels. Bosses set out measures being taken to protect customer supplies after severe drought was declared in parts of England last week, including sending less water from reservoirs into local rivers and reducing water pressure, where appropriate, overnight. Water companies are also speeding up leak detection and working to transfer water from elsewhere in the network to support the lowest reservoirs. These steps come after the government told water companies and the Environment Agency to put public supplies first. Water Minister Emma Hardy, who chaired yesterday’s meeting, said: Having instructed water companies to carry out daily monitoring of reservoir and river levels, while improving water quality checks, it’s right that the National Drought Group has now heard directly from water company bosses on the action they’re taking. It’s encouraging that these efforts are starting to ease the pressure on public supplies, but water companies must continue to step up their efforts, and we will keep holding them to account. While customer water supplies will not be interrupted, declaring a severe drought allowed us to ensure proactive steps are taken to safeguard water. Although water companies remain responsible for maintaining public water supplies, we can all help by thinking about ways to use water wisely over the coming weeks. The National Drought Group heard that while the first half of October has been dry, wet weather is also expected to spread in later this week which could help water resources. The Environment Agency has said at least 120% of average rainfall is needed over the next six months for the country to be considered out of drought by the start of spring. The expert group – which includes the Met Office, Government, regulators, water companies, the National Farmers’ Union, the Canal & River Trust, anglers, hydrologists, and conservation experts – has again urged people to use water wisely in the coming weeks and months to protect supplies and the environment. Last week, the Government declared severe drought in parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex. The South East and South West have experienced their driest April to September in over a century, impacting reservoir levels in that area – particularly Ardingly in West Sussex and Wimbleball in Somerset. While customer supplies are uninterrupted, declaring severe drought allowed additional proactive steps to be taken to safeguard water before any disruption occurs. Since then, enhanced engagement has started with Local Resilience Forums in the severe drought areas to coordinate risk assessment and preparedness across local communities. The National Drought Group have been meeting regularly since August to coordinate the response to this year’s unprecedented dry weather and hold organisations to account for their actions. The Environment Agency has stressed the need for drought plans to be translated into timely action, including quickly fixing leaks, communicating with customers about using water wisely, and submitting early applications to the government where restrictions on non-essential business use may be needed. - The Environment Agency has granted drought permits to South West Water and South East Water to reduce the amount of water released from its reservoirs into local rivers. (Wimbleball into the River Exe and Ardingly into the River Ouse) - Temporary pumps have also been put in place to help move water around the area supplied by South West Water’s Stithians reservoir in Cornwall, and Wessex Water is preparing applications for seven further drought permits, which the Environment Agency will prioritise on receipt. - Applications for non-essential use bans by South East Water, South West Water and Southern Water are under consideration by the Environment Secretary. - Fish rescue plans are being put in place in case reservoir levels fall further and action is needed to protect wildlife. Environment Agency Chief Executive Philip Duffy said: The rain is welcome, but the drought is far from over. It will bring some welcome respite for farmers and the environment, but we need sustained rainfall to refill depleted reservoirs and help rivers and wildlife recover. Water companies must act now to secure public water supplies and reduce pressure on our rivers and wildlife. The public can help too. Small changes in how we use water can make a real difference. Every drop counts. Met Office Business Manager, John Loynd, said: September and the first half of October continued the pattern of below-average rainfall across many parts of England, adding to existing drought pressures in some areas. While more unsettled conditions are now affecting parts of the UK and bringing spells of rain and strong winds, it remains too early to say whether this will deliver the widespread, sustained rainfall needed to make a significant difference to the drought situation. The Met Office will continue to work closely with the Environment Agency and water companies to monitor conditions and provide the latest forecasts and climate information. CEO of Waterwise, Nicci Russell, said: Water is scarce in England - and we all need to make sure we waste less, at home and at work. There are more of us than ever before, we’re using on average more than we used to, and the climate emergency means the water isn’t always available when we need it. Nothing happens without water.
