state: Attorney General's speech at the London Conference on International Law 2026 Full text of the speech given by the Rt Hon Ellie Reeves KC MP at the London Conference on International Law 2026, on 1 October 2026. Thank you for the invitation to speak here today. This is my first speech on international law as Attorney General, and I’m really glad to be giving it at the London Conference, in front of an audience who understands its importance and has contributed to its development. Today is a day that I will look back on with pride. This morning I was at the Royal Courts of Justice, where I took my oath and was sworn in as Attorney General for England and Wales. Taking part in that ceremony was a reminder of the history and significance of the job. I’m joining a long line of Attorneys General who have had to contend with the thorniest issues of their day. Before entering politics, I spent more than a decade as an employment rights lawyer. I represented trade unions and their members, before establishing my own consultancy to support women facing discrimination at work. What that experience taught me is that law does not exist in a vacuum, just as international law is not some abstract concept we can do away with. It determines whether people are treated fairly, whether they can provide for their families, and whether they can assert their rights when things go wrong. Integral to my role as Attorney General is upholding the rule of law within government, including our obligations under international law. This is personal to me. In 2007, and then again in 2012, I visited Colombia and I saw and heard about the grave human rights violations happening there. Those conversations followed me through the doors of Parliament where I continued to advocate and speak up. The experience only continued to strengthen my belief in the importance of standing up for human rights, and my support for international law. But I am concerned in recent years those values and beliefs have come under repeated assault. [Redacted political content] The crises we face are spilling out on multiple fronts, and trust and public confidence in the institutions built to protect ordinary people are eroding. Whether it’s the ECHR, NATO or the UN, the rules-based order and international law are under threat. Making the case for international law has never been more important, not least because we can no longer separate events happening around the world from their impact here at home. We’ve seen it in the closing of the Strait of Hormuz raising prices at the petrol pumps, the ongoing war in Ukraine increasing the cost of the weekly shop, and foreign state-backed cyberattacks disrupting critical care and patient safety in our hospitals. International law determines what happens here, just as much as domestic law does. But it is no secret to anyone here that international law and the rules-based order face real challenges. When international law enters public debate, people often question its relevance in today’s world, or even whether they believe in it at all. I think that is an understandable reaction. We have all turned on the news or checked our phones and seen the horrendous suffering in places like Sudan, Gaza and Ukraine. When those responsible for that suffering appear to act with impunity, without fear or accountability, it is natural for people to question what role international law really plays. It is vital that we take that criticism head on. We have to listen. But we also have to make the case for why international law matters, and why people should continue to believe in it. One of the best routes to doing that is not through theory, but through evidence, by making the practical, pragmatic case for how international law affects people’s everyday lives. So let me be clear: this government and I are steadfast in our commitment to institutions like the European Convention on Human Rights, the International Court of Justice and the UN, and to the treaties and multilateral agreements that allow people to get on with their everyday lives. That commitment is partly pragmatic. We understand the material benefits of international law, the security it provides, the prosperity it creates. But it is also about our values. When Russia launched its illegal invasion of Ukraine, in flagrant breach of the UN Charter, it was a reminder of what is at stake when international law is cast aside. Our commitment to international law speaks to who we are as a country and the role we want to play in the world, one that stands with Ukraine’s inalienable right to sovereignty, not with those who would trample on it. So today, I don’t intend to labour the case for international law on principle alone. I think that everyone in this room already agrees with me about why international law matters for its own sake. Instead, I want to speak to its specific practical benefits - and I invite anyone who thinks we can do away with international law – or that we can discard multilateral frameworks to explain away the practical difference, it makes to millions of people every day. There are four main points I want to speak about today: international law’s integral role in our prosperity; in enabling the opportunities people enjoy; in keeping the public safe on our streets; and in protecting individuals from the overreach of the state. Prosperity: I’ll begin with prosperity. A few weeks ago, the Bank of England announced a rise of inflation to 3.1%. The government is providing support to alleviate some of the financial pressure, such as cutting VAT on energy bills, but every house across the UK will feel the squeeze in their household budgets. Part of that squeeze can be traced to events happening thousands of miles away. The illegal invasion of Ukraine has thrown energy markets into turmoil, and the price of oil and gas spiked as supply from the region was disrupted. Households up and down this country are feeling that impact directly, in higher petrol prices and in energy bills that pushed inflation to levels not seen in decades. More recently, Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz has resulted in a huge number of commercial ships being unable to navigate the Strait and continue their journeys across the globe. Our financial security and prosperity depends on international banking systems, the WTO, and international trade law, but it also depends on multilateral regimes like the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz in contravention of international law has resulted in higher oil prices, higher household bills, and higher mortgage rates. UNCLOS is a cornerstone of international commerce. It protects access to vital shipping routes that allow food to reach our supermarket shelves, British manufacturers to export their goods around the world, and the global economy to flourish. Every day more than 400 commercial vessels pass unimpeded through the Dover Strait, exercising their right of transit passage guaranteed under UNCLOS. Before the outbreak of the US-Iran conflict and the closure of the Strait, I imagine few people beyond law of the sea specialists spent much time thinking about that right – or about the extent to which it also exists in customary international law – or about whether a state which claims a 12-nautical-mile territorial sea can, at the same time, credibly deny rights of passage through an international strait which forms part of that sea. Of course, many of those specialists are in this room. London remains one of the world’s leading centres for commercial shipping and expertise in the law of the sea. But these legal issues have come to the fore this year because long-standing rules on the law of the sea have been violated. But that does not mean we should question the relevance of those rules. If anything, it only reinforces their importance to our everyday lives. So, whilst the UK will continue to work tirelessly with our allies to seek to restore freedom of navigation in the Strait. There is no doubt that the blocking of commercial vessels from exercising their right of transit passage through the Strait of Hormuz has directly impacted millions of people across this country. Things people enjoy: My second point is opportunities. International law is also vital for things that make our lives special. Like going on holiday. Most people outside this room have never heard of the Chicago Convention, but millions of people rely on it every year. Every time a family wheels a suitcase through an airport terminal. Every time a boarding pass flashes green at the gate. Every time a Jet2 flight lifts off for Corfu or Tenerife or Faro. The Chicago Convention establishes the international legal framework for international civil aviation, governing everything from rights of overflight to safety standards for aviation. And Air Services Agreements between States give our commercial airlines the certainty they need to operate – without the quiet operation of international law, families across Britain would not have been able to enjoy their holidays this summer. And the same is true of many other legal frameworks that operate on the international or bilateral level. They might seem quite mundane, even to us as lawyers. But their importance cannot be understated. After all, it is a treaty between the UK and France that allows us to get to Paris by Eurostar in less than two hours. And when children set off on their school coach trip to France, it is made all the easier because States have agreed, as a matter of international law, for the mutual recognition of foreign driving licences. International law provides the stability we need to get on with our lives. This is my challenge to anyone who dismisses international law as some sort of ambiguous or foreign concept, where its only purpose is to constrain States’ freedom and stop them acting however they want. Consider the practical difference it makes. The ability to board a flight, cross borders, and travel with confidence depends on a framework of international rules and cooperation that most of us rarely think about but rely on every day. Keeping us safe: The same principle extends to criminal justice, which is my third argument, how international law keeps people safe on our streets. The UK relies on a range of international criminal cooperation agreements, from UN-led treaties to Council of Europe, EU and bilateral arrangements, to extradite suspects, share evidence and pursue cross-border crime. When I was appointed as Attorney General in July, the Prime Minister wrote to me and asked that I help deliver the government’s ambition to make our streets safer, halve violence against women and girls, and restore public confidence in the justice systems. International law has a role in that too. No one would accept a world where offenders could evade justice simply by hiding overseas. Nor would anyone accept a world where criminals abroad could help commit crimes on our streets and get away with it. But when it comes to criminal justice, successful prosecutions for cross-border crime cannot be achieved through ungoverned, sporadic dealings between States. There is no point in seeking the extradition of an offender if they can evade prosecution because their extradition process was unfair. And there is no point gathering evidence from abroad through mutual legal assistance if that evidence then gets thrown out of court because it was obtained unlawfully. Due process underpinned by legal certainty is essential for securing the justice that victims of crime deserve. And it is international law – in the form of those criminal justice treaties - that gives us the confidence that due process will be followed even when the crime, or the suspect, crosses borders. We’ve recently seen this play out in practice. Last year, ten members of a major organised crime gang were sentenced to a combined total of 207 years in prison. Their operation was worth an estimated £26 million and involved drugs, firearms and money moving across borders. The gang leader was directing parts of the enterprise from Spain, believing he could evade justice by using the encrypted messaging platform EncroChat. But he was wrong. Through cooperation between multinational law enforcement agencies, sharing intelligence, tracking suspects and working together, the organised crime gang was brought home to face justice. International law was crucial to that outcome, resulting in safer communities here in Britain. ECHR: And finally, my fourth point, protecting individuals from the overreach of the state. International law doesn’t just keep us safe, it protects our rights and freedoms too. The European Convention on Human Rights, brought home to the UK from Strasbourg in 1998 through the Human Rights Act, has delivered benefits to people across this country that are all too often overlooked. It has allowed people to object when doctors put “do not resuscitate” orders on their bed without their consent. It has allowed people with learning disabilities imprisoned in locked units to be reunited with their families. It has allowed elderly married couples in residential care to object when care home managers try to separate them. And it is the reason victims of rapists such as John Worboys have been able to force the police to investigate cases of rape, rather than being turned away. Of course, institutions like the ECHR are under strain. But they were never intended to stand frozen in time. To remain effective, they must evolve alongside the societies they serve. That is why this Government has worked with partners across Europe and through the Council of Europe to strengthen and modernise the Convention for the challenges of the twenty-first century. West Bank So far, I’ve spoken about the practical, everyday benefits that international law delivers. But I also want to speak about its arguably most important role - maintaining peace and security. The Prime Minister has made clear that, in a difficult and dangerous world, it is more important than ever that Britain stands for something. Last month, we saw what that means in practice. Alongside twelve other countries, the Foreign Secretary gave a statement to Parliament announcing UK’s shift in policy on Israel and Palestine. The UK has long considered Israeli settlements in the West Bank to be a violation of Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention. But for the first time, the Foreign Secretary announced a formal change in the view of the British Government – that the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory is, itself, unlawful. There was no requirement or legal obligation on the Government to make that view public. As the Prime Minister said, that conclusion is in line with, but independent of, the conclusion of the International Court of Justice in its Advisory Opinion on the Occupied Palestinian Territories. The Government reached this conclusion after considering all of Israel’s actions in the occupied territory, in particular their scope and intended permanence. The unlawfulness of the occupation should be reflected in the economic relationships that the UK chooses to have with the occupied territories. For that reason, the Government will introduce an import ban on goods from illegal settlements. And we will ban the advertising in the UK of illegal settlements. This is Britain standing for something. It is about holding true to our values, supporting accountability, and upholding respect for international law. I am proud to serve in a government that is prepared to do that. And one that will work with our allies, to maximise our collective influence, uphold international law, and demonstrate the vital role that cooperation plays in our response to the challenges we face. So, to finish, international law is not perfect. And I am not here today to pretend that the challenges it faces are not real. But imperfection does not mean unimportant. Anyone who dismisses international law must also explain away the practical difference it makes to millions of people every single day. Today, I have set out how international law helps make our country safer, more prosperous and stronger. It gives Britain influence beyond our size. It allows us to work with allies to pursue criminals, challenge aggression, uphold human rights and hold rogue actors to account. But just as much, it matters to people at home. To the parent worried about the bills arriving at the end of the month. To the family looking forward to a holiday booked months in advance. To the victim waiting for justice. Law and legal certainty underpin so much of our daily freedoms, the fact that it operates in the background does not make it any less important. Today we see conflict spreading, trade under strain, and trust in our institutions being tested, but the answer should never be to look inward or to do less. It should be to do more… more cooperation, recommitting ourselves to our international obligations and to speak with absolute confidence about the benefits it brings. And in an increasingly uncertain world it is one of the most practical, tangible and important responsibilities we share. Thank you very much.

state: CMA outlines proposals to unlock contactless technology on Apple iPhone Opening up iPhone contactless technology could boost innovation, lower costs and help UK fintechs grow. - Apple’s fees and rules are blocking UK fintechs and other businesses from innovating and growing. - Proposals expected to result in substantially lower access fees, helping make it commercially viable for more businesses to innovate and compete. - Proposals would require Apple to grant access through the main contactless technology standards used internationally and give businesses more choice. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is consulting on proposals to transform how UK businesses build digital products and services on Apple’s iPhone. The UK is one of the world’s leading fintech hubs, with the sector generating around £214 billion in turnover and supporting more than 360,000 jobs. Fintechs are a UK success story, but Apple’s fees and access rules for key mobile contactless technology, known as near field communication (NFC), risk blocking their ability to innovate and grow. The CMA has heard concerns from businesses in the UK that Apple’s current NFC access arrangements may not be commercially viable, that fees, and other terms may be onerous, and that different technical approaches across jurisdictions and platforms can make it harder to scale and compete effectively. Contactless services in the UK Contactless technology is already central to everyday life in the UK. People increasingly use their phones to pay, travel, access buildings and hold important credentials. The increasing importance of this technology is clear from changes in contactless payments, currently the most popular use of this technology, which now represents 39% of all payments compared to just 3% of transactions a decade ago. Meanwhile, more than 60% of adults currently use a digital wallet, with Apple Wallet being the most popular choice in the UK. However, unlike in the EU, not a single firm has launched a wallet-type product to compete with Apple’s in the UK. Just six months after Apple agreed to provide NFC access for payments in the EU, Vipps launched the first alternative payment app, followed by PayPal, Klarna, Curve, and BBVA. The CMA wants to ensure that businesses in the UK with great ideas have a genuine opportunity to compete with existing wallets and develop the technologies and services of the future. Better access to the technology underpinning these services could help UK businesses develop a wide range of new products, such as account-to-account payments, digital IDs, travel passes and digital keys. What the CMA is proposing For businesses to compete effectively, access to the technology needs to work both technically and commercially. The CMA’s proposals therefore address two barriers: giving businesses access to the technologies they need and ensuring that access is available on terms which allow viable business models to develop. Giving businesses a choice of technology: The CMA proposals would require Apple to provide access through the main contactless technology standards used internationally. Evidence seen by the CMA suggests that neither technology raises inherent security concerns and that access to both standards would support the widest range of innovative use cases and enable UK firms to roll out payment services that are already offered in the EU. Making access commercially viable: Even where technical access is available, high fees can prevent businesses from developing viable products and competing effectively. Pricing is therefore a key part of ensuring that businesses have effective access to contactless technology. The CMA is not proposing to set the price and terms of contactless functionality access. Instead, it has proposed principles for how this should be determined, with the expectation that charges would be substantially lower than Apple’s current fees while still fairly rewarding Apple for providing access. These proposals are consistent with the CMA’s proportionate approach to intervention and principles set out in digital markets legislation. The measures would help UK fintechs and other businesses seize the potential of this technology, which makes everyday experiences faster and more seamless. It will not only improve people’s lives now by offering more choice, but create the conditions for a new generation of contactless products and services to be developed in the future. This could include: - digital wallets and payment services - digital IDs and age-verification tools - digital car, hotel and workplace keys - tickets and travel passes - loyalty and rewards services Sarah Cardell, Chief Executive of the CMA, said: These proposals open the door to more innovation, more choice and economic growth, including in the UK’s important fintech sector. We have heard that high fees, strict terms, and technical restrictions relating to Apple’s contactless technology make it too difficult for challengers to innovate and compete. By removing barriers to entry, we can help create the conditions for brilliant British businesses with great ideas to develop new products and services here - from payment apps and digital IDs to travel passes and digital keys. David Geale, Executive Director for Consumers, Payments and Competition at the FCA, said: We welcome steps the CMA has taken to boost competition and innovation. Improved access and substantially lower fees should create greater competition and more choice for consumers and businesses. Opening up this technology will also support the expansion of open banking, enabling more people to make payments directly from their bank accounts.” The consultation will close on Tuesday 17 November 2026, and a final decision will be made after responses have been assessed. Visit the case page to find out more about the consultation and submit a response. Notes to editors - The CMA is consulting on a proposed conduct requirement under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024. The consultation follows the CMA’s designation of Apple as having Strategic Market Status in relation to its mobile platform. - UK Finance (2026) estimates that contactless payments – whether made using a physical card or a mobile device – rose by 2% to 19.2 billion in 2025, representing 39% of all payments. A decade ago, contactless made up just 3% of transactions. - The Data City (2025) estimates that the fintech sector employs 362,651 people across 3,348 companies and generates a combined turnover of £213.6 billion from 3,583 businesses. - Which? (2026) found that 62% of UK adults currently use a digital wallet, with Apple Wallet (50%) being the most popular. - The two main contactless technology standards used internationally are known as secure element (SE), which stores information on-device and host-based card emulation (HCE), which stores data off-device. Both HCE and SE are established technologies, not developed by Apple, and used across mobile ecosystems to enable a range of contactless services. Apple currently only offers SE in the UK, and the proposals mean that it would be required to offer both HCE and SE. On bank holidays, use our out of hours number.

state: Separation Agreement Joint Committee between the UK and EEA EFTA states: joint statement from the seventh meeting This page shows the statement following the meeting of the Separation Agreement Joint Committee on 20 October 2026. The seventh meeting of the Separation Agreement Joint Committee was held online on 20 October 2026, chaired by officials from the Principality of Liechtenstein, with representatives from Iceland, the Kingdom of Norway and the United Kingdom participating. The Committee was established by the Separation Agreement to monitor its implementation and application. The Separation Agreement ensures that nationals of Iceland, Liechtenstein or Norway (‘the EEA EFTA States’) already living in the UK, or UK nationals living in the EEA EFTA States at the end of the transition period, have largely the same rights as before the UK left the EU. In addition to the right of residence, these include entitlements to social security and the recognition of professional qualifications. During the meeting, representatives from the EEA EFTA States and the UK updated each other on their implementation and application of the Separation Agreement, focusing on the provisions relating to citizens’ rights. Representatives of the EFTA Surveillance Authority and the Independent Monitoring Authority also presented information on the monitoring of the implementation and application of the Separation Agreement. The EEA EFTA States and the UK adopted a Decision amending Part I of Annex I to the Separation Agreement, in order to include two recent relevant Decisions of the Administrative Commission for the Coordination of Social Security Systems. The EEA EFTA States and the UK continue to work together to ensure the correct implementation and application of the Separation Agreement, to provide certainty to citizens.

state: Marine Licensing Decisions Deliver Safer Communities, Stronger Infrastructure and Healthier Seas From Harbour Bridges to Oyster Reefs: Marine Licensing Enables Vital Coastal Projects. Mussel farm relocation approved to boost sustainable seafood industry in Devon Plans to relocate an offshore mussel farm into deeper waters in Babbacombe Bay, Devon, have been approved, supporting the growth of sustainable aquaculture in the region. Offshore Shellfish Ltd. will install 140 screw anchors on the seabed to support 68 mussel-growing longlines across four sections in Torbay Harbour. The move shifts the operation into a new offshore environment designed to improve long-term resilience and productivity. The project required a marine licence due to seabed works and underwent environmental assessment to ensure protected habitats in Lyme Bay and Torbay were not harmed. The MMO Marine Licensing team worked closely with regulators and the fishing industry to address concerns around site location and impacts. The relocated farm is expected to strengthen mussel production, safeguard local jobs, and support the regional economy, while contributing to more sustainable seafood practices that can enhance biodiversity and water quality. Fast-tracked harbour bridge approved ahead of Porthleven Food Festival A temporary pedestrian bridge over Porthleven Harbour was approved just days before the town’s popular food festival, ensuring safe movement for large crowds. The scaffold footbridge was designed to improve crowd flow around the busy harbour during the event. The application was submitted on 27 March 2025, with construction scheduled for 30 April. As the structure would sit below Mean High Water Springs, it required a marine licence application from the organisers. With limited time and the bridge considered vital for public safety, the MMO Marine Licensing team fast-tracked the decision and issued approval on 28 April. The bridge allowed organisers to manage visitor numbers more effectively, helping reduce congestion and ensuring a safer experience for festival goers and residents. Storm-damaged sandbanks jetty to be rebuilt in major upgrade project Plans to rebuild and improve the Sandbanks ferry terminal in Poole have been approved, paving the way for a major long-term upgrade to a key gateway for visitors to Brownsea Island. The National Trust will replace the ageing jetty at Sandbanks, located next to the chain ferry slipway, with a new pier and upgraded infrastructure. The project includes new vessel berths, a replacement quay wall, a vehicle ramp, and improved loading facilities. Work is set to run from May 2025 through to October 2029. The need for the project became urgent after severe storm damage caused part of the seabed beneath the pier to wash away, leaving the structure unstable. Emergency works were carried out shortly after, with the damaged jetty removed. Due to the site’s environmental sensitivity, the application required a detailed habitat assessment covering multiple protected areas, with Natural England supporting the final approach. The MMO Marine Licensing team worked closely with the National Trust to address concerns raised during consultation, helping move the project forward. Once complete, the upgraded terminal will improve access to Brownsea Island, one of the region’s most popular attractions, supporting tourism and ensuring a reliable link for visitors, staff, and essential supplies. Maintenance dredging approved to keep Burnham Marina accessible A marine licence has been granted for annual maintenance dredging at Burnham Yacht Harbour, ensuring safe access for vessels using the marina. The project will involve removing up to 17,500 cubic metres of sediment each year from the marina basin, with dredging taking place between December and May. The material will be dispersed into the River Crouch. The application prompted discussions between the MMO, Natural England and the applicant over environmental safeguards, including a condition relating to freezing weather. Following consultation, a final agreement was reached and the licence was approved. The dredging is essential to maintain navigational depth at the harbour, allowing boats to continue operating safely and supporting ongoing use of the marina by the local boating community. Native oyster reef pilot project launched to boost marine life in Tyne and Wear A pioneering project to restore native oyster populations in Tyne and Wear has been approved, marking a significant step in efforts to improve marine biodiversity and water quality. Led by the Zoological Society of London in partnership with Groundwork Northeast & Cumbria, the Wild Oysters Project will create an artificial reef using specially designed structures and oyster “cultch” placed on the seabed. The initiative required a marine licence for the reef construction, with the MMO Marine Licensing team working closely with the project team to refine plans and ensure regulatory requirements were met. Native oysters play a vital role in marine ecosystems, helping to create habitats for other species and naturally filtering water. The restored reef could support local fisheries, improve water quality, and strengthen the wider marine environment. As a pilot scheme, the project is also expected to inform future oyster restoration efforts across the UK, helping tackle long-term declines in native oyster populations.

state: The United Kindgom welcomes the continued consolidation of peace and stability in the Central African Republic: UK statement at the UN Security Council Statement by Jess Jambert-Gray, Deputy Political Coordinator, at the UN Security Council meeting on the Central African Republic. I will make three points on supporting lasting stability in the Central African Republic. First, the United Kingdom welcomes the continued consolidation of peace and stability gains and stresses the importance of protecting them. The development of national and local institutions following elections, alongside progress in implementing the Political Agreement for Peace and Reconciliation, are encouraging steps. We also welcome continued progress on the disarmament and demobilisation of combatants. However, growing conflict and insecurity in parts of the region pose risks, and it is important to ensure that hard-won gains are not rolled back. We urge further steps to address persistent insecurity in the border areas. Recent escalations including in the CAR, Chad, and Sudan tri-border area underscore the impact of regional instability, including spillover from the conflict in Sudan. With more than 416,000 people internally displaced and around two million facing food insecurity, it is critical to ensure humanitarian access. Second, sustained security sector reform remains crucial. Long-term stability will rest on the Central African Republic’s security institutions assuming greater responsibility for national security. These institutions need to be accountable and inclusive. Continued efforts on disarmament and demobilisation are important, especially supporting reintegration opportunities for former combatants to prevent return to armed groups. We encourage the Government of the Central African Republic to sustain momentum on reforms, with support from international partners and MINUSCA. And third, we welcome the significant work undertaken by MINUSCA, in coordination with the Government of the Central African Republic, to reconfigure the Mission and establish a clear pathway for its transition. We commend the SRSG for all of her leadership, and thank her for all of her work over the last four years. As this Council considers MINUSCA’s mandate in the coming weeks, it will be important that any transition is gradual, conditions-based, carefully sequenced, and guided by realities on the ground. This will be essential to protect stability in the Central African Republic and to support the protection of civilians.

state: Skills Minister Jacqui Smith speech at Parliamentary reception for WorldSkills UK Skills Minister Jacqui Smith delivers a speech at a Parliamentary reception for WorldSkills UK, 19 October 2026. It’s a real pleasure and an honour to be here today and to be able to welcome colleagues and partners, employers, educators, family members and most importantly, Team UK here to Parliament. It’s a brilliant opportunity to celebrate your enormous success at WorldSkills Shanghai. When I met up with the team in advance of the welcoming ceremony in Shanghai, I could see a few nerves about what was to come. But overwhelmingly, what I felt was that you were an enormously well-prepared and ready to go group of people. And seeing you all walking out as part of that amazing opening ceremony was brilliant. I was very proud. You may have seen me standing up and clapping loudly and enthusiastically. It was a brilliant opening ceremony, wasn’t it? Notwithstanding being slightly spooked by the sight of those robots dancing with those ballerinas! Clearly the way of the future, and thank goodness that we’ve got you Peter and Pratham to take forward our robotic skills as well. You did so well, as a team. Simply earning a place in Team UK is a remarkable achievement and reflects years of hard work and dedication and resilience. In Shanghai you demonstrated the very best of UK technical and vocational education, competing against the world’s most talented young people and winning. This year’s competition was particularly significant because you, Team UK, delivered our best WorldSkills performance in almost a decade. And that’s testament to your talent and your determination and professionalism, and also to the strength of the UK’s skills system. Every competitor should be immensely proud, regardless of the medal or the result achieved, because success at WorldSkills is about excellence, growth, and representing your country on a global stage. As others have said though, I’d also like to recognise all of those people who helped you to make that possible. Your training managers and technical experts. The colleges, training providers and universities that are training and supporting you. The employers who invested in talent development. And I’m sure as well your families and friends who would have given you unwavering support for all those months and years when you were focused on what is necessary in order to achieve the sort of excellence that you have achieved. Medals are brilliant. But WorldSkills is about more than medals as well. It allows us to benchmark ourselves against the very best in the world. It helps us identify and adopt international best practice. It raises standards across education, training and industry throughout the UK. And the skills represented by Team UK are vital to our country’s future as well, helping to drive economic growth, supporting innovation and productivity, building the workforce that our industries need for the future. And by competing at this level, you’re also inspiring the next generation to pursue technical education, apprenticeships and skilled careers. You’ll have heard, I hope, the Prime Minister talking about how important it is that we provide the focus and the resource and the importance to technical and vocational education and you’re the manifestation of that. Shanghai also highlighted the importance of international collaboration and learning. And I’m pleased that we are going to be able to continue this collaboration with China following that recent visit. There’ll be a UK-China Education Summit on the 24 and 25 November 2026 in Beijing, to continue the ministerial dialogue that I began with my counterparts whilst in Beijing and Shanghai. International engagement of this kind help strengthen educational partnerships, share expertise, and create opportunities for future collaboration. As we celebrate today, I hope that every member of Team UK reflects on what you’ve achieved. You represented the United Kingdom with distinction. You demonstrated excellence on the world stage and you helped to secure Britain’s strongest WorldSkills result for nearly 10 years. So on behalf of the government, can I thank you for everything that you’ve achieved and for being outstanding ambassadors for UK skills. Congratulations once again to Team UK and you thoroughly deserve to enjoy today’s celebration. Thank you.

state: Readout of the Civil Society Council: 15 October 2026 On Thursday 15 October, the Civil Society Council met at the King’s Trust in Manchester. On Thursday 15 October, the Civil Society Council met at the King’s Trust in Manchester. The Prime Minister opened by recognising the vital contribution that civil society organisations make in our communities. He reflected that “if you start where people live, with organisations they trust, all kinds of things are possible”. He argued for a whole-government, whole-society approach to supporting people as they grow up and to tackle youth unemployment as part of the 10-year plan to be published later this year. The PM reflected on the power of partnership with civil society and the importance of coming together to deliver better outcomes. He reiterated the need “to face the same way and pull in the same direction. It’s about empowering people and places to find their own solutions and trusting them to do so.” He drew on the experience of Covid, and the particular contribution of faith communities during that time. The PM then spoke about Live Well in Greater Manchester where a joined-up, person-centred approach, with civil society as an equal partner, meant people could access the support they need. In this, he reflected that “civil society in all its many iterations is absolutely critical to the success of our country.” In response, the Council proposed a deep dive into the principles of Live Well and other community-led models. This will be taken forward by a coalition of partners with DHSC’s sponsorship, learning from and informing wider work on the transition to neighbourhood health. Culture Secretary, Lisa Nandy MP reflected that as civil society organisations are dealing with the realities of peoples live everyday across the country, they should be a respected and trusted partner of government at every level, with a critical role to play as devolution is accelerated. Sally Jameson MP, Minister for the No10 North Devolution strategy, then joined a session on rewiring the state. Minister Jameson set out more details of the Government’s vision for devolution and public service reform, and invited Council Members’ reflections on the structures, capability and incentives needed to shift power closer to communities. Finally, Vicky Foxcroft MP, Minister for Civil Society and Youth, joined Council Members to discuss opportunities for young people. This focused particularly on how government and civil society can work together in giving young people the confidence, skills and support they need as they transition into the world of work. The Council Chair, Kate Lee, closed the discussion by thanking Council Members for their contributions. She reflected on progress since the last Council Meeting – across civil service capability building, embedding public participation, changes to procurement processes and work underway on volunteering rates – and agreed actions to be taken forward ahead of the next meeting.

state: SS Richard Montgomery mast removal project All 3 masts of SS Richard Montgomery have been successfully removed and have been transferred to the Historic Dockyard Chatham for conservation and preservation. I wish to inform the House that the SS Richard Montgomery mast removal project has now been completed, with all 3 masts successfully removed and delivered to the Historic Dockyard Chatham. The wreck is a World War 2 cargo ship that sank in the Thames Estuary in 1944 while carrying an estimated 1,400 tonnes of munitions cargo. The removal of the 3 masts was recommended by an expert advisory group formed to consider the management of the wreck. As the vessel has aged, the masts continued to place significant load on the structure and their removal has reduced that risk and supports the long-term safe management of the site. This was a complex project requiring specialist programme, engineering and risk management expertise to address a unique risk and a challenging site. Nonetheless, the project was completed ahead of schedule and below forecast costs. This was achieved through close collaboration between the Department for Transport (DfT), the United States Maritime Administration, industry and local partners and I would like to place on record my thanks to all those whose expertise and professionalism contributed to its successful delivery. In recognition of the historic significance of the SS Richard Montgomery and its role in supporting the Allied forces’ efforts during World War 2, the recovered masts and associated artefacts have been transferred to the Historic Dockyard Chatham for conservation and preservation. This will help ensure that an important part of the region’s heritage is protected for future generations. The wreck will continue to be subject to continuous monitoring and control via the established exclusion zone. Existing restrictions on flying in the vicinity of the site also remain in force. The government remains committed to the safe and responsible management of the SS Richard Montgomery, with public safety remaining our highest priority.

state: Families of missing Brits abroad to benefit from new support as government partners with charity Missing People The families of British people missing abroad are set to receive improved support, as a result of a new partnership between the UK Government and the charity Missing People. - UK government announces new partnership with charity Missing People to support those with a missing loved one in the UK and abroad. - Agreement will see Foreign Office directly refer consenting families to services provided by Missing People to ensure they have access to all available support. - Support on offer will include peer support networks and family events to help manage emotional strain of a loved one going missing. The families of British people missing abroad are set to receive improved support, as a result of a new partnership between the UK Government and the charity Missing People. Under the new agreement, Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) consular assistance teams will directly refer consenting families they are supporting to Missing People for tailored assistance. This could include engagement with trained family support teams, as well as a host of other family-centred services and events designed to help manage the emotional burden of a loved one going missing. The partnership will ensure more people can access Missing People’s vital services and will mean families whose loved ones are missing in another country will be able to more easily access the support they need, when they need it the most. FCDO Minister for Consular, Stephen Doughty MP, said: Not knowing where a loved one is, or what has happened to them, is a truly awful experience for any family – and when they have gone missing in a distant part of the world, accessing support can be even harder. We are committed to strengthening our support for British people with a modern consular service that ensures they receive compassionate and professional support at every step. As part of that, our new partnership with Missing People will help provide enhanced support to families and friends in some of their most difficult moments. The FCDO deals with hundreds of cases a year of people going missing abroad and can help families contact and arrange meetings with local authorities as well as helping to keep them informed of new developments. Missing People bolsters that support by working directly with the family and friends of the missing person. They support around 10,000 people affected each year and already work with several departments across National and devolved governments. Director of Services at Missing People, Sophie Lapham, said: When someone goes missing abroad, families can find themselves facing enormous uncertainty and distress. They are forced to navigate unfamiliar systems and language barriers, often from thousands of miles away. We are delighted to be partnering with the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) to ensure more families can access support during some of the most difficult moments of their lives. For more than 30 years, Missing People has been supporting missing people, as well as families and friends living through the trauma of a disappearance. This partnership will strengthen our ability to work alongside the FCDO, offering missing people and families hope, guidance and a trusted source of support for as long as they need. The new partnership comes as part of the overall strengthening of approach to consular services as the UK Government works to ensure it provides British nationals with support when they need it most.

state: GAD uses actuarial modelling to support pandemic preparedness GAD modelling explored how uncertainty in vaccine development could affect pandemic response decisions and their economic impact. The Government Actuary’s Department (GAD) worked with the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) to explore how uncertainty in vaccine development could influence the economic consequences of pandemic response decisions. This included uncertainty in development timescales and the number of vaccine candidates. Building on wider preparedness activity, the proof of concept combined scientific input, economic evidence and actuarial techniques to demonstrate how a range of possible outcomes could be explored, rather than relying on a single estimate. It showed how actuarial modelling can help decision-makers understand uncertainty and quantify risk. The ask The UK’s pandemic preparedness strategy emphasises the use of analysis, scientific evidence and expert advice. UKHSA asked GAD to test whether actuarial techniques could support understanding of uncertainty in vaccine development and help frame its potential implications for the UK economy. This was exploratory work. It was designed to demonstrate a modelling approach, not to recommend a particular response or replace the scientific, operational and policy judgements for which decision-makers remain responsible. What GAD did GAD and UKHSA developed a simplified, hypothetical model to explore how uncertainty in vaccine-development timescales could interact with the economic effects of pandemic response choices. UKHSA brought public health and subject-matter expertise, while GAD designed the modelling approach and interpretation of risk. Drawing on expert input and desk-based research, GAD represented a sequence of uncertain vaccine-development milestones and tested many plausible pathways through them. The model then linked the resulting timescales to a measure of potential economic impact. Rather than producing a single forecast, the analysis generated a distribution of outcomes. This allowed the team to examine central estimates, less likely but more severe outcomes, and the assumptions that had the greatest influence on results. How GAD added value The actuarial approach made uncertainty explicit and connected it to consequences that matter to decision-makers. It provided a consistent framework for comparing options, testing sensitivities and showing how new evidence could change the assessment of risk. The work also illustrated the importance of diversification: relying on fewer vaccine candidates could increase expected development times. Such delays could lead to higher economic costs. The value of actuarial analysis This project showed how actuarial modelling can complement scientific and economic analysis in pandemic preparedness. It can quantify uncertainty, compare possible outcomes and highlight concentration risk, helping decision-makers consider trade-offs and the implications of emerging evidence. “GAD worked closely with UKHSA to deliver a useful and clearly presented piece of analysis within a challenging timescale. The team helped sharpen the focus of the work, communicated clearly throughout the project and produced a valuable output for us. We were impressed by the team’s technical expertise and would welcome opportunities to work with GAD again in future.” Michael West, Deputy Chief Economist, UK Health Security Agency Supporting future decisions The analysis was a hypothetical, non-advisory proof of concept. Further research, validation and assurance would be needed before adapting the model to support live decisions. As evidence develops, a future model could be updated to reflect observed development times, changes in the number of vaccine candidates and revised economic assumptions. This could show how the risk picture changes and help communicate complex information in a form relevant to decision-makers.

state: Over 100,000 job and training opportunities a year to give young people a route into Britain’s growth industries as part of industrial strategy Young people will get thousands more opportunities to start skilled careers in some of Britain’s fastest-growing industries, as government and businesses join forces to expand apprenticeships, work experience and training. - Young people to benefit from thousands more routes into skilled careers, including 22,400 new under-25 apprenticeships a year in professional and business services and 40,000 construction placements every year - Industrial Strategy plans come ahead of Milburn review into young people, opening up routes into good jobs while building the skilled workforce Britain needs to grow and reindustrialise - Devolution at heart of plans, with mayors and local skills partnerships helping shape training around the jobs and skills their areas need Young people will get thousands more opportunities to start skilled careers in some of Britain’s fastest-growing industries, as government and businesses join forces to expand apprenticeships, work experience and training. Industrial Strategy Jobs Plans published today for Professional and Business Services and Construction will support 22,400 new under-25 apprenticeships a year in businesses such as accountants, legal services, and consultants. This will come alongside 40,000 construction placements annually as part of a previously announced construction industry ambition to create 100,000 job opportunities a year. They mark the start of a week of Jobs Plans, with further plans for Digital and Technologies and Defence due to be published later this week. The Defence Jobs Plan will help deliver thousands of opportunities for young people, including an increase in the number of people supported through apprenticeship programmes in the defence sector to at least 14,000 annually by 2035. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said: Reindustrialising Britain means giving workers the skills they need to get good jobs in growing industries. Too many young people are being denied the chance to get a foot on the career ladder. These Jobs Plans bring government and industry together to change that, opening up more apprenticeships, training and vocational routes into rewarding careers. Our Modern Industrial Strategy is backing the industries where Britain can lead and making sure people in every part of the country benefit from our industrial renewal.” Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said: Too many young people have been locked out of opportunities for too long. These commitments will help change that by creating clear pathways into apprenticeships, training and good jobs. It’s encouraging to see even more industries backing young people with new opportunities to gain the skills, training and experience needed to succeed in the growing sectors of our economy. By working hand in hand with employers, we’re building a skills system that meets the needs of modern industry while delivering our Youth Guarantee and helping more young people build rewarding careers. From accountancy and law to bricklaying, engineering and defence, the plans will create clearer routes into skilled careers while helping businesses recruit the workforce they need to grow. Coming ahead of the final Milburn review into young people and employment, the plans will help connect more young people, including those not in education, employment or training, with opportunities to earn, learn and build a career. By bringing government, businesses and local areas together behind investment, skills and good jobs, the plans will also support the drive to reindustrialise Britain and spread the benefits of growth across the country. The Jobs Plans will put local partnerships at the heart of tackling skills shortages, with mayors, employers and Local Skills Improvement Plans shaping stronger routes into work through apprenticeships, work experience and vocational training. The Plans include: Professional and Business Services: - PBS firms have committed to recruiting 22,400 new apprentices aged under 25 each year over the next five years, alongside a 20% increase in work experience opportunities for young people. The sector will also establish systems to measure and track recruitment and support for young people not in education, employment or training. - Opportunities will range from accountancy, business and law to AI, cyber security and data analytics, with commitments supported by leading employers and representative organisations across the PBS sector. - Employers will support good jobs and workforce development through commitments including wider adoption of the Living Wage, a new PBS Good Jobs Standard, AI literacy training and tracking greater salary transparency in early-career recruitment. Construction: - Industry will strengthen workforce planning for construction, identifying jobs and skills needs nationally, regionally and locally, with sector-specific plans for sectors including homebuilding, infrastructure, repair and maintenance, and professional and technical roles. *Major projects and new technology will be used to boost skills, productivity and job quality, including stronger employment and skills outcomes through procurement and social value, and preparing workers for AI and industrialised construction. - A Construction Apprenticeship Network will be created to boost apprentice recruitment and participation by smaller firms. - Opportunities will span skilled trades such as bricklaying, carpentry, electrical work and plumbing, alongside careers in engineering, surveying, planning and construction management, supported by industry bodies including the Construction Skills Mission Board and the Construction Leadership Council. Defence: - Following September’s agreement, defence firms will expand work experience and pathways for young people not in education employment or training by 25%. - Industry will also introduce a “no wrong door” approach to help suitable candidates access opportunities across the defence supply chain. This is supported by the government’s £2.5 billion youth employment package, which will deliver almost one million opportunities for young people to earn or learn through apprenticeships, work experience and training. The apprenticeship system is being pivoted towards the next generation, including 50,000 additional apprenticeships for young people and a new incentive of up to £2,000 for SMEs that take on a 16 to 24-year-old apprentice. Businesses will also be supported to back young talent through the continued National Insurance exemption for under-21s and apprentices under 25. These plans are also underpinned by wider government action to put technical education on a par with academic learning and ensure more young people have access to high-quality technical education. Alongside the UK’s world-leading universities, Technical Excellence Colleges, new V Levels and expanded T Levels, and new Vocational GCSEs, will arm young people with the skills and confidence for the world of work. Phil Smith, Chair of Skills England and member of the Industrial Strategy Advisory Council, said: World class apprenticeships and skills training will be absolutely vital to supporting thousands more young people into rewarding careers and making sure these Jobs Plans deliver for key industries and sectors. That includes through new foundation apprenticeships, for people starting out their careers, and shorter apprenticeship units to help them develop fast once they’re in work. Bringing government, businesses and local areas together through these plans makes perfect sense. It reflects the collaborative approach now being taken to ensure the skills system delivers what businesses and our emerging workforce needs. Notes to editors - The new plans build on Jobs Plans already published for Financial Services, Clean Energy Industries and Life Sciences. Jobs Plans are being developed across all eight growth-driving sectors identified in the Modern Industrial Strategy, as well as Construction, complementing the Sector Plans published in 2025. - The Advanced Manufacturing and Creative Industries Jobs Plans will follow shortly, setting out further action to build the workforce needed for Britain’s industrial renewal. - The latest Industrial Strategy quarterly update shows progress across the eight growth-driving sectors, including over £1 billion of automotive investment supporting more than 5,000 jobs, over £3 billion of public-private investment in Life Sciences since publication of the Sector Plan, and a £600 million package for British aerospace, including £500 million for cutting-edge R&D. It also highlights £1.5 billion committed by ScottishPower to repower Whitelee windfarm, £800 million from EDF and Centrica to refurbish Sizewell B, and a £26 billion programme to modernise Royal Navy bases. - On average, jobs in the eight Industrial Strategy priority sectors pay around £8,000 more a year than jobs across the wider economy. - The government is also making reforms to computing education, including a new Computing GCSE, will ensure all pupils develop the digital and AI skills needed for future jobs and careers.

state: Helping communities stay ahead of flooding along the Great Ouse After months of extreme weather, the Environment Agency have been stepping up efforts to protect the country from weather whiplash. This is where prolonged dry conditions can be followed by periods of heavy rainfall and flooding. With severe drought recently declared in parts of southern England, and a heightened potential for a wet winter, communities can face contrasting challenges of water scarcity and flooding, sometimes in the same season. The Environment Agency is encouraging communities to prepare for the risks ahead as part of its Flood Action Week campaign. Across the Great Ouse catchment communities are strengthening their flood preparedness now. Thirty-five communities across the Great Ouse catchment have already developed community flood plans and received a start-up emergency flood kit. Tailored to each community the kits typically include high visibility jackets, a submersible pump, roadside ‘Flood’ signs, temporary barriers, a first aid kit, two-way radios, and torches. These are practical tools that can make a real difference when flooding threatens. Adam Foster, Flood Risk Manager from the Environment Agency said: “We’re facing extreme weather, with flood and drought placing communities under growing pressure. Building resilience has never been more important. “Through flood groups, community flood plans, and emergency flood kits, this project is equipping local volunteers and communities to respond quickly and effectively when water levels rise. We can’t always prevent flooding, but we can help communities understand their risk, be better prepared and hopefully recover more quickly.” One example of community preparedness in action is Riseley, Bedfordshire, where residents have shown the value of getting organised before flooding strikes. Residents formed a flood group and worked with the Environment Agency and Bedford Borough Council to develop a community flood plan, identify vulnerable residents, and spread the word through door-knocking, social media and leaflets. And, when flooding later hit the village, their preparation paid off. Alongside the kits, CCTV cameras are being installed at flood-risk locations across the catchment, letting communities, the Environment Agency and partners monitor conditions remotely. For residents, that means they can check water levels online and make informed decisions without leaving home. Nine cameras are already in place, with a tenth installed in Newport Pagnell last week. As the weather becomes increasingly unpredictable, knowing your flood risk and understanding what to do when warnings are issued can help households prepare for changing conditions. During Flood Action Week, people are being encouraged to take simple, proactive steps: check their flood risk, prepare a flood plan, and sign up for flood warnings. Households can also visit Flood Action Online, a one-stop hub where people can check their flood risk, sign up for warnings, access Met Office alerts, and find practical advice on making their homes more resilient. Notes to editors: - The Great Ouse catchment flood resilience project is funded through the local levy programme and delivered in partnership with local authorities. - Communities in the catchment can apply for a flood kit and flood monitoring camera after developing a suitable community flood plan with support from the Environment Agency. - Communities with flood kits: Alconbury, Alconbury Weston, Biggleswade, Blunham, Brampton, Buckden, Buckingham, Cambridge, Cottenham, Cranfield, Elsworth, Fen Drayton, Great Barford, Harrold, Houghton and Wyton, Kempston West, Kempston, Langford, Newport Pagnell, Northill, Oakington and Westwick, Potton, Riseley, Sandy, Shefford, St Ives, Stevington, Stony Stratford, Stotfold, Swavesey, Swineshead, Walsham le Willows, Wistow, Woughton, Yelden and Melchbourne. - Communities with flood monitoring cameras: Alconbury, Alconbury Weston, Cambridge, Harrold, Newport Pagnell, Riseley, St Ives, Stony Stratford, Wistow, Yelden and Melchbourne. - Only communities within the Great Ouse catchment are eligible for community flood kits and flood monitoring cameras. The catchment crosses county boundaries and includes parts of Northamptonshire, Buckinghamshire, Hertfordshire, Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire, Norfolk, Suffolk, and Essex. Communities located within these counties but outside the catchment are not eligible. For information about Community Flood Plans

state: MHRA authorises plozasiran (Redemplo) for adults with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has today, 19 October 2026, authorised plozasiran (Redemplo) The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has today, 19 October 2026, authorised plozasiran (Redemplo) to reduce triglyceride levels in adults with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome (FCS), alongside a low-fat diet. FCS is a rare condition that causes abnormally high levels of fats called triglycerides in the blood. This can lead to inflammation of the pancreas, known as pancreatitis, causing severe abdominal pain. Plozasiran blocks the production of apolipoprotein C3, a protein made in the liver that slows the breakdown of fats. Reducing production of this protein helps lower triglyceride levels in the blood. The medicine is administered as a 25 mg injection under the skin once every three months. Patients or their caregivers can give the injection after receiving training. Julian Beach, Executive Director, Operations, said: “This authorisation provides an additional treatment option for adults with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome, a rare condition that can cause serious and painful complications. “Clinical trial data showed that plozasiran substantially reduced triglyceride levels when used alongside a controlled diet. “As with all medicines, we will continue to monitor the safety of plozasiran closely.” The authorisation is supported by a main study involving 75 adults with FCS. All participants followed a controlled diet, with 50 receiving plozasiran and 25 receiving placebo. After 10 months, participants receiving plozasiran had a median reduction in triglyceride levels of around 80%, compared with 17% among those receiving placebo. The study also recorded fewer episodes of acute pancreatitis in participants receiving plozasiran. The most common side effect reported with plozasiran is hyperglycaemia (raised blood sugar), which may affect more than one in 10 people. Other common side effects, which may affect up to one in 10 people, include headache, nausea and reactions at the injection site. Anyone who suspects they are experiencing a side effect should speak to their doctor, pharmacist or nurse and report it directly through the Yellow Card scheme at https://yellowcard.mhra.gov.uk or via the MHRA Yellow Card app. Notes to editors - The marketing authorisation was granted on 19 October 2026 to Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals Ireland Limited. - It was approved through the International Recognition Procedure (IRP), Route B, with the European Medicines Agency (EMA) as the reference regulator. - More information can be found in the Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC) and Patient Information Leaflet (PIL), which will be published on the MHRA Products website in due course. - The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) is responsible for regulating all medicines and medical devices in the UK by ensuring they work and are acceptably safe. All our work is underpinned by robust and fact-based judgements to ensure that the benefits justify any risks. - The MHRA is an executive agency of the Department of Health and Social Care. - For media enquiries, please contact newscentre@mhra.gov.uk, or call 020 3080 7651.

state: Troubles Bill strengthened to deliver greater truth and accountability for victims and better protections for veterans The Government will today [Monday 19 October] strengthen the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill through a substantial package of amendments. The Government will today [Monday 19 October] strengthen the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill through a substantial package of amendments designed to deliver greater truth and accountability for victims and families, while providing clear protections for veterans. The changes include measures to strengthen the new Legacy Commission, such as by setting deadlines for public bodies to hand over information. The strengthened Bill is intended to address the long-standing legacy commitments of the Good Friday Agreement and give families the greatest possible opportunity to get the answers they have waited years for. Other amendments enable the Commission to use the expertise of police forces to assist investigations and introduce regular inspections of the Commission’s work. During Committee Stage, the House of Commons will also debate the measures brought forward by the Government to ensure that legacy processes treat our veterans who served in Northern Ireland fairly, and with dignity and respect. This includes protection from repeated investigations, protection from cold calling, and a formal recognition of the operational context in which members of the security forces served in protecting the rule of law. The bolstered Bill carefully navigates one of the most sensitive challenges of legacy reform by striking a clear, balanced path forward: delivering meaningful information and acknowledgement for victims and survivors, while safeguarding service personnel and veterans who served with distinction under lawful authority. Speaking ahead of the House of Commons Committee Stage, the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, Sir Chris Bryant said: At its heart, this legislation exists to deliver the unfinished business of the Good Friday Agreement. For far too long, families and victims have been left without the clear, transparent answers they deserve, while veterans have faced prolonged uncertainty and anxiety. We must right the wrongs of the Legacy Act, which compounded those harms and failed to deliver the confidence of veterans, victims and families across Northern Ireland and Great Britain. Last week’s substantial amendments will strengthen our Bill immeasurably and I am confident that this framework turns a corner on legacy by putting truth and accountability first whilst upholding our lasting commitment to those who served. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: Veterans who served honourably in Northern Ireland in extremely challenging circumstances to protect lives and uphold the rule of law should not face an endless cycle of reinvestigation. The amendments to the Bill – developed in consultation with veterans – rightly ensure they have the strong and lasting legal protections they deserve after the service they have given to our country. As the Bill enters its final stages of debate in the House of Commons, the Government remains focused on securing a lasting legacy solution - one grounded in truth, integrity and accountability for all communities affected by the Troubles. It will deliver legacy mechanisms which command broad public confidence and give families the greatest possible opportunity to obtain answers by: - Scrapping the Legacy Act’s conditional immunity scheme which would have allowed terrorists to escape justice for their crimes; - Fundamentally reforming the Independent Commission for Reconciliation for Information Recovery, to be renamed Legacy Commission; - Unlocking the fullest possible cooperation by the Irish Government with the reformed Commission. - Implementing clear and workable protections for former service personnel; and; - Establishing the Independent Commission on Information Retrieval (ICIR) under the Joint Framework agreed with the Irish Government. The Bill is expected to conclude its passage through the House of Commons tomorrow, after which it will proceed to the House of Lords.

state: Have your say on the future of Part K of the building regulations Help inform the Building Safety Regulator's review of Part K and Approved Document K by sharing evidence, research and experience. The Building Safety Regulator (BSR) is launching a call for evidence on Part K of the building regulations and its associated statutory guidance, Approved Document K. Part K covers protection from falling, collision and impact in and around buildings. It includes requirements and guidance on features including stairs, ramps, handrails, guarding, windows, doors, glazing and vehicle barriers. As part of its duties under the Building Safety Act 2022, BSR keeps the safety and standards of buildings under review to ensure regulations and guidance are fit for purpose and reflect best practice. Reviewing Part K and Approved Document K is an important part of that wider programme of work. Part K is one part of a wider system of building regulations that collectively shape the design, construction and use of buildings. Keeping these standards under review helps make sure they continue to work effectively together and support safe, accessible and high-quality buildings and homes. The call for evidence is an opportunity for professionals, organisations, researchers, building owners, occupants and members of the public to share their views, experiences and evidence to help inform that work. Why are we seeking evidence? Part K and Approved Document K help protect people from accidents involving falls, collisions and impacts in and around buildings. It has been more than 20 years since a substantial review of Part K and Approved Document K took place. We want to gather evidence on whether the current requirements and guidance are effective, and if there are areas that need greater clarity, strengthening, more research or further development. This call for evidence is not proposing policy changes. Instead, it is intended to help BSR build a stronger evidence base and identify priorities for future work. The current requirements and guidance remain in place while the review is undertaken. What are we looking for feedback on? We are seeking feedback on all areas of Part K and Approved Document K, including those covering: - stairs and ladders - ramps and handrails - guarding and protection from falls - windows, doors and gates - glazing - vehicle barriers We are particularly interested in evidence, experience and research that can help us understand where existing requirements and guidance work well and where further consideration may be needed. We want to hear from people who design, construct, manage and use buildings. You can tell us where guidance may no longer reflect current practice, where greater clarity is needed, and where innovations in design, construction and building use should be considered in future guidance. We also want to hear from people who live in, work in and visit buildings. Their experiences can help us understand how buildings are used in practice and whether existing requirements and guidance continue to support safe and accessible environments. The call for evidence is also an opportunity for respondents to comment on issues that have been raised by stakeholders. This includes the consistency of guidance across Approved Documents and approaches to protecting people from falls in different building types. Supporting research publications BSR, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) and the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) have published research looking at stair safety and whether guidance relating to stairs in dwellings and other buildings may need to be strengthened. These findings contribute to our understanding of the issues and form part of the wider evidence base for the review of Part K and Approved Document K. Read the research reports: - Evidence to support potential changes to Approved Document K guidance on domestic stairs - RR1228: Safety of stairs for limited access in dwellings: A mixed methods study - HSE What happens next? The call for evidence will help inform the next stage of the review of Part K and Approved Document K. Every response received will contribute to the evidence base that supports the review. Once the evidence-gathering phase is complete, BSR will analyse the responses alongside other research and evidence. This will help us prioritise future work and inform the ongoing review of Part K and Approved Document K. Any future proposals for changes to building regulations or statutory guidance will be subject to further consultation. Some issues raised through the call for evidence may require longer-term consideration and may form part of BSR’s ongoing programme of work reviewing building standards and guidance. Take part The call for evidence will run for 10 weeks. We encourage respondents to submit their views through the online survey, which will support the efficient analysis of responses. Information on alternative ways to respond are in the call for evidence documentation.
