state: SEC Censures OTC Link LLC for Repeated Compliance Failures Related to Regulation SCI Washington D.C., Sept. 22, 2026 — The Securities and Exchange Commission today censured New York-based broker dealer OTC Link LLC and ordered it to pay a $575,000 civil penalty for longstanding violations of Regulation Systems Compliance and Integrity (SCI). According to the SEC’s settled order, between August 2016 and March 2025, OTC Link LLC failed to establish, maintain, and enforce certain written policies and procedures required by Regulation SCI for OTC Link ATS—an alternative trading system for over-the-counter securities that it operates—including policies and procedures pertaining to system security, access control, and application vulnerability management, testing, and remediation. Although staff in the SEC’s Division of Examinations examined OTC Link ATS several times during the relevant period and each time flagged certain required policies and procedures that the firm had not established or kept in draft form and failed to finalize or enforce, the SEC’s order finds that OTC Link LLC repeatedly failed to promptly remediate such deficiencies. “OTC Link’s continual failure to remediate deficiencies even after they were repeatedly flagged by Division of Examinations staff reflects a disregard for their findings and the overall examinations process and justifies a meaningful penalty,” said Laura D’Allaird, Chief of the Division of Enforcement’s Cyber and Emerging Technologies Unit. “All SCI entities are expected to take their regulatory responsibilities seriously and promptly fix issues when they're identified.” The SEC’s order finds that OTC Link LLC lacked written policies and procedures that were reasonably designed to ensure that OTC Link ATS’s SCI systems and, for purposes of security standards, indirect SCI systems, had levels of capacity, integrity, resiliency, availability, and security adequate to maintain OTC Link ATS’s operational capability and promote the maintenance of fair and orderly markets in violation of Rule 1001(a)(1) of Regulation SCI. By failing to have required minimum policies and procedures, to periodically review the effectiveness of its policies and procedures, and to take prompt action to remedy its deficiencies, the SEC’s order also finds that OTC Link LLC violated Rules 1001(a)(2) and 1001(a)(3). Without admitting the findings, OTC Link LLC agreed to a cease-and-desist order, a censure, and a civil penalty of $575,000. ### Last Reviewed or Updated: Sept. 22, 2026

Key Highlights: First Half 2026 In the first half of 2026, IPO and follow-on offering activity showed year-over-year growth: - IPOs: There were 208 IPOs raising over $137 billion in the first half of 2026, compared with 180 IPOs raising over $27 billion in the first half of 2025. state: SEC Charges Founder and His Two New Jersey-Based Companies in Alleged $16 Million Ponzi Scheme Washington D.C., Sept. 10, 2026 — The Securities and Exchange Commission today charged Ernest Ossei Boateng and two New Jersey-based companies he controls, Intercontinental Wealth Network LLC and I Wealth Network LP, for allegedly raising approximately $16 million from more than 200 inexperienced investors through a Ponzi scheme he operated from at least January 2020 until at least March 2026. According to the SEC’s complaint, Boateng, acting through his two companies, solicited, recommended, and sold interests in an alleged investment fund, primarily targeting Christians of Ghanaian heritage in New York and New Jersey, many of whom had no prior investing experience. The complaint alleges that Boateng told investors that their investments would generate guaranteed fixed returns and that the investment fund would pursue a low-risk investment strategy. Rather than investing the money as promised, however, Boateng allegedly misappropriated more than $5.8 million for his personal expenses, including the purchase, renovation, and furnishing of his home. Boateng also allegedly used approximately $6.6 million to make Ponzi-like payments to earlier investors. The complaint further alleges that, to the limited extent Boateng did invest the money, he failed to do so in low-risk investments with fixed returns. Instead, according to the complaint, Boateng used investor money to engage in high-risk, speculative day trading, leading to more than $750,000 in trading losses. “We allege that the defendants’ investors included retirees, taxi drivers, home health care providers, students, an ailing widow with young children, and at least two churches and one prayer group,” said Thomas P. Smith, Jr., Associate Director of the SEC’s New York Regional Office. “The defendants’ sales pitch to victims included assuring them that their investments were safe and without risk—telling many their money was protected by so-called ‘financial, investment insurance.’ That’s as big of a red flag as we see in these types of scams.” The SEC’s complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York, charges Boateng, Intercontinental, and I Wealth with violating the antifraud provisions of the Securities Act of 1933 and Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and Boateng and Intercontinental with violating the antifraud provisions of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. The complaint seeks permanent injunctive relief, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with pre-judgment interest, and civil penalties against all of the defendants, as well as conduct-based injunctions against Boateng and Intercontinental. ### Last Reviewed or Updated: Sept. 10, 2026

state: SEC Charges Meyer Global Management and Its CEO With Defrauding Retail Investors in Private Funds That Held Interests in SpaceX and Other Pre-IPO Securities Washington D.C., Sept. 30, 2026 — The Securities and Exchange Commission today charged private fund adviser Meyer Global Management LLC (MGM) and its CEO, Owen E.H. Meyer, with defrauding investors and MGM-managed funds in connection with investments in SpaceX and other pre-IPO securities. According to the SEC’s complaint, in a series of schemes from at least December 2021 to the present, the defendants violated their fiduciary duties by misusing client fund assets, and lied to the underlying investors in the funds. In at least three of those schemes, the defendants allegedly misappropriated client assets from certain MGM-managed funds to pay for Meyer’s personal expenses. As outlined in the complaint, the defendants concealed their actions in one scheme by sending statements to investors that inflated their account values. The complaint also alleges that, in one of the misappropriation schemes involving three MGM-managed funds, defendants misappropriated portions of investor proceeds and required investors to sign releases accepting distributions of amounts that were less than they were owed in order to get any money at all. Finally, the complaint alleges that defendants repeatedly failed to address a capital call deficiency owed by an MGM-managed fund in connection with its investment in SpaceX, resulting in the fund forfeiting its nearly $3,000,000 investment. “This case is a reminder that fraudsters can exploit the allure of exclusive, high-return pre-IPO access to take advantage of retail investors,” said Corey A. Schuster, Chief of the Enforcement Division’s Asset Management Unit. “The defendants in this matter were investment advisers entrusted with acting as fiduciaries to their clients. Nevertheless, they allegedly engaged in multiple fraudulent acts to enrich themselves.” The complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, charges the defendants with violating antifraud provisions of the Advisers Act of 1940. The SEC seeks permanent injunctive relief, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties against both defendants, as well as a conduct-based injunction against Meyer. ### Last Reviewed or Updated: Sept. 30, 2026

state: SEC Issues “Innovation Exemption” to Facilitate the Trading of Tokenized NMS Stock and Request for Comment Washington D.C., Sept. 17, 2026 — The Securities and Exchange Commission today issued an order granting temporary, conditional exemptive relief to Tokenized Securities Venues each a “TSV” from the definition of “exchange” in the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (Exchange Act) to trade tokenized National Market System (NMS) stock using innovative permissioned automated market makers and liquidity pools (together “AMM Liquidity Pools”). “Today, the Securities and Exchange Commission is taking a significant step forward, within its statutory authority, to bring America’s capital markets into the digital age by facilitating onchain trading of certain tokenized stocks through the ‘Innovation Exemption,’” said SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins in a statement. “The Innovation Exemption, while temporary, would allow TSVs to trade tokenized NMS stock in a permissioned environment today while the Commission considers the need for additional action to facilitate onchain trading. As we take this important first step, we invite public comment on all aspects of the Innovation Exemption to help inform the Commission as it considers further changes.” “Today’s approval of exemptive relief for on-chain secondary trading on a TSV – known as the ‘Innovation Exemption’ – marks an important milestone for the Commission’s work to open our capital markets for tokenized securities,” said Jamie Selway, Director of the SEC Division of Trading and Markets. “The division stands ready to work with interested parties seeking to operate a TSV and field questions from investors and market participants.” TSVs bring together buyers and sellers of tokenized NMS stock by: (1) providing one or more AMM Liquidity Pool(s) for permissioned participants to interact and agree to terms of a trade and (2) setting standards for persons to access trading on such AMM Liquidity Pool(s). The exemption from the definition of “exchange” for TSVs is subject to conditions designed to ensure the exemptive relief is in the public interest and consistent with the protection of investors, including that: - Tokenized NMS stocks traded on a TSV are subject to limits on the number of symbols and volume traded; - A TSV must verify that the tokenized NMS stock made available for trading on the TSV provides holders the same rights and privileges as does traditional NMS stock of an equivalent class; - Before making available for trading a tokenized NMS stock that is tokenized by an unaffiliated third party, the TSV must provide written notice and an opportunity to object to the issuer of the underlying NMS stock; - Smart contracts used by a TSV must be auditable, public, and deployed on a public, permissionless distributed ledger; - A TSV must stop trading in a tokenized NMS stock concurrently with any stoppage of trading in the underlying NMS stock on the primary listing exchange; and - A TSV must provide public notice about its operations, trading activities, and the trading activities of its affiliates on the TSV. In addition, the order also will temporarily grant a conditional exemption from the definition of “dealer” as defined in section 3(a)(5) of the Exchange Act to liquidity providers in an AMM Liquidity Pool used by a TSV that supply liquidity in the form of tokenized NMS stock using proprietary capital and may also be engaged in additional activities that are indicia of dealing activity, such as quoting pricing to customers or entering into agreements to provide committed capital. The exemptions are set to expire five years after publication. The order solicits public comment about possible modifications to the exemptive relief and potential next steps. The order will be published on SEC.gov and in the Federal Register. The SEC looks forward to continued public engagement on the temporary exemptions. ### Last Reviewed or Updated: Sept. 17, 2026

state: SEC Proposal Would Address How Investment Advisers and Funds Can Custody Crypto Assets Under the Federal Securities Laws Washington D.C., Oct. 1, 2026 — The Securities and Exchange Commission today proposed new rules and amendments to provide a tailored framework for the custody of crypto assets for registered investment advisers and regulated funds, i.e. registered investment companies and business development companies. It would also allow regulated funds to offer clients access to a wider range of crypto asset-related investment strategies. “Since the advent of Bitcoin in 2008, the crypto asset market has grown from a niche curiosity into a multi-trillion-dollar asset class to which investors actively seek exposure. Unfortunately, our rules and regulations have not kept pace. To that end, today’s proposal would provide a clear regulatory framework for the custody of crypto assets, giving investment advisers and funds a compliant pathway where none existed before—and replacing the grey of uncertainty created by custody rules crafted for a bygone era,” said SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins in a statement. The proposed rules and amendments under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and the Investment Company Act of 1940 would better address current industry practices and update a number of requirements relating to, among other things, financial statement audits for registered investment advisers and broker-dealer custodial services for regulated funds. The proposal would also permit crypto assets to be held in self-custody under certain circumstances and allow the use of state trust companies as custodians for client and regulated fund crypto assets. The public comment period will remain open for 60 days following the publication of the SEC’s proposing release in the Federal Register. ### Last Reviewed or Updated: Oct. 1, 2026

state: SEC Proposes Amendments to Expand Responsible Retailization of Private Markets Washington D.C., Sept. 30, 2026 — The Securities and Exchange Commission today voted to propose rule amendments that would facilitate capital formation in the public and private markets by expanding retail investor choice and promoting innovation in regulated fund structures while preserving appropriate investor protections and safeguards. The Commission is separately requesting public comment as it considers providing individual investors with additional ways to qualify as an accredited investor by holding in good standing certain professional certifications, designations, or credentials. “Investor demand for private market investment opportunities is growing, and one of my priorities for the Commission is to explore ways to facilitate the ability of individual investors to participate in private markets, while at the same time protecting those investors from bad actors and fraud. The Commission’s efforts in this regard — focused on expanding opportunities for investors’ post-tax, pre-retirement dollars — complement efforts undertaken pursuant to President Trump’s Executive Order on Democratizing Access to Alternative Assets for 401(k) Investors,” said SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins in a statement. The use of performance-based compensation has long been a common and defining characteristic of investment strategies that are associated with private funds, such as hedge fund, private equity, and venture capital strategies. Because performance‑based arrangements have traditionally been associated with private funds, access to these strategies, as a practical matter, has been limited to a narrow group of eligible investors. By permitting similar incentives to, for example, advisers to regulated funds, such advisers may be more likely to offer private market strategies to regulated funds. The proposals would: - Expand the ability of registered investment advisers to receive performance-based compensation from certain categories of clients, including regulated funds, that is calculated on the basis of capital gains or capital appreciation. - Amend certain fund registration and reporting forms to require disclosure of performance-based compensation. - Modernize the interval fund framework, including by allowing the scheduling of repurchases at certain times that better match the liquidity profile of the portfolio. - Replace existing exemptive orders with an exemptive rules-based framework for regulated closed-end funds to issue multiple share classes. Together, these proposed amendments would offer expanded retail access to diversified investment opportunities, while promoting transparency and aligning incentives across the advisory ecosystem. The Commission separately seeks comment on the potential designation of the passage of an accredited investor exam to be developed by the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) as an additional method for investors to be accredited investors. An exam would provide a non-financial pathway for investors to demonstrate their sophistication in the areas of securities, investing, and financial and business matters to appropriately evaluate the merits and risks of a prospective investment. The Commission also seeks comment on the potential designation of holding, in good standing, certain licenses, certifications, or other credentials as additional ways for individuals to qualify as accredited investors. Among the designations the Commission is considering: - A license as a U.S. certified public accountant (CPA) - A charter as a Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA) - A certification as a Certified Financial Planner (CFP) in the United States - The FINRA Investment Banking Representative license (Series 79) - The FINRA Research Analyst license (Series 86 and Series 87) The public comment periods will remain open for 60 days after the date of publication of the proposing releases and the notices in the Federal Register. ### Last Reviewed or Updated: Sept. 30, 2026

state: SEC Proposes Rescission of Shareholder Proposal Rule and Reforms to Proxy Solicitation Process Washington D.C., Sept. 16, 2026 — The Securities and Exchange Commission today proposed to rescind Rule 14a-8 under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, which exceeds the scope of the Commission's statutory authority and intrudes into matters of state law. The Commission outlined independent policy reasons for its proposed rescission of Rule 14a-8. Many of the justifications for adopting the rule either have not been substantiated in practice or are less compelling today, and the rule has had unintended consequences, including the implication of federal preemption that may have discouraged states from developing their own laws governing shareholder proposals. Rescinding Rule 14a-8 would leave determinations about the role of shareholder proposals to state law and company governing documents. "Today, the Commission issued two proposing releases related to its proxy rules under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. The proposals reflect two of my highest regulatory priorities. First, ensuring that the Commission does not improperly intrude into state corporate law when applying the federal securities laws. Second, updating the Commission’s rules to reflect developments in market practice and technology, and other innovations, since the rules’ adoption or last amendment," said SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins in a statement. "Today’s proposals demonstrate my focus on ensuring that the Commission’s rules are within the agency’s statutory authority and reflect policy positions grounded in current and anticipated market practice and modern technologies. I look forward to receiving and reviewing the public’s feedback on both proposals." The Commission also proposed amendments to Rule 14a-4(c) under the Exchange Act to provide companies with greater flexibility and shareholders with greater control regarding proposals for which a company may seek discretionary proxy voting authority. The Commission separately proposed rule amendments to modernize the proxy solicitation process. Reflecting advancements in technology and current realities of shareholder communications, those amendments would: - Eliminate the requirement that companies deliver an annual report to security holders. - Eliminate the delivery deadline when documents are incorporated by reference into a proxy statement. - Eliminate the requirement and the ability to submit Notices of Exempt Solicitation. - Shorten the minimum broker search period from 20 business days to five business days. The public comment periods will remain open for 60 days following the publication of the proposing releases in the Federal Register. ### Last Reviewed or Updated: Sept. 16, 2026

According to the SEC’s complaint, from at least October 2023 through August 2024, Williams, of Port St. Lucie, Florida, made numerous false and misleading statements in order to convince clients to invest in two funds that he controlled. The investors, many of whom trusted Williams because he worked for a third-party police and firefighter pension plan administrator, were allegedly told that one of the funds had a portfolio value of more than $5 million and achieved returns exceeding 140 percent. “We allege that one of the tactics the defendants used to trick investors was to send them cropped screenshots of graphics that showed exorbitant trading profits,” said Stephanie N. Moot, Director of the SEC’s Miami Regional Office. “We strongly urge all investors to use caution when entrusting their funds to others and to be wary of anyone promising high returns with little to no risk.” Williams allegedly misappropriated approximately $384,000 of investor and client funds to pay for personal expenses, including credit card balances, a sports car, and vacations. According to the complaint, Williams began repaying certain investors in August 2024 and has repaid more than $375,000 to certain investors. The SEC’s complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, charges Williams and CMI Capital, which is also known to do business as Check Mate Investments, with violating antifraud and registration provisions of the Securities Act of 1933 and antifraud provisions of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Investment Advisers Act of 1940. Without admitting the allegations in the complaint, the defendants consented to the entry of judgments, subject to court approval, that would permanently enjoin them from violating the charged provisions of the federal securities laws and further enjoin Williams from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any security except for certain transactions in his personal accounts. The proposed judgments further provide that the Court shall order disgorgement with prejudgment interest against Williams and civil penalties against the defendants in amounts to be determined by the Court. Williams also agreed to a forthcoming associational bar against him. ### Last Reviewed or Updated: Sept. 23, 2026

state: SEC Charges Registered Investment Adviser Zoe Financial for Failure to Disclose Conflict of Interest Washington D.C., Sept. 28, 2026 — The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced settled charges against New York-based investment adviser Zoe Financial Inc. for failing to fully and fairly disclose material facts concerning conflicts of interest to its clients and prospective clients. According to the SEC order, Zoe Financial operated a referral service which used an algorithm to match third-party investment advisers in its network with individuals seeking a recommendation for an investment adviser. Zoe Financial salespeople typically would then follow up with individuals who did not schedule a meeting with one of the matches generated by the algorithm, and in ensuing conversations, salespeople often recommended additional advisers to the client, beyond the recommendations generated by the algorithm. In January 2023, Zoe Financial launched Zoe Wealth, through which Zoe Financial offered sub-advisory services, account onboarding assistance, and other back-office support for its network of investment advisers. The order finds that Zoe Financial had a financial incentive for advisers in its network to use Zoe Wealth and encouraged advisers to do so. Further, as described in the order, while Zoe Financial’s algorithm did not consider whether an adviser used Zoe Wealth when it generated recommendations, salespeople often became involved in the referral process, and on many occasions suggested advisers that had not been initially recommended by the algorithm. The order finds that Zoe Financial did not adequately disclose the resulting conflict of interest in its Form ADV Brochure until December 2024. In addition, according to the order, while Zoe Financial disclosed that certain advisory firms held indirect minority interests in Zoe Financial and that this presented a conflict, Zoe Financial did not accurately describe how it mitigated that conflict. “Investment advisers have a fiduciary obligation to fully and fairly disclose material conflicts of interest,” said Sheldon Pollock, Associate Director of the SEC’s New York Regional Office. “Advisers must live up to those disclosure obligations in all aspects of their advisory services, including when they offer a new technology or new feature to their clients.” Accordingly, the order finds that Zoe Financial willfully violated Section 206(2) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. Without admitting the SEC’s findings, Zoe Financial agreed to a cease-and-desist order, a censure, and to pay a civil monetary penalty of $450,000. The order acknowledges certain remedial measures taken by Zoe Financial, including making compliance manual revisions and hiring an in-house chief compliance officer. ### Last Reviewed or Updated: Sept. 28, 2026

state: SEC Charges Two Individuals With Orchestrating Fraud Scheme That Targeted Veterans Washington D.C., Sept. 30, 2026 — The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced charges against Christopher Kenji Dinelli and Jacob David “Kobe” Frankel for allegedly orchestrating a fraud scheme that raised more than $8.7 million from 35 investors through their fund, Beyond Alpha Ventures LLC (BAV), and advisory firm, Beyond Equity LLC. According to the complaint, Dinelli, a former naval officer, targeted veterans as well as individuals who provide medical services to veterans, telling them and other investors that their money would be invested in the BAV fund that was represented to have an options trading strategy and/or affiliated special purpose vehicles (SPVs) that purported to hold pre-IPO securities in two private companies. To induce these investments, the defendants allegedly repeatedly made material misrepresentations concerning, among other things, the past performance of the fund and pre-IPO investments, the amount of assets under management, and BAV’s client base and current and past holdings. Despite consistent losses in the fund, the complaint alleges that Dinelli and Frankel continued to tout wildly successful returns of up to 153% and a sprawling client base, including in a document titled, “Trading Fund Overview 2024,” which claimed a “153% Net Return on Investment.” “The bonds between service members are as strong, if not stronger, than in any other profession,” said Thomas P. Smith, Jr., Associate Director of the SEC’s New York Regional Office. “Through their alleged actions, the defendants took advantage of those relationships for greedy and self-serving purposes. We will hold them accountable for their actions.” The complaint also alleges that without investors’ knowledge, the defendants diverted money provided by pre-IPO securities investors to the fund’s brokerage accounts, where the vast majority of it was lost due to failed options trades. In addition, the complaint alleges Dinelli misappropriated over $1 million and Frankel misappropriated over $340,000. The SEC’s complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, charges Dinelli and Frankel with violating the antifraud provisions of the Securities Act of 1933, the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and, additionally as to Frankel, the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. The complaint seeks permanent injunctions, disgorgement with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties against both defendants. In a parallel criminal action concerning the same conduct, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York this week announced criminal charges against Dinelli and Frankel. Investors can learn more about the risks of investing in pre-IPO offerings in this Investor Alert. ### Last Reviewed or Updated: Sept. 30, 2026

state: SEC Seeks Final Judgment Against Former Western Asset Co-CIO Ken Leech in Cherry Picking Case Washington D.C., Oct. 6, 2026 — The Securities and Exchange Commission today moved for entry of a final judgment by consent against Stephen Kenneth Leech II, the former co-chief investment officer of registered investment adviser Western Asset Management Company LLC, whom the SEC previously charged with a multi-year cherry-picking allocation scheme. As alleged in the SEC’s November 2024 complaint, from at least January 2021 through October 2023, Leech placed trades and then routinely delayed allocations until near or after futures markets set daily settlement prices, allowing him to observe price movements and disproportionally allocate hundreds of millions of dollars in realized and unrealized first‑day gains to favored portfolios and a similar amount of realized and unrealized first‑day losses to disfavored portfolios. Without admitting the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, Leech consented to entry of a final judgment, subject to court approval, that would order him to pay a $3 million penalty, impose an officer-and-director bar and permanently enjoin him from violating antifraud provisions of federal securities laws. Leech also agreed to a forthcoming associational bar against him. In June 2026, the Commission instituted settled public administrative proceedings against Western Asset, ordering the firm to pay a $100 million civil penalty and establishing a Fair Fund to distribute money to affected investors in the disfavored portfolios. “The conduct by Leech and Western Asset was an egregious breach of fiduciary obligations to their clients,” said Brent Wilner, Associate Director of the SEC’s Los Angeles Regional Office. “Together, the resolution with Leech, if approved by the court, and the SEC’s prior settlement with Western Asset will return $103 million and provide meaningful relief to harmed investors, and reinforce that advisers must put clients first, every time.” Also in June 2026, Leech pleaded guilty in U.S. District Court in the Southern District of New York to obstruction of justice charges related to false and misleading testimony he provided to the SEC during its investigation; sentencing will take place in the coming weeks. The SEC acknowledges the assistance of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York and the FBI. ### Last Reviewed or Updated: Oct. 6, 2026

state: SEC Proposes Rescission of Political Contribution Rule for Investment Advisers Washington D.C., Sept. 3, 2026 — The Securities and Exchange Commission today issued a proposal to rescind its “pay-to-play” rule that prohibits investment advisers from providing compensated investment advisory services to a government client for two years after making a political contribution to certain elected officials or candidates, and related recordkeeping requirements. All other requirements of the Advisers Act and its associated rules, including prohibitions on fraud, fiduciary duty requirements, the compliance rule, and the code of ethics rule, would continue to apply. The Commission has determined that the political contribution rule, since its adoption in 2010, has led to significant unintended consequences, such as prohibitions by some advisers on political contributions at the state and local level. Advisers have indicated that the rule is operationally challenging to implement, and creates a de facto strict liability standard, which can lead to situations where small donations or “foot faults” potentially trigger substantial prohibitions and fines. “After more than 15 years of experience administering the ‘pay-to-play’ rule, it is clear that it is overly prescriptive and has produced a host of unintended consequences. Beyond operational implementation challenges, it has imposed serious penalties for small, often impulsive donations to candidates in both parties, and routinely punishes and handicaps advisory firms for an employee making a donation even before joining the business. Furthermore, advisers’ implementation of the rule has effectively resulted in the suppression of political speech,” said SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins in a statement. “Ultimately, matters involving political contributions are more properly governed by local ordinances, state laws, and federal election regulations—not by the SEC.” Specifically, the proposal would rescind Advisers Act Rule 206(4)-5 and amend the Advisers Act recordkeeping rule to eliminate the corresponding provisions related to the political contribution rule. The public comment period will remain open for 60 days after the proposing release is published in the Federal Register. ### Last Reviewed or Updated: Sept. 3, 2026

state: SEC Proposes Expanding Securities Eligible for Cross Trading by Registered Funds Washington D.C., Oct. 9, 2026 — The Securities and Exchange Commission today proposed amendments to the Investment Company Act “cross-trading rule,” which permits transactions in securities between a registered fund and its affiliates under certain conditions. The proposed amendments would modernize and expand the cross-trading rule and would allow cross trades that are beneficial to registered funds and their shareholders (by, for example, reducing a fund’s trading costs), subject to enhanced investor protection measures. “Today, the Commission took another step toward modernizing our regulatory frameworks to meet the realities of today’s markets by proposing amendments to Rule 17a-7 under the Investment Company Act of 1940, which permits trades in securities between registered funds and certain affiliates. When executed appropriately, cross trades allow registered funds to avoid costs associated with open market trades and to then pass those savings on to investors. The amendments we are proposing today would modernize and expand the cross-trading rule, helping to deliver additional cost savings to those investors,” said SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins in a statement. Following the initial adoption of Rule 17a-7 in 1966, registered funds relied on the cross-trading rule to trade both equity and fixed-income securities. However, adoption of the Investment Company Act’s “fund valuation rule” in 2020 effectively restricted cross trading most fixed-income securities, although at the time the Commission recognized that potential revisions to the cross-trading rule were under consideration. The proposed amendments would restore the ability to cross trade most fixed-income securities and modernize the rule’s conditions, including those related to pricing and oversight of cross trades. These modernizations would, among other things, recognize market developments that have led to pricing that is more verifiable and transparent. The proposal would also require aggregated reporting of trading activity and cross trades by registered funds that engage in cross trading to provide additional transparency. The proposal will be published on SEC.gov and in the Federal Register. The comment period will remain open for 60 days after publication in the Federal Register. ### Last Reviewed or Updated: Oct. 9, 2026

state: SEC Charges Multiple Entities in Fraud Schemes Totaling at Least $15 Million That Used WhatsApp and Other Platforms to Lure Investors Washington D.C., Sept. 29, 2026 — The Securities and Exchange Commission today charged multiple entities that are likely operated by individuals located overseas for defrauding hundreds of retail investors, including many in the U.S., through so-called investment confidence scams where the perpetrators sought to build online relationships with unsuspecting clients before stealing their money. In two separate complaints, both filed in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, the SEC charged Cryptoaiml Ltd. and Cryptoaiml Capital Foundation as well as TSAI Pro Ltd. and TSAI Capital Foundation with fraud in connection with schemes that feigned SEC compliance while misappropriating more than $12.5 and $2.8 million, respectively, from investors through online platforms. “Although the methods used to bilk innocent investors in these fraudulent investment scams varied, the goal was the same – promise potential investors outsized returns, claim that they were legitimate entities regulated by the SEC, and then steal their money,” said David Woodcock, Director of the SEC’s Division of Enforcement. “We encourage the public to report these types of schemes as they occur using our online tip portal.” According to the SEC complaint against Cryptoaiml and Cryptoaiml Capital Foundation, from at least August 2024 through March 2025, the entities formed WhatsApp group chats where they gained investor trust by impersonating investment professionals and issuing supposed AI-generated trading “signals” or tips claiming to produce large profits. The defendants allegedly directed investors and clients to open accounts on their fake trading platform and manipulated them into transferring crypto assets to the platform. In some cases, the defendants allegedly established an investment adviser client relationship with unwitting investors who signed investment management agreements that were represented to be legitimate. As alleged, the entities also lured investors and clients to their platform by falsely claiming to be certified by regulators, including the SEC, and posted a screenshot on their website of a falsified Form D filed by Cryptoaiml Ltd. with the SEC. The complaint alleges that there was no genuine trading platform as no trading took place, the reflected profits were fictitious, and investors who attempted to withdraw funds were told that their accounts were frozen until they paid fraudulent advance fees. According to the SEC’s complaint against TSAI Pro Ltd. and TSAI Capital Foundation, from September 2024 to March 2025, the entities represented to investors through their website, WhatsApp chats, and public Facebook that they could earn guaranteed profits by, among other things, depositing funds on their online platform for the purpose of renting bots programmed with artificial intelligence to trade on investors’ behalf. The defendants also told investors that they could earn money by recruiting others to invest in the AI-trading bot program. They also falsely represented that TSAI—which offered and sold the bot program to investors—was fully regulated by the SEC and posted a phony certificate from the agency on their website that referenced a falsified Form D filed by TSAI Pro Ltd. As alleged, the entire AI-trading bot program was a fraud: there were no AI trading bots and deposited funds never were used to earn returns for investors. The SEC’s Office of Investor Education and Assistance has issued investor alerts warning investors that fraudsters may use popular group chats or claim to be officially registered with the SEC to lure investors into scams. The SEC encourages investors to use Investor.gov to check the background of anyone offering or selling them an investment. Separately, the Forms D filed by Cryptoaiml Ltd. and TSAI Pro Ltd. have been removed from the Commission website. ### Last Reviewed or Updated: Sept. 29, 2026

state: Gaza: Funding cuts leave half a million without food assistance Funding shortages have forced the World Food Programme (WFP) to slash assistance to hungry families in the Gaza Strip by roughly one third – a move that will affect some 500,000 people as winter approaches, the UN agency announced on Monday. WFP said that its food assistance “has provided a lifeline for up to 90 per cent of families in Gaza” over the past three years. Since the October 2025 ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas fighters, teams have reached around 1.6 million people monthly with food parcels, wheat flour, bread, hot meals, nutrition support, school snacks and cash assistance. “Improved humanitarian access and delivery of assistance since October 2025 have helped reduce food insecurity, but these gains remain fragile and could quickly be reversed if humanitarian funding continues to decline,” the agency warned. Rations, cash and hot meals reduced This month, WFP is supporting 1.1 million of the most vulnerable people in the war-torn enclave, down from 1.6 million in September. Rations have been cut in half, meaning families will now receive one food parcel instead of two, and a smaller bag of wheat flour. The value of cash assistance given to 75,000 families has also been reduced, while the number of hot mails provided daily across Gaza will drop from 250,000 to 150,000. “Families living in hard-to-reach areas, including near the ‘yellow line’ of Israeli military control, will receive a hot meal every other day instead of daily,” the agency said. For now, WFP is able to continue supporting bakeries that cover a third of Gaza’s bread needs, provide nutrition assistance to 300,000 women and children and deliver healthy school snacks to 200,000 students. Crisis-level hunger The cuts come at a critical time in Gaza, where more than 80 per cent of the population is unemployed, leaving many families unable to afford fresh produce or protein-rich foods, even when they are available. Roughly 67 per cent of Gazans –an estimated 1.4 million people – is experiencing acute food insecurity at crisis levels or worse. Although this is down from 77 per cent at the end of 2025, “improvement remains modest and fragile”, WFP said. Some 200,000 people remain in emergency conditions and immediate food assistance is needed to prevent them from dying from hunger. Meanwhile, only one in five children consumes a sufficiently diverse diet, and access to healthcare and other essential services remains limited. Critical funding needs WFP stressed that as winter approaches, additional resources are urgently needed to sustain emergency food assistance, provide critical engineering support and prevent malnutrition among young children and pregnant and breastfeeding women. Funding for its operations in Palestine in 2026 amount to less than half received in previous years, and the agency urgently requires $450 million to maintain critical operations in Gaza and the West Bank through March. WFP noted that funding shortages have also affected its operations in the West Bank, where the number of people receiving assistance was cut by half – from 400,000 to 200,000 – in September.

state: Inside the New York ‘time machine’ racing to save a century of sound and film “I tell my kids I work in a time machine,” said Rhony Dostaly. In a basement beneath Lincoln Center, the media preservation engineer rescues moments from the past. “I go back in time, and I grab elements, and I make them available for people today.” He and his colleagues at the New York Public Library (NYPL) are working against the clock to preserve the contents of film, tape, discs and cylinders that hold more than a century of sound and moving images. The records are decaying, and the machines that can play them are disappearing. Learning from the past For Mr. Dostaly, it’s not just about technology. He has watched other people’s lives unfold through the archive. Harry Belafonte, the legendary American singer, actor, civil rights activist – and longtime UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador – filmed his family for decades, from teaching his son to ride a bike in Central Park to trips abroad. “I’ve actually seen his kids from toddlers all the way to adults,” Mr. Dostaly said. Films of the African American civil rights leader Malcolm X’s travels, including footage from Mecca, moved him the most. “I’m the one who’s going to be making it available for everyone to see,” he remembered thinking. By looking through footage like this – he hopes – young people “will realize the importance of events that took place before they were here on Earth.” Cultural heritage Next door, Casey McNamara, a media preservation coordinator, bends over a reel of film with a jeweller’s loupe or magnifying glass, checking it frame by frame for tears, splices and shrinkage. On the white leader she has written “BHARATA NATYAM,” the name of one of the oldest Indian classical dance forms. Films may reach her “in a rusty tin, on an old projection reel, or in a lab box, in plastic bags.” Without the work she does, some collections “would remain mostly unseen.” The lab is part of NYPL’s Digital Collections Operations. Once digitized, most of the material will be accessible to anyone with a library card. “The tapes and the decks are no longer being manufactured, but the history needs to be preserved,” explained lab manager Shahed Dowlatshahi. Work like this is exactly the kind of project that the UN’s World Day for Audiovisual Heritage, marked annually on 27 October, is designed to highlight and assist. Preserving UN history In the audio room, Jeff Willens slides a 16-inch disc from a brown paper sleeve marked: A Year To Remember. The UN Radio Division produced it for broadcast on New Year’s Day 1949, when the Organization was still headquartered at Lake Success on Long Island. Copies would have been mailed to radio stations and UN offices around the world. Mr. Willens places it on a turntable with a microscope mounted above it, and the voices of actor Fredric March and sportscaster Ted Husing fill the room. Down the corridor, engineers are digitizing the archive of William Greaves, a pioneering African American documentary filmmaker. His 2001 film Ralph Bunche: An American Odyssey tells the story of the American diplomat who won the 1950 Nobel Peace Prize for mediating the armistice agreements between Israel and Arab States. Mr. Bunche was the first Black Nobel laureate and later became UN Under-Secretary-General. ‘Kind of like surgery’ Time is working against all of it. The acetate film which the New York Public Library is trying to preserve suffers from “vinegar syndrome,” a chemical decay that leaves it brittle, warped and smelling of vinegar. “Once that process starts, there’s no stopping it,” Ms. McNamara said. “You can slow it down with cold storage, but it will never reverse.” Audiotape can arrive crinkled or stuck together and must be repaired by hand. “To be able to repair it and then play it and get a successful transfer is kind of like surgery,” said media preservation engineer Victoria Fajardo. “It really is such a privilege to be one of the first people to listen to a lot of this content for the first time since it’s been recorded.” Even Digital Betacam cassettes, once considered robust, have started to shed. Francis Dougherty, the specialist who originally built the video lab, now has to clean his deck between tapes. “Every year this job gets more difficult,” he said. “Every year physical media degrades.” The last of the repairmen “The machines are getting rarer,” Mr. Dougherty added. “The old men who repair the machines are getting even rarer.” Asked how urgent the work is, he does not hesitate: “It should have been dealt with 20 years ago.” Universities train young specialists but there are fewer and fewer machines for them to work on. “Without people to maintain and repair and service them, we won’t be able to do this,” Mr. Dowlatshahi added. “And there’s only a few people that do it now.” Work in progress Some solutions are built by hand. The turntable that played the UN disc was made by Nick Bergh, a California engineer who builds playback machines as “sort of a hobby.” The library has one of the first in the world. It isn’t even finished. For now, its microscope lets engineers inspect record grooves for scratches; eventually, a second arm will read discs optically, without touching them. Bergh’s earlier machine uses lasers to align warped wax cylinders to within microns and to read broken ones without contact. The library used it to re-transfer the Mapleson Cylinders, recorded at the Metropolitan Opera in the early 1900s. They hold “unique performances by singers who were never otherwise recorded.” The paradox according to Mr. Willens is that as playback technology improves, the original recordings keep deteriorating. Every year of waiting means less heritage left to save.

state: Protecting Earth’s fragile biodiversity takes spotlight at Armenia talks Biodiversity losses continue to upend the lives of billions of people whose future prosperity depends on countries taking urgent action to protect our planet, the top UN official leading talks at the UN Biodiversity Conference in Yerevan, said on Monday. The aim of the talks in the Armenian capital is to assess progress so far and build on an agreed blueprint for biodiversity protection known as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted four years ago. “In 2022, 196 countries made commitments. But we are all accountable to each other and to future generations. What happens here in Yerevan matters. Billions of people whose lives are being upended by the impacts of biodiversity loss depend on progress being made here in the next two weeks,” said Executive Secretary of the UN Convention on Biodiversity, Astrid Schomaker. Tapping into indigenous ideas Insisting that “taking action for nature does work”, Ms. Schomaker called for the “untapped energy and ideas” of Indigenous Peoples and local communities, women and youth to contribute to the decisions made at the talks. “We need even greater engagement from cities, businesses and financial institutions…the science is clear. No nation, no economy, no society is immune from the impacts of biodiversity loss,” she said. The goals of the Convention include tackling the main drivers of biodiversity loss, including changes in how land and seas are used, the unsustainable exploitation of species, climate change, pollution and invasive species. Perhaps the Kunming-Montreal framework’s best-known ambition is “30 by 30”: conserving 30 per cent of land and sea by 2030, the deadline for achieving the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). To do this, national action plans must align with international goals, finance must match current needs and consumption and production should be in accord with “the finite resources of our planet”, Ms. Schomaker maintained. Why do these talks matter? A core aim of the Yerevan talks – also known as COP17, or the 17th Conference Of Parties – is “to turn commitments into measurable progress on the ground”, insisted Armenia’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Paruyr Hovhannisyan. “We want COP17 to send a clear political signal that addressing biodiversity loss requires coordinated action by governments, international organizations, the private sector and civil society,” he told UN News. “This means strengthening implementation, mobilizing adequate resources, and improving monitoring and accountability.” Among the big issues governments will grapple with in Yerevan: - Taking stock: Countries will conduct the very first global review of collective progress under the framework by presenting their national reports and updated national biodiversity strategies and action plans. This will show what has been achieved since 2022 and where faster action is needed. - Closing the implementation gap: The question is how to translate national targets and plans into measurable results on the ground. - Finding the money: The framework calls for at least $200 billion annually from all sources by 2030, including at least $30 billion in international biodiversity finance, according to Armenia’s UN Ambassador Mr. Hovhannisyan. - Making the Cali Fund work: This global financial mechanism established under the UN Convention on Biodiversity was agreed at COP16 in Cali, Colombia. Talks at Yerevan aim to advance practical arrangements for the fund, which was designed to collect funds from companies that use digital genetic data and redistribute these monies to protect biodiversity and Indigenous Peoples. - Tracking progress: Better monitoring, data, capacity and cooperation are needed so countries can measure whether commitments are actually delivering results. - Changing the economics: Some of the areas furthest behind require action outside environment ministries, including on finance, business, sustainable consumption and harmful incentives. The meeting follows warnings from UN chief António Guterres in Yerevan on Friday that more than one million species face extinction. War on nature In his call for an end to the “war on nature”, the UN Secretary-General appealed to governments, business and communities to accelerate efforts to protect biodiversity for future generations. “Every day, humankind saws another branch through the tree of life. Climate chaos, invasive species, overgrazing and overfishing, excessive fertilizers, pesticides, plastics and heavy metals, all these and more are driving the triple planetary crisis of pollution, biodiversity loss and climate chaos,” he said. The UN chief warned that the world is edging ever closer towards becoming uninhabitable. But he also pointed to international biodiversity action agreed under the Kunming-Montreal Framework. It had inspired action worldwide, Mr. Guterres insisted, noting that since 2022, an additional 1.3 million square kilometres of land and six million square kilometres of ocean have received formal protection. But “progress is uneven and far too slow” and countries risk falling “well short” of the goal of conserving 30 per cent of the world’s land and sea by 2030, the UN chief said.

state: Haiti: Elections on hold as gangs adapt to security crackdown, Security Council hears Armed groups in Haiti are adapting to intensified security operations, stepping up reprisals against civilians and extending their reach into rural areas, the UN warned the Security Council on Monday. The briefing came two weeks after presidential and legislative elections planned for 13 December were postponed indefinitely, with the UN’s top official in the country cautioning against setting new dates without a realistic assessment of whether a vote can be held. Key points - 1,123 Haitians were killed and 440 injured in gang-related violence between July and early October - Sexual violence remains widespread, with 689 women and girls reportedly raped by gang members in July and August - The Security Council-authorised Gang Suppression Force is not yet fully deployed Changing tactics In Haiti, security forces are intensifying their operations, but the gangs are not giving up. They are adapting their tactics, increasing reprisals against civilians and spreading violence to rural areas, according to the Secretary-General’s latest report. “What is particularly worrying is the gangs’ ability to adapt their tactics as security operations intensify,” said Carlos Ruiz Massieu, the UN’s top official in Haiti. Armed groups are increasingly resorting to hostage-taking, intimidation and reprisals against civilians to maintain their territory and challenge state authority. Deadly attacks The attack carried out on 23 and 24 August in Kenscoff, a mountainous town southeast of the capital, Port-au-Prince, illustrates this strategy. At least 47 people were killed, 22 wounded, and 52 taken hostage, 13 of whom were later freed thanks to local initiatives supported by the UN. In the West and Artibonite departments, 241 people were killed for allegedly resisting gangs. Other attacks – notably in Saint-Michel-de-l’Atalaye, Marigot, and Léogâne – indicate a spread of violence into rural areas. Armed groups are also targeting farmland, homes and public infrastructure. Security force operations also contribute to the rising death toll. They account for 52 per cent of Haitians killed or wounded since the beginning of July, or 808 people, including 148 not associated with gangs. GSF a work in progress Faced with this violence, the Security Council-backed Gang Suppression Force, logistically supported by the UN, is continuing its deployment. As of 12 October, it had 1,563 uniformed members, far fewer than the 5,550 authorised by the Security Council. It has notably established a base in the Artibonite region, beyond the capital. But, armed groups retain the capacity to retaliate. On Sunday, an armoured vehicle transporting Salvadoran soldiers from the force was attacked in Croix-des-Bouquets, in the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area. Four soldiers were still missing on Monday, according to media reports. Power vacuum For Mr. Ruiz Massieu, retaking territory will not be enough. “Experience has shown that security operations alone cannot bring about lasting stabilisation,” he warned, calling for the permanent restoration of the State’s presence and the development of disarmament and reintegration programmes, particularly for children recruited by gangs. This persistent insecurity also jeopardises the return to democracy, he said. Presidential and legislative elections, initially scheduled for 13 December, have been postponed indefinitely. Haiti has not held national elections since 2016. Nevertheless, preparations are ongoing. More than 35 political parties and groups, and 3,500 candidates have registered, according to Mr. Ruiz Massieu. As of 5 October, however, only 759,257 potential voters were on the lists, out of an estimated electorate of 6.5 million people. Insecurity and mass displacement are further complicating the organization of the election. “Setting new dates for elections without a realistic assessment of their feasibility will only erode public confidence and the credibility of Haitian institutions,” he warned. Humanitarian crisis Adding to this political uncertainty is a humanitarian crisis. Nearly 1.5 million people have fled their homes, including more than 740,000 children. The economy is expected to contract for the seventh consecutive year, while the UN’s 2026 humanitarian plan is only about half funded. The country thus remains faced with a dual emergency: restoring security essential for holding elections, without which a return to democratic institutions remains out of reach.

state: ‘Season of fear’: Escalating Israeli attacks on West Bank olive farmers, deadly strikes on Gaza Israeli attacks on war-torn Gaza over the weekend killed at least six Palestinians, including children, despite a year-old ceasefire agreement. Meanwhile, in the occupied West Bank, settler violence continued through the ongoing olive harvest, with UN independent experts on Monday urging Israel to protect Palestinian farmers. Key points - West Bank: Five Palestinians were killed and over 240 injured by Israeli forces or settlers over the past two weeks, with 200 olive harvest-related attacks documented since the start of September - Gaza: Israeli attacks have continued to cause deaths and injuries as nearly one million Palestinians face winter flood risks - Funding shortages have forced UN agencies to make major cuts to food programmes Death, demolitions along so-called ‘yellow line’ In the Gaza Strip, deadly Israeli airstrikes, gunfire and shelling occurred alongside incursions, demolitions and reported shifts in the so-called “yellow line” imposed by Israel since the year-old ceasefire agreement. The attacks raised concerns and risks of further displacement, according to the latest updates from the UN emergency aid coordination office, OCHA. Local health authorities told OCHA 57 Palestinians were reported killed and 319 injured between 29 September and 12 October, bringing the total number of casualties since the October 2025 ceasefire agreement to 1,493 fatalities and 5,299 injuries. Winter storms and growing hunger Meanwhile, around 950,000 displaced people have been assessed as living in sites at medium to high risk of flooding, including over 400,000 at high risk. Available supplies offered partial assistance to only 18 per cent of the 294,250 families requiring shelter support for the rainy season, OCHA reported. Daily cooked-meal production has declined by 12 per cent to approximately 614,000 amid funding constraints, while shortages of fuel, engine oil and essential supplies threaten the continuity of health and water services, the UN agency said. Settler violence must end: Independent experts Five Palestinians were killed and over 240 injured by Israeli forces or settler attacks in the occupied West Bank over the past two weeks, OCHA reported. During the same period, 160 olive harvest-related settler attacks resulted in casualties, property damage or both while record demolitions displaced 96 Palestinians, the agency said. UN independent human rights experts warned on Monday that Palestinian farmers are facing renewed threats as the annual olive harvest gets underway, urging Israel to guarantee their protection and safe access to their land. ‘Maximum pressure’ needed “The olive harvest should be a time when farmers can enjoy, in safety and dignity, the food and livelihoods their nature and land provide, not another season of fear, loss, violence and destruction,” said the Human Rights Council-appointed experts, who are not UN staff and do not receive a salary. “Israel is under an international legal obligation to end its occupation of Palestinian land, immediately cease new settlement activities, evacuate settlers from the Occupied Palestinian Territory and provide full reparation for the damage caused by its violations, including by returning land and allowing displaced Palestinians to return to their homes,” the experts said. “The international community, especially States with power and influence, must exercise maximum pressure to protect Palestinian civilians, halt and reverse the rapidly expanding policies and practices of annexation and ensure accountability for decades of violations of Palestinian rights under international law,” they said, warning that the situation could worsen following new Israeli orders for uprooting olive trees and restrictions on farmers in the West Bank.

state: Hunger is ‘an avoidable tragedy’ in a world of plenty: Türk More than a quarter of humanity struggles to get enough food, even though the world produces enough for everyone, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said on Monday, blaming injustice and the denial of human rights for hunger in a world of plenty. Addressing the UN-hosted Committee on World Food Security in Rome, the High Commissioner said that while the right to food has found its way into treaties and laws, “for too many people, it has yet to find its way onto their dinner plates”. Global food supply now exceeds 3,000 calories per person per day – a historic high – yet hunger reduction has not kept pace. “Too much of that abundance is swallowed up by injustice and the denial of human rights,” Mr. Türk said. Waste, inequality and war Every day, households alone throw away more than one billion meals, he said. Just one per cent of the world’s farms operate more than 70 per cent of global farmland, while women farmers and Indigenous Peoples often lack government support and access to land. Conflict is also driving acute hunger in 12 of the 13 current hunger hotspots, the High Commissioner said, with restrictions on humanitarian aid and attacks on aid workers “cutting off the last lifelines”. He called for a human rights economy built on social protection, fair taxation and agricultural policies that reduce poverty, as well as equitable access to land, water and seeds, and meaningful climate action. “We must do our utmost to ensure the rules of war are upheld and hunger is never used as a method of warfare,” he said. Famine ‘with impunity’ Addressing the Committee for the first time as the independent expert on the right food, UN Special Rapporteur Sofía Monsalve Suárez said the issue that concerned her most was the rapid increase in famine and the use of starvation as a weapon of war. While chronic hunger declined in 2025, acute hunger has been rising steadily since 2016, she said. Today, 1.4 million people in six countries face catastrophic conditions – nine times more than in 2016 – and 266 million people face acute hunger every day, in countries including Sudan, South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Yemen, as well as in Gaza. “The return of famine and the deliberate use of starvation as a weapon of war is an unprecedented moral challenge for our generation. These crimes continue with impunity,” she said. Ms. Suárez called for a stronger framework for accountability and prevention, and better coordination between the Security Council, the Committee, the human rights system and food security monitors to improve early warning.

state: UN condemns deadly wave of drone strikes in war-torn Sudan Drone strikes killed and injured dozens across Sudan on Monday as the ongoing war continues to cause soaring displacement and hunger. “We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting essential services,” UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric told journalists in New York. The rising use of armed drones during the war between rival militaries comes at a time when 20 million people face acute hunger, with a rising risk of famine in parts of Darfur and Greater Kordofan. Fighting erupted in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) – former allies who had jointly seized power in a 2021 coup. This latest escalation comes on the heels of a spate of deadly drone attacks last week. Bloody Monday On Monday alone, drone strikes injured at least 19 people in a busy market in Abyei and targeted several locations in the capital, Khartoum, including an area near the airport. One civilian was reportedly killed and some flights were cancelled following the attacks. Over the weekend, drone attacks reportedly killed at least 19, including 10 children, and injured others across West Darfur, South Darfur and North Kordofan States. “We condemn all of these attacks unequivocally,” Mr. Dujarric said. In response to the increasing use of armed drones in Sudan, Rosemary DiCarlo, Under-Secretary-General for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, urged external actors to stop fuelling the violence and drone usage. She called once gain on the warring parties to return to the negotiating table, during a briefing to the Security Council last Friday. Aid workers targeted Another grave concern has been the targeting of aid workers, the UN Spokesperson said. Since the conflict began, 25 Sudanese Red Crescent volunteers have reportedly been killed while on duty. He expressed deep sadness over the killing of a Sudanese Red Crescent volunteer last week who was providing first aid at a health centre in Um Darfa in Blue Nile State following a drone attack on the facilities. “The targeting of those who put their own lives at risk to help others in humanitarian settings is particularly heinous,” Mr. Dujarric said, reiterating that civilians and civilian infrastructure, including medical facilities and personnel, must be protected in accordance with international humanitarian law. Crucial aid delivered Despite these immense challenges, the UN and its humanitarian partners continue to deliver crucial assistance wherever they can, Mr. Dujarric said. In Central Darfur state, UN partners recently rehabilitated a water facility in Zalingei, restoring access to safe water for some 2,500 people. More than 2,000 families have received water, sanitation and hygiene support. “Once again, we need more funding to sustain all of these lifesaving operations,” he said, emphasising that Sudan’s humanitarian response plan is just over 43 per cent funded.

state: Yemen war continues to force families from homes amid hunger and disease More than 250,000 people have now fled renewed fighting in Yemen, the UN said on Tuesday, citing particular concern for those sheltering in the southwestern city of Taiz and the wider governorate, where access is “essentially blocked”. “The Houthis’ closure of the only supply route linking Taiz to Aden is placing civilians at grave risk, blocking humanitarian aid and cutting off essential supplies,” said UN human rights chief Volker Türk. In an appeal to Houthi fighters who he said had encircled Taiz City to allow aid in immediately, the High Commissioner for Human Rights noted that 32 civilians have been confirmed killed across the governorate, including 14 children and nine women. He warned of a significant uptick in the risk of death and injury as fighting moves closer to densely populated areas of the city. The development follows the resumption last month of clashes between Houthi fighters – formally known as Ansar Allah – and the internationally recognized Government based in Aden, ending the relative calm brought about by the 2022 truce. The situation in Taiz is particularly worrying because around half of those recently uprooted by the violence have sought shelter there. ‘An ocean of concerns’ “Taiz is certainly the number one concern at the moment in an ocean of concerns,” said Akhil Iyer, United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) Representative in Yemen. “Many people have fled repeatedly. They are arriving in already overcrowded camps or communities with little or no food. Clean water is almost non-existent when they arrive. They’ve literally arrived with just the clothes on their backs, and they have almost nothing left to sustain themselves.” According to the UN World Food Programme (WFP), wheat flour stocks in affected areas of Taiz are nearly exhausted. “This is an alarming development in a governorate that already faces some of Yemen’s highest levels of food insecurity,” with 10 out of 16 districts already classified at emergency levels, Mr. Iyer stressed. Briefing journalists from Aden, the UNICEF official described the deteriorating situation in conflict-affected areas, where “garbage is piling up – particularly in Taiz city – as sanitation services come to a halt”. The ongoing hostilities have made it extremely difficult and dangerous for humanitarian agencies to reach vulnerable communities and deliver fuel and other necessities. Health emergency The result could be an even more acute health emergency in a country already facing outbreaks of cholera and measles, along with suspected cases of diphtheria and dengue. “We are very worried about the water and sanitation situation in Taiz because diesel fuel is essential to run pumping stations in and around the city. Supplies have been threatened by the lack of access and the blockage of supply routes, particularly from Aden to Taiz city,” Mr. Iyer explained. He noted that although UNICEF had pre-positioned enough ready-to-use therapeutic food before the conflict escalated early last month, the supplies could not be distributed to health facilities because “all of the routes are closed”. “We’re calling on all parties to protect children and civilians, safeguard water systems and health facilities, and uphold their obligations under international humanitarian law. That includes allowing humanitarian actors access.” Oxygen running out World Health Organization (WHO) spokesperson Tarik Jasarevic reported that 12 hospitals in Taiz had approximately four days of fuel remaining. The oxygen cylinders they require are in “daily deficit”, while 115 of 127 essential medicines have sufficient stocks for about one week or less, he said. Matthew Saltmarsh, spokesperson for the UN refugee agency (UNHCR), stressed that access problems were preventing aid teams from reaching those most in need, although protection activities continued “where access allows”. “Let’s not forget that there are some 65,000 refugees and asylum-seekers who are also urgently in need of support; most are from Somalia and Ethiopia,” he added.

state: Guterres honours Indonesian troops who paid ‘ultimate sacrifice’ UN Secretary-General António Guterres paid tribute to Indonesian peacekeepers on Monday, laying a wreath in honour of four who recently lost their lives in Lebanon and offering a robust defence of UN peacekeeping in what he called “testing times for peace”. Speaking to troops at the Indonesia Armed Forces Peacekeeping Centre in Sentul – some of whom are deploying to the Central African Republic (CAR) – Mr. Guterres said the fallen had paid the “ultimate sacrifice” to protect others in very difficult circumstances. “Their service and their sacrifice will never be forgotten. No one should die serving the cause of peace,” he said, extending his deepest condolences to their families. “Attacks on peacekeepers are grave violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes. These violations demand accountability,” the UN chief stressed, pledging to keep calling on Member States to ensure the safety and security of UN personnel at all times. ‘A source of hope’ Mr. Guterres described UN ‘blue helmets’ as “a source of hope in some of the world’s most troubled places” and, for him, “a source of enormous pride”. Far from home and in some of the world’s most dangerous settings, the UN’s 50,000 peacekeepers de-escalate tensions between hostile parties, oversee vital aid delivery, protect civilians and create space for political solutions to take hold, he said. Indonesia is the world’s sixth-largest contributor to UN peacekeeping, with nearly 2,000 uniformed women and men serving across seven missions. Next year, it will co-host the UN Peacekeeping Ministerial with the Netherlands. ‘Success story’ to be concluded Addressing those troops preparing to deploy to the CAR, Mr. Guterres – who has worked with the country for 20 years, first as UN High Commissioner for Refugees – called it “a success story that still needs to be completed”. Most armed groups have “celebrated…agreements with the Government and are giving up their arms”, he said, and the troops’ mission will be decisive in helping State institutions function across the whole territory. With their success, the UN could then progressively downsize its mission in the country, he added. Mr. Guterres had opened his remarks on a lighter note, telling the troops he was convinced that “no bad guys in [the Central African Republic] will dare confront the Indonesians”. ‘Better multilateralism’ In Jakarta, speaking at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Guterres hailed Indonesia as “a pillar of multilateralism” and a diplomatic bridge-builder between North and South. With conflicts multiplying, inequality deepening and trust in institutions declining, he said many people question whether international cooperation can still deliver. “The answer to deepening frustration with multilateralism is not less multilateralism. It is better multilateralism,” he said, calling for reform of international financial institutions and the Security Council to reflect today’s world. ‘The nightmare must end’ Speaking to reporters alongside Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir, Mr. Guterres said that in Gaza, “the nightmare must end.” “The peace plan must be fully implemented – and we cannot allow the two-State solution to disappear before our eyes,” he said, paying tribute to Indonesia for always being at the forefront of support for the Palestinian people. He also voiced concern over Myanmar’s deepening crisis, renewing his appeal for protection of those fleeing violence and persecution, including Rohingya refugees across the region.

Director General of the ANMCC Boulevard de Tokyo, Ankadievo Alasora, Antananarivo 103 - Madagascar Email: [email protected] Website: www.anmcc.org� 5. Provide the deadlines and procedures for importers, exporters and other interested parties to present evidence and their views, including: (i) deadlines and procedures for Members and exporters to identify themselves as interested parties, if so required, to participate in the investigation and (ii) the date of an intended public hearing as provided for in Article 3.1. [..] Interested parties have 30 days from the initiation of the investigation to make themselves known to the ANMCC, submit their comments, and request a questionnaire. Responses to the questionnaire and other relevant information must be submitted within 30 working days. Public hearings may be held at the request of the parties or on the ANMCC's own initiative. If responses are not submitted within the prescribed deadlines, or if the information provided is inaccurate or incomplete, determinations may be made on the basis of the best information available." The notification is available in G/SG/N/6/MDG/21. (Currently available in French only) What is a safeguard investigation? A safeguard investigation seeks to determine whether increased imports of a product are causing, or are threatening to cause, serious injury to a domestic industry. During a safeguard investigation, importers, exporters and other interested parties may present evidence and views and respond to the presentations of other parties. A WTO member may take a safeguard action (i.e. restrict imports of a product temporarily) only if the increased imports of the product are found to be causing, or threatening to cause, serious injury.
